In this study, we investigate regional variability in RI frequency and magnitude across the Gulf, Caribbean, and Atlantic, as well as relationships between RI, landfall timing, and intensity forecast error. A total of 725 North Atlantic TCs from 1980-2025 are analyzed using IBTrACS best-track data and classified throughout their lifetimes using predefined Gulf and Caribbean polygons. A total of 725 North Atlantic TCs from 1980–2025 are analyzed using IBTrACS best-track data and classified throughout their lifetimes using predefined Gulf and Caribbean polygons. The locations of key lifecycle stages, including genesis, RI, extreme RI (ERI), and landfall, are recorded by region. RI is defined using the standard threshold of a ≥30-kt increase in maximum sustained 1-min winds over 24 h, while ERI is defined as an increase of ≥50 kt over 24 h. Statistical analyses are conducted to compare RI frequency, magnitude, and timing relative to landfall across the Gulf, Caribbean, and Atlantic. NHC 24-h intensity forecast errors are also evaluated to quantify regional differences in forecast performance during RI and landfall. Our results indicate that RI occurs most frequently in the Caribbean and reaches greater magnitudes in the Gulf. Among storms that entered each basin during their lifetimes, 21.7% of Gulf storms, 33.2% of Caribbean storms, and 26.4% of Atlantic storms experienced RI within the respective basin. ERI occurred in 5.5%, 8.5%, and 3.5% of storms in the Gulf, Caribbean, and Atlantic, respectively. The upper-quartile RI rate was greater in the Gulf (34 kt 24 h⁻¹) than in the Caribbean and Atlantic (30 kt 24 h⁻¹). Landfall analyses further reveal substantial regional differences in the proximity of RI to landfall. Among storms with RI onset in the Gulf, 97.6% subsequently made landfall within the Gulf region. RI also occurred closer to landfall in the Gulf and Caribbean. Among storms with RI onset in each region, 9.5% of storms in the Gulf and 19.1% of storms in the Caribbean, experiencing RI onset within 24 h of landfall, compared with 2.2% in the Atlantic. These results indicate a shorter window between RI onset and potential coastal impacts for Gulf and Caribbean TCs, reducing the time available for preparation and emergency response. NHC 24-h intensity forecast errors show greater negative errors, indicating intensity underforecasting, and broader error distributions during RI than during non-RI periods across all three regions. The underforecasting signature is most pronounced in the Caribbean. Many of the largest 24-h intensity forecast errors, approximately 55–75 kt, are associated with major hurricanes that underwent RI in the Gulf and/or Caribbean. Ongoing analyses further examine intensity forecast errors at landfall and environmental conditions associated with regional differences in RI. Preliminary ERA5 analyses suggest that warm SSTs in the Gulf and northwestern Caribbean may contribute to the observed regional patterns. These findings highlight the operational importance of understanding regional differences in RI, particularly where intensification occurs close to landfall and limits preparation time for coastal communities.

498418.title: Validation of NOAA's Automatic Preparation, Evaluation, and Calibration (AUTO-SPEC) Testing Unit on Electrochemical Concentration Cell (ECC) Ozonesonde Preformance
498418.authors: Mia Robinson, Jackson State University, terry, MS
498418.abstract: Accurate and precise ozonesonde data are increasingly vital for validating long-term satellite observations [GAW, 2021; JOSIE, 2007]. While current standard operating procedures (SOPs) used with manual testing units can achieve measurement uncertainties as low as 5% [GAW, 2021], small variations in preparation and correction procedures can significantly impact an Electrochemical Concentration Cell (ECC) ozonesonde’s performance [JOSIE, 2007]. Minimizing human error and subjective assumptions is therefore critical to improving the accuracy, precision, and reliability of these measurements. To address this, NOAA designed the Automatic Sonde Preparation, Evaluation, and Calibration (AUTO-SPEC) testing unit to improve the uniformity and repeatability of ECC ozonesonde data preparation. This three-phase study evaluates whether the AUTO-SPEC testing unit optimizes preparation by comparing its automated procedure to the manual procedure of the historically utilized EN-SCI Ozonesonde testing unit. By tracking four new EN-SCI model 2Z ECC ozonesondes during each phase, key metrics (cell current, ozone partial pressure, and bubble flow rate) and confidence levels regarding pump variability will be compared between the manual and automatic units. Additionally, this study will elucidate ozonesonde instrument specification drift during a maximum flight duration window of 2.5 hours, analyzing its correlation to pump motor temperature and ambient laboratory conditions. Through conservative alterations to the pre-existing standard operational procedures (SOPs) and improvements to the AUTO-SPEC testing unit, we can enhance ECC ozonesonde reliability across global sounding laboratories by significantly reducing calibration errors.

498423.title: Case Study of the 27 May 2024 QLCS-Supercell Merger
498423.authors: Joshua Stephen Honick, Ohio University, Athens, OH; and D. V. Blount
498423.abstract: In 2025, severe weather events, including damaging winds, resulted in billions of dollars of damage in the United States. Some of these events were caused by supercells and QLCSs highlighting the importance of understanding these convective modes, particularly when they interact. Previous idealized studies focused on supercells that merge into a QLCS. These studies have shown that damaging winds and tornado probabilities can increase after a QLCS-supercell merger. An observation study noted that these cases occur in two types of environments. A strong forcing environment (SF) classified by an intense surface cyclone and strong 500 mb trough, and a weak forcing environment (WF) classified by a weak surface cyclone and weak 500 mb trough. On 27 May 2024, a supercell in eastern Kentucky produced an EF-3 tornado that was on the ground for over 1 hour. At the same time, a QLCS producing 60-70 mph straight line winds approached then merged with the supercell at 0225 UTC. After the QLCS-supercell merger, an increase in straight line wind speed could be observed with one damage report recording 100 mph winds. This study will examine the synoptic and mesoscale environments preceding, during, and after the 27 May 2024 QLCS-supercell merger event. This will be accomplished by leveraging HRRR analyses and observational datasets (e.g., NEXRAD data, sounding, etc.) to examine upper-level patterns and convective parameters present near the merger event. Building on previous research, we will examine if this case exhibits similarities or differences to the idealized conceptual models of a merger event and environments in which these mergers occur. This will help determine whether the environmental factors led to the development of strong damaging winds or if storm-scale dynamics had a large factor in their development.

498424.title: From Ice-Nucleating Particles to Climate Intervention: How Cloud and Precipitation Phases Control Mixed-Phase Cloud Radiative Effects (Invited Presentation)
498424.authors: Diego Villanueva, ETH, Zürich, Zürich, Switzerland
498424.abstract: Ice-nucleating particles (INPs) provide a pathway for modifying mixed-phase clouds, bridging processes traditionally studied in weather modification with emerging concepts for climate intervention. Yet predicting the climatic response to such perturbations requires understanding how changes in ice nucleation propagate through cloud phase, precipitation formation, cloud lifetime, and radiation. We combine satellite observations with climate-model experiments to trace this causal chain across scales. Using 35 years of satellite observations, we find that mineral dust strongly controls cloud-top glaciation in the northern extratropics at temperatures between approximately −30 and −15 °C. The observed sensitivities of cloud-top phase to temperature and dust are consistent with laboratory measurements of immersion droplet freezing, providing observational evidence that natural variations in INPs measurably perturb cloud phase. Climate simulations show, however, that changes in cloud phase alone do not determine the radiative response. Instead, the key intermediary is precipitation phase. Snow-forming mixed-phase clouds remove condensate more efficiently than rain-forming clouds through ice growth, riming, and Wegener–Bergeron–Findeisen processes. Anthropogenic perturbations to cloud microphysics, whether through INP seeding or climate warming, shift the balance between snow formation and less efficient warm-rain formation, altering cloud liquid water and solar albedo. Across perturbed-parameter ensemble (PPE) experiments, we find that the liquid-water response to warming or INP perturbations is much more tightly coupled to the cloud radiative effect than is the ice-to-liquid partition itself. The same relationship holds across CMIP6 models under climate warming, where differences in liquid-water responses associated with precipitation phase explain a substantial fraction of intermodel differences in cloud feedback. This relationship suggests that the intermodel spread in responses to INP perturbations may be at least as large as the spread in cloud feedback. These results provide a mechanistic framework for interpreting mixed-phase cloud thinning (MCT), in which additional INPs are introduced over polar oceans to enhance glaciation, reduce cloud water, and increase outgoing longwave radiation. Previous simulations indicate that such perturbations can cool the polar surface and increase sea-ice area. Together, these findings suggest that assessing glaciogenic cloud modification requires constraining not only the response of cloud ice to INPs but also the complete chain from INPs → ice formation → precipitation phase → cloud water → radiation. Our results further suggest that the responses of mixed-phase clouds to warming are closely linked to their sensitivity to INPs, thereby connecting key questions in the cloud-based climate-intervention and cloud-feedback research communities.

498425.title: Evolution of Black Carbon Mixing State in the Summertime NY Urban Plume
498425.authors: Adam Jozef De Groodt, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and L. Garofalo, D. Farmer, and J. Mak
498425.abstract: Black Carbon (BC), a refractory product of incomplete combustion reactions, impacts the climate through direct and indirect radiative forcing and human health through respiratory uptake. In the atmosphere BC mixes with other species which has been shown to enhance its radiative impact. Thus, understanding the evolution of BC mixing state is essential to evaluating the atmospheric impact of the pollutant. With more than 23 million people, the New York Metropolitan Area (NYMA) is an urban landscape with complex chemical emissions. Despite the decreasing trend of BC concentration over the last two decades, the evolution of BC mixing state in the urban plume remains poorly understood. To investigate BC mixing state in the urban plume and the chemical composition of particles we deployed a single-particle soot photometer (SP2) and high-resolution aerosol mass spectrometer (HR-AMS) aboard the NSF/NCAR C-130 aircraft during the Greater New York Oxidant, Trace gas, Halogen, and Aerosol Airborne Mission (GOTHAAM; July-August 2025). Preliminary results suggest that BC becomes more coated as the NY plume ages, with the fraction of thinly coated particles (fthin; < 30% coating by volume) decreasing and thickly coated particles (fthick; > 30%) increasing as we intercepted the plume at multiple locations downwind of NYC through a pseudo-Lagrangian sampling approach. During periods influenced by aged wildfire smoke, fthick increased by a factor of 3 relative to urban air. Thus, while coating thickness grows in the urban plume, transported Canadian wildfire smoke brings the most thickly coated particles, likely having differing impacts on both air quality and human health. Further, both urban and other BC sources can age over the ocean, providing the opportunity to explore fate and evolution of BCCPs. Our observations indicate BCCPs become thickly coated in the urban plume, which will impact the radiative role as well as the lifetime of the particle.

498426.title: Atmospheric Conditions Affecting Snowfall Intensity During Lake-Effect and Synoptic-Scale Snowfall Events in the Great Lakes Region
498426.authors: Lauren Rachel Burge, The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and X. Chen
498426.abstract: Snowstorms are a major hazard in the Great Lakes region during winter, and severe events have caused extensive economic and infrastructure losses. Better understanding of their physical processes is critical to advancing our knowledge and projection of these hazards. Winter storms usually fall into two categories: those triggered by lake-effect, and those produced by synoptic-scale weather systems. Therefore, it is necessary to identify and characterize the dependence of snowfall intensity during these storms by their unique atmospheric conditions, including thermodynamic structure, moisture availability, and wind and convection fields. In this research study, we present an analysis of eight high-impact snowstorms in the Great Lakes region from the NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information database during the 2000-2024 period: four synoptic-scale storms and four lake-effect storms. Using the CONUS404 downscaled reanalysis set, we analyzed how their meteorological conditions evolved in the 48-hour window surrounding the peak intensity value: temperature, humidity, wind speed and direction, and instability as approximated by convective available potential energy (CAPE). Using a Python time-series analysis, we summarized the common meteorological ingredients contributing to peak snowfall intensity across both categories. These in-depth analyses will contribute to deeper understanding, and improved modeling and projection of these hazardous snowstorms in the Great Lakes region.

498427.title: When Seasons Don’t Speak Clearly: Climate Change Impacts in Haa Dzongkhag, Bhutan
498427.authors: Valentina Mendoza Cruz, Denison University, Columbus, OH
498427.abstract: This study aims to investigate climate change indicators and community perceptions in Haa Dzongkhag, Bhutan, with a focus on how environmental changes are impacting local livelihoods and shaping adaptation strategies. A mixed-method approach was used to ensure a deeper understanding that includes both qualitative and quantitative data. That data was collected through a survey of close-ended questions and semi-structured interviews with open-ended questions. Further, data the weather station was incorporated to understand specific trends in the study area. Investigating three northern gewogs of Haa (Bji, Katsho, and Eusu), our research captures major trends around culture, climate, and landscape. Findings indicate that community members perceive a variety of interconnected environmental changes, including changes in climate, pests, diseases, and wildlife. Many of the farmers interviewed are entering a commercial market which encourages them to continue an agricultural livelihood, moving beyond subsistence farming. Climate change awareness in these villages is influenced by differences in education, age, and access to sources of information. The weather trends show a decrease in minimum temperature, and an increase in maximum temperature over the last 30 years. Overall, the research highlights the interconnected nature of environmental changes, adaptation strategies, and awareness in rural communities.

498429.title: Urban VOC Observations from Volatile Chemical Products During the FROG-NY 2023 Field Campaign
498429.authors: Rose Rossell, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and E. B. Franklin, A. Bélanger, L. Tonnesen, C. Osburn, and D. Farmer
498429.abstract: Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are a class of highly reactive chemicals that can form atmospheric pollutants, including ozone, through a series of complex atmospheric reactions. A subset of VOCs associated with cleaning goods, personal care products, and manufacturing emissions are classified as volatile chemical products (VCPs). VCPs play an increasingly important role in urban atmospheres as traffic emissions decrease. However, there are high uncertainties surrounding VCP identities, quantities, and their temporal and spatial variability – complicating any future regulations. The Fluxes of Reactive Organic Gases in New York (FROG-NY) field campaign took place in Mineola, NY during summer 2023. We quantified VOCs using offline cartridge samples for isomer-resolved analysis at the field site and nearby locations, including a train station, botanical garden, and landfill. We used positive matrix factorization to separate regional and local influences and examined corresponding impacts to urban atmospheric chemistry through reactivity against the hydroxyl radical and ability to form ozone. Within our suite of observed VOCs, functional groups such as siloxanes, acetates, and ethers were especially prominent and are potentially representative of artificial fragrance additives. At the ground site, our measured compounds contributed a median of 6.6 ppb ozone, with acetates highly contributing to both hydroxyl reactivity and ozone. Local anthropogenic emissions highly influenced urban VOC loadings but were spatially dynamic. VOC concentrations at the gas station totaled over 200 ppb, while the train station and botanical garden represented local point sources of VCPs from personal care products.

498430.title: Multifaceted investigation of Saharan dust and sea spray aerosol interactions to resolve heterogenous production mechanisms of chlorine radicals
498430.authors: Emma Joyce Pellerin, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and K. Richard, M. Selby, T. Berg, A. J. De Groodt, L. Garofalo, V. Shah, and D. Farmer
498430.abstract: The African Easterly Jet can transport hundreds of teragrams of Saharan dust over the Atlantic every year. Investigating this transport can improve our understanding of potential heterogeneous chemistry that occurs when iron-rich dust aerosols interact with sea-spray and sea-salt aerosols leading to formation of chlorine radicals. Radical chlorine is extremely reactive with large regional influence on the lifetime of greenhouse gases and formation of secondary organic aerosols. Here, we show measurements of molecular chlorine (Cl2), a precursor of radical chlorine, and various other gas and particle components from a ground site in Puerto Rico. The data demonstrates that mid-morning production outcompetes Cl2 photolysis as a chlorine radical source. The interaction and mixing of dust and sea-spray or sea-salt aerosols in the troposphere is explored through comparing Atmospheric Tomography mission (ATom) vertical profiles of aerosol mass concentrations with Modern-Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2 (MERRA-2) model reanalysis mass concentration vertical profiles. This comparison revealed interaction at the 1 - 2 km, and 5 - 7 km range indicating that the marine boundary layer (MBL) is not the only area where these aerosols interact. ATom single particle composition profiles were compared to Cloud-Aerosol Lidar with Orthogonal Polarization (CALIOP) depolarization ratios as well indicating potential for internal mixing of these aerosols outside the MBL. Through probing vertical transport of the Sahara dust layer over Puerto Rico via these comprehensive datasets, a clearer understanding is resolved of where these aerosols species are likely to interact in our troposphere, and where that interaction may lead to heterogeneous formation of chlorine precursors.

498436.title: Do Street Block Features Affect PM2.5 Concentrations on Smoke and Non-Smoke Days in Downtown Salt Lake City, Utah?
498436.authors: Leslie Rubi Navarro, Texas A&M University, New Caney, TX
498436.abstract: As the Southwestern U.S. becomes warmer and drier due to climate change, wildfire smoke emissions are on the rise. Increasingly, wildfire smoke is degrading air quality in urban areas. The combination of more smoke events and high pedestrian foot traffic in downtown urban areas exposes residents to increased levels of fine particulate matter (≤2.5 µm diameter, PM2.5), threatening public health and welfare. This study analyzed how street block features affect PM2.5 concentrations at the street level, on smoke and non-smoke days in downtown Salt Lake City, Utah. In June 2026, and as part of a personal exposure monitoring campaign, measurements of PM2.5 and black carbon (BC) were collected in West Downtown and East Downtown using the low-cost wearable Airbeam3 sensor and the portable MicroAeth MA200. To capture the street level environment, urban features, such as trees, buildings, and businesses were quantified for each block. Smoke model data, BC data, and PM2.5 data were then used to determine smoke vs. non-smoke days. Smoke days were defined as days when the model indicated smoke over the study area and when there were elevated levels of both PM2.5 and biomass (as opposed to fossil fuel) BC. Street block differences in PM2.5 concentrations and relationships between PM2.5 and street block features were examined for smoke and non-smoke days. We found that PM2.5 was approximately 10 times higher on smoke than on non-smoke days for both West and East Downtown routes. PM2.5 concentrations showed greater block-to-block variability on non-smoke days compared to smoke days. This indicates that on smoke days, PM2.5 from wildfire smoke had a greater impact on spatial patterns of PM2.5 concentrations than local sources. In addition, some street block features were related to PM2.5 concentrations. On non-smoke days, the total count of businesses was positively related to PM2.5 likely because businesses attract people and increase activities such as cooking and transportation that emit PM2.5. The number of buildings was also positively related to PM2.5 for both non-smoke and smoke days which may be due to buildings preventing PM2.5 from mixing and dispersing (creating an urban canyon effect). Urban planners should therefore consider how street block features can either improve or worsen the exposure of residents to poor air quality, especially during smoke events. Further research could examine additional street block features and meteorological variables not measured here as they may be playing a greater role in PM2.5 concentration patterns.

498438.title: Comparing Federally Declared Disasters Against Reported Storm Events to Assess the 1996-2025 Weather Hazard Climatology Across Kentucky
498438.authors: Ian Michael Pfeiffer, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY
498438.abstract: Kentucky is a state that experiences a perpetual state of disaster response and recovery, with some counties leading the country in declared disasters. Previous research has examined historical occurrences of federally declared disasters for Kentucky, which may serve as a first proxy for understanding weather disasters in the Commonwealth. However, non-weather-related factors may introduce bias in this understanding. The purpose of the current study is to employ the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, National Centers for Environmental Information Storm Events Database from 1996-2025 to compare against federally declared disasters to determine a more comprehensive inspection of Kentucky’s weather hazard and disaster record over the past thirty years. Initial findings show declared disasters only account for 21% of recorded storm events (79% non-declared). However, by category, declared disasters account for 62%, 67%, and 76% of injuries, fatalities, and total damage costs, respectively, the latter totaling ~$3.54 billion. Overall, declared disasters only offer a limiting perspective of total weather hazard frequency of occurrence, while accounting for two-thirds of casualties and three quarters of the costs. Since both declared disasters and reported storm events appear less representative across rural and less populated areas, population bias correction may highlight potential for missing or lesser-impactful events.

498441.title: Engaging the Weather Enterprise in Public Health Communication: A Survey of Weather Professionals at the 2026 American Meteorological Society Annual Meeting
498441.authors: Sarah Gillani, Center for Outbreak Response Innovation, washington, DC
498441.abstract: Weather and health are intrinsically linked, yet the potential for weather professionals to serve as health communicators remains underexplored. This study examined the attitudes, practices, and training needs of individuals working in weather-related fields regarding the delivery of health information, as well as interest in health forecasting among the broader weather-engaged community. A digital survey was administered by the Center for Outbreak Response Innovation (CORI) at Johns Hopkins at the 2026 American Meteorological Society Annual Meeting in Houston, Texas, with 271 respondents including working meteorologists who provide information to the public (n=49) and other AMS attendees representing the broader weather-interested community (n=222). Among weather professionals who communicate with the public, 55.1% (n=27) had previously delivered weather-related health information such as air quality indices and heat advisories, and 95.9% (n=47) believed meteorologists should have a role in broader health communication. However, only 65.3% (n=32) felt comfortable delivering health updates, with those who expressed discomfort (n=17) citing needs for training, credible resources, and localized data. Among other AMS attendees, 59.5% (n=132) actively sought health information for daily planning, 76.1% (n=169) had seen meteorologists deliver health content, and 95.9% (n=162) of those found it helpful. Interest in a recurring health forecast was high at 87.4% (n=194), with most preferring weekly or daily updates. These findings demonstrate that weather professionals and the broader AMS community share strong interest in integrating health information into weather communication. The results reveal a clear need for training and resources to support weather professionals in this expanded role.

498442.title: A Calibration Assessment of PotThunder from the National Blend of Models in the National Weather Service Caribou, Maine, County Warning Area
498442.abstract: Luca Guyer (2), Todd Foisy (1), and Perry Samson, PhD (2) (1) National Weather Service, Caribou, Maine (2) Department of Climate and Space Sciences and Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor Introduction Thunderstorm forecasts are an important part of operational weather prediction because they support public safety, emergency preparedness, and aviation operations. The National Blend of Models (NBM) provides Probabilistic Thunderstorm Guidance (PotThunder), which National Weather Service forecasters regularly use as a starting point for their official thunderstorm probability forecasts. However, its local performance has not been closely evaluated for the NWS Caribou County Warning Area (CWA) in northern and eastern Maine. Local validation is especially important in this region for two reasons. First, Caribou is located near the edge of the National Lightning Detection Network (NLDN), where fewer lightning strikes may be detected. Second, the CWA includes interior, coastal, and over-water areas with potentially different thunderstorm environments. This study evaluates the calibration of NBM PotThunder across the Caribou forecast area. Methodology Lightning activity in the CWA was compiled from an operational forecast database for May through August 2024, and again for May through July 2025. The corresponding 3-hour (T03), 6-hour (T06), and 12-hour (T12) NBM guidance valid at each observation time was also recorded, producing a verification dataset of nearly 9,000 forecast points. Forecast probabilities were compared with observed thunderstorm occurrence using reliability diagrams. The analysis was conducted for the full CWA and separately for northern interior, central, coastal, and over-water sites. Results Across all sites, the average forecast probability increased with the length of the forecast period: 21.2% at T03, 29.7% at T06, and 40.7% at T12, as expected. The reliability diagrams showed a consistent pattern among the forecast periods. The 3-hour guidance underpredicted thunderstorm occurrence, meaning that thunderstorms occurred more often than forecasted. The 12-hour guidance overpredicted thunderstorm occurrence, while the 6-hour guidance was the best calibrated. This pattern was clearest at the northern interior sites. Calibration was weaker and less consistent near the coast and over the water, where the reliability curves showed greater departures from the ideal diagonal. The 12-hour guidance over water also exhibited greater variability. Conclusion NBM PotThunder is not uniformly calibrated across the Caribou CWA. At northern interior sites, the guidance tends to underpredict thunderstorm occurrence at shorter forecast periods and overpredict it at longer forecast periods. The 6-hour guidance showed the best overall calibration. Calibration was poorest near the coast and over the water. Two factors may contribute to this reduced performance, and the available data cannot fully distinguish between them. The detection network may record fewer lightning strikes near its coverage edge, while marine conditions may also make thunderstorms less likely than the model predicts. These results identify local biases that may help forecasters interpret PotThunder in the Caribou CWA. A larger, multiseason dataset, combined with a comparison of NLDN and Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) total-lightning data, would help confirm these patterns. Such an analysis could also determine whether the coastal issue is primarily caused by missed lightning detections or by the model overpredicting thunderstorm occurrence in that area.

498443.title: MPAS‑Viewer: Python‑Based Exploration of MPAS UnstructuredMesh data with UGRID export for QGIS visualization
498443.authors: Jorge Bravo, Stevens Institute of Technology, Hoboken, NJ
498443.abstract: As the Model for Prediction Across Scales- Atmosphere (MPAS-A) gains prominence as a successor to the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF)model, one of the primary challenges associated with this transition is data visualization, largely due to MPAS-A'sunstructured mesh. Although several tools, both software-based andprogramming-based, are capable of visualizing unstructured data, many rely on iterative, polygon-by-polygon mesh generation, which significantly slows the visualization process. Given that Python is the most widely used programming language for scientific data processing and visualization, this work presents the continued development of MPAS-viewer(https://github.com/jhbravo/mpasviewer), a Python package designed for efficient visualization of the Spherical Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation mesh used byMPAS-A. While MPAS-viewer has demonstrated better visualization speed compared to similar tools, this presentation highlights a newly added data-writing capability. Specifically, it demonstrates how data read by MPAS-viewer can be saved using UGRID standards, allowing seamless visualization within Geographic Information Systems (GIS) such as QGIS through a simple drag-and-drop workflow. The use of robust QGIS software further enhances MPAS data visualization by enabling the integration of additional geographic information, including vector and raster layers, without compromising the representation of MPAS data on its native unstructured mesh; moreover, it supports dynamic visualization across both spatial and temporal dimensions, as well as the simultaneous display of multiple datasets.

498444.title: Assessing the Sensitivity of the June 29-30, 2012 Derecho-Producing MCS to the Appalachian Mountains
498444.authors: Max Murtough, Ohio University, Athens, OH; and D. V. Blount
498444.abstract: Mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) are distinguished from other severe convective storm modes by their production of widespread rain and wind impacts over timescales of 6-12 hours or more. While the atmospheric processes that influence MCS genesis, maintenance, and decay are well studied and observed, the influence of the physical topography of Earth’s surface on MCS behavior has proven to be an area where more work is needed. Past research has shown that idealized ridge-and-valley mountain ranges of similar (or greater) height to the Appalachian Mountains are sufficiently large to disrupt continuous MCS forward propagation by blocking the advancement of the gust front and delaying new updraft production. In anomalously strong MCS cases, however, the Appalachians have often proven to be insufficient in disrupting crossing. One example of this comes from June 29-30, 2012, when an intense MCS moved through the Ohio Valley and Mid-Atlantic regions, crossing the Appalachians while producing significant severe wind gusts (65 kt+) across the entire width of the mountains. This study simulates this case by using the WRF-ARW model to examine the sensitivity to the terrain. This will be tested by scaling the terrain, greater than 500 meters, to 40% above and below its real-world height. Parameters such as updraft velocity, rear inflow and cold pool strength, and 10-meter wind speed will be analyzed for each case before, during, and after interaction with the terrain. The goal of this study is to determine if an anomalously strong MCS like the June 2012 case simply require a greater terrain height to effectively disrupt new updraft formation at the gust front, or if some other characteristic of extreme cases (such as strong rear inflow) allows for continuous forward propagation despite gust front blocking.

498446.title: Investigating Graupel Riming Through Numerical Simulation
498446.authors: Sage Branham, CU Boulder, Boulder, CO; and B. Baker
498446.abstract: Riming, the freezing of super-cooled water droplets onto ice particles, is a fundamental process in mixed phase clouds. Actively riming graupel seems to play a central role in thunderstorm electrification. During the riming of graupel, latent heat released by freezing maintains a riming droplet near 0°C, while it is freezing. When the graupel is substantially colder, this results in strong localized gradients in temperature and water vapor density that enhance vapor deposition onto the nearby graupel surface. It has been hypothesized from laboratory models of mixed phase cloud electrification that these regions of enhanced growth of the graupel are key to understanding charge transfer during ice-ice interactions, in the lab and in clouds. Existing analytical descriptions of this process are limited to simplified geometries and idealized assumptions. We develop a numerical model that explicitly represents a graupel particle, a freezing super-cooled droplet, and the surrounding air as coupled domains. The model simultaneously handles heat conduction, phase change, and vapor diffusion, allowing the evolution of temperature and vapor density fields to be simulated for realistic geometries throughout the period during which the droplet is freezing. The numerical model is intended as an open and extensible research tool for studying localized vapor deposition during graupel riming and its potential implications for thunderstorm electrification

498447.title: Characterizing Atmospheric Boundary Layer Height Across an Urban-Rural-Coastal Gradient in the Washington DC - Baltimore Region
498447.authors: Akye C Johnson, NOAA, Capitol Heights, MD; NOAA, Capitol Heights, MD
498447.abstract: The atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) mediates surface-atmosphere exchange, yet its spatial variability across adjacent urban, rural, and coastal surfaces remains poorly constrained. We characterize ABL height (ABLH) across a four-site gradient in the Washington-Baltimore-Chesapeake Bay region during July 2025 to investigate how contrasting land surfaces, including urban and coastal environments, influence ABL structure and development : Mt. Airy, MD (rural), Baltimore, MD (urban), Kent Island, MD (bay), and Washington, DC (urban core). ABLH is retrieved from HALO Doppler lidar and ceilometer observations and paired with co-located eddy-covariance measurements of sensible and latent heat flux, with all sites referenced to Local Standard Time for direct diurnal comparison. Observations from the CoURAGE and UrbanNet campaigns are evaluated against WRF simulations using correlation, bias, and RMSD at each site. Across all sites, daytime ABLH is strongly associated with sensible heat flux and near-surface air temperature under convective conditions, highlighting the role of surface heating in boundary - layer growth. The urban sites depart from this baseline in both magnitude and timing: the urban heat island sustains a deeper boundary layer through the afternoon and delays evening collapse well past sunset, when the rural site has already stabilized. The bay site behaves oppositely - cool marine air advected over Kent Island suppresses sensible heat flux and air temperature, limiting ABL growth while producing the largest day-to-day variability of the four sites. Comparisons among the urban, rural, and coastal sites highlight the distinct influences of urbanization and marine processes on ABL characteristics. These results quantify the surface heterogeneity that mesoscale models must resolve to represent boundary layer structure across the urban-rural-coastal transition, while evaluation against Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations provides insight into model performance across contrasting environments. Together, these findings improve understanding of lower - atmospheric processes across heterogeneous landscapes and provide guidance for improving representation of the ABL in numerical models.

498453.title: The importance of pre-existing outflow boundaries on warm-season Midwestern tornado events
498453.authors: Nathan Love, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and J. W. Frame
498453.abstract: We analyzed archived radar imagery, surface data, and storm reports to obtain a set of 19 severe weather events in which a supercellular tornado occurred along or on the cool side of a preexisting outflow boundary in Illinois or surrounding states. We then examined representative Rapid Refresh (RAP) model proximity soundings from either side of each boundary and compared thermodynamic and wind shear parameters. In general, the immediate cool sides of these boundaries featured lower temperatures, higher dewpoints, and stronger wind shear, particularly near the surface, than the warm sides. Thus, it is possible that at least some these tornadoes would not have occurred without the presence of the preexisting outflow boundary.

498459.title: State-Aware Dual-Stream Graph Neural Emulation of Lagrangian Ice-Particle Dynamics in Cirrus Clouds
498459.authors: Zesheng Liu, Lehigh University, Bethlehem, PA; and J. Liu, F. Li, J. Ko, K. D. Lamb, K. K. Chandrakar, and M. Rahnemoonfar
498459.abstract: Cirrus clouds play an important role in Earth’s climate, yet their evolution depends on ice-particle microphysical processes that occur at scales much finer than those resolved by global climate models. Cloud Model 1 (CM1), used in a large-eddy simulation (LES) configuration, enables high-resolution simulation of the three-dimensional atmospheric environment. Within CM1, the Super-Droplet Method (SDM) represents cloud microphysics by tracking Lagrangian superdroplets and the evolution of their positions and microphysical properties. The coupled CM1-SDM framework provides a detailed representation of cirrus cloud evolution, but the resulting particle-resolved simulations are computationally expensive. This motivates machine-learning emulators that can reproduce the evolution of SDM particles conditioned on the surrounding CM1 environment. We develop a state-aware emulator for superdroplet evolution in CM1-SDM cirrus simulations using a dual-stream architecture, where a graph neural network encodes the states and interactions of Lagrangian superdroplets, while a three-dimensional U-Net independently encodes spatially structured CM1 fields, including thermodynamic, humidity, and wind variables. The particle and atmospheric-field representations are combined through a structured fusion mechanism that separates particle self- and interaction dynamics, direct local atmospheric forcing, and learned three-dimensional environmental context. An adaptive gate controls the contribution of the learned environmental correction according to particle state and forecast horizon. The experiments use output from a CM1-SDM simulation of a cirrus case from the ICEBall field campaign. To accommodate coupled simulation outputs that may be archived at different temporal cadences between particle and atmospheric fields, the emulator uses a block-based, multi-horizon forecasting formulation. In the dataset considered here, SDM particle states are saved every 15 s, while CM1 atmospheric fields are saved every 60 s. From each CM1 output time, the model directly predicts particle positions and microphysical states at 15-, 30-, 45-, and 60-s lead times, with the 60-s prediction initializing the next rollout block. The state-aware component accounts for particles whose radius and effective density take fixed values in the SDM output, while separately modeling particles with continuously evolving microphysical properties. The training objectives capture particle trajectories, transitions between fixed-value and continuously evolving particle states, and population-level radius and effective density distributions. On particle-level tests, the dual-stream model substantially improves over particle-only multi-layer perceptron and graph neural network baselines. Under the inductive particle split, RMSE aggregated over all evaluated particle forecasts at 15-, 30-, 45-, and 60-s lead times was 2.08 m in x, 2.09 m in y, 4.29 m in z, 0.28 microns in equivalent radius, and 12.25 kg/m3 in effective density. Comparable performance between inductive and transductive particle splits further indicates that the learned representation is not dependent on individual particle identities. These results demonstrate the potential of coupled particle-field neural emulation as an efficient surrogate for resolving detailed ice-particle evolution within high-fidelity cirrus simulations.

498460.title: METGOAT: Meteorological and Environmental Tool for Graphical Object Annotation and Tracking
498460.authors: Ezekiel Caldon, Ohio University, Athens, OH; Ohio University, Athens, OH; and A. J. Drager
498460.abstract: The Meteorological and Environmental Tool for Graphical Object Annotation and Tracking (METGOAT) is a modular, open-source web application that empowers researchers to easily draw, manipulate, and tag analyzed meteorological features on maps and imagery for a variety of research applications. METGOAT started as a tool allowing researchers to label and track cold pool outflow boundaries, sea-breeze fronts, and convective cells in multivariate observational data or simulation outputs associated with the DOE ARM TRacking Aerosol Convection Interactions ExpeRiment (TRACER) campaign. However, the app remains under active development, and it can be used across a variety of applications requiring human labeling of meteorological features from time-evolving maps of one or more variable. METGOAT is also being expanded so that it can be used in conjunction with machine learning (ML) frameworks to create training and testing datasets for new tracking algorithms, as well as be used to edit machine-generated labels and tracks by hand. One example of a future use case for the tool is refining outputs from the tobac Python module to better characterize storm cell merger and splitting events. The main component of the tool is a web user interface that allows users to import sets of map images and data, draw and manipulate contours on a canvas, and export these contours into usable data formats such as KML, GeoJSON, and CSV. The intuitive interface empowers the user to precisely plot, modify, and track objects: users can zoom and pan, toggle between plotted variables, forward and backward through time, and display overlays to help track features’ evolution. The implementation as a simple, open-source web application allows for interoperability, ease of use, and the development of companion modules across the scientific and development communities. Roadmaps for an attendant Python module, application programming interface (API), and database framework are also identified to allow METGOAT to be used as a collaborative and connective tool within scientific workflows. The METGOAT-Python module would be a conduit for users to directly port data to and from the web interface, such as human and ML-made feature contours and meteorological images and data. The associated database and API framework would enable persistent storage of annotation data on a remote server and collaborative use of the application in a self-hosted environment. This modular approach to the tool’s development maintains the accessibility and interoperability of METGOAT across scientific applications, while building its capabilities as a powerful analysis tool. This presentation will include a live demonstration of the user interface, as well as a description of the architecture and development of the application. Finally, we would like to enthusiastically invite interested developers to learn about and contribute to the web interface, Python module, and/or database code stack for METGOAT. The GitHub repository for the project can be accessed at https://github.com/METGOAT, released under the Apache 2.0 license.

498461.title: Multi-Modal Data Assimilation for Improved Space Weather Forecasting
498461.authors: Preston Robert Schenk, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; Air Force Research Laboratory / Space Warefare Directorate, Albuquerque, NM; and S. J. Schonfeld and C. J. Henney
498461.abstract: Accurate predictions of the solar wind are essential for understanding and forecasting behavior of Earth’s upper atmosphere. Solar wind forecasts depend strongly on representations of the Sun’s photospheric magnetic fields, yet observations of the solar poles remain limited, introducing uncertainty into assimilated magnetic field maps used to initialize heliospheric models. Previous work demonstrated modifying polar flux of Air Force Data Assimilative Photospheric Flux Transport (ADAPT) global magnetic maps to match observed coronal hole boundaries improved solar wind model performance during solar minimum. Here, we extend this work, evaluating the method's impact on coronal hole representation and resultant solar wind forecast skill during 2010-2014, covering the rise and maximum of a solar cycle. ADAPT global magnetic maps are modified following Schonfeld et al, 2022 and processed through the Wang-Sheeley-Arge (WSA) heliospheric model. We evaluate the method’s performance by using binary image processing metrics (Markedness and Informedness) to evaluate coronal hole predictions and the WSA Prediction Metric for solar wind forecasts. We find that polar flux modification results in little to no improvement in coronal hole prediction or mean WSA-ADAPT ensemble forecast skill. However, individual WSA-ADAPT realizations exhibit rare episodes of significant skill improvement accompanying increased variance across the ensemble. These results suggest that polar flux redistribution does not systematically improve mean forecast skill but can alter the distribution of ensemble outcomes. Episodic improvements in individual realizations may provide value for retroactive solar wind analyses and motivate further investigation into polar field uncertainty as a source of forecast spread.

498462.title: Estimating Greenland Ice-Sheet Internal Layer Thickness from Polar Radar Imagery with Deep Graph Transformers
498462.authors: Zesheng Liu, Lehigh University, Bethlehem, PA; and M. Rahnemoonfar
498462.abstract: Characterizing the internal stratigraphy of the Greenland Ice Sheet is important for investigating past snow accumulation, ice deformation, and the long-term evolution of the ice sheet. Ice-penetrating radar provides extensive observations of internal layers, but older and deeper horizons are often more difficult to estimate because their geometry reflects accumulated deformation and increasing spatial variability. Predicting deeper layer thickness from better-observed shallow layers therefore requires a model that can preserve local layer continuity while learning dependencies across a long sequence of layers formed at different times. We present GRIT-LP, a deep graph transformer designed to estimate the thickness of deeper internal ice layers from polar radar observations. Each internal layer is represented as a geometric graph, with GraphSAGE used to extract spatial variations along the radar transect and temporal self-attention used to model relationships across the ordered layer sequence. GRIT-LP introduces adaptive long-range skip connections that repeatedly integrate the original spatial representations into deeper attention blocks, improving information propagation and reducing representation degradation in deep architectures. It also employs partitioned spatial graphs composed of overlapping, fully connected local neighborhoods, which preserve spatial coherence while avoiding potentially noisy and computationally expensive connections between distant locations. We evaluate GRIT-LP on the SRED Greenland radar stratigraphy dataset, using younger internal layers corresponding to 2007--2011 to estimate the thicknesses of older and deeper layers corresponding to 1992--2006. The proposed model reduces root mean squared error by 24.92% relative to the current state-of-the-art approach and maintains consistent performance across radargrams collected at different locations. Additional experiments show stable predictions when the target sequence is extended to as many as twenty-one deeper layers. These results demonstrate that combining locality-preserving graph representations with long-range information propagation can improve the estimation of Greenland ice-sheet internal stratigraphy and provide more reliable representations of subsurface layer geometry for subsequent analyses of accumulation patterns and ice-sheet dynamics.

498463.title: Using Explainable Machine Learning Techniques to Investigate Marine Stratocumulus Processes in the Eastern North Atlantic
498463.authors: Ezekiel Caldon, Ohio University, Athens, OH; and V. P. Ghate
498463.abstract: Turbulence and microphysical processes are tightly coupled in marine stratocumulus topped boundary layers, influencing cloud structure, precipitation, and radiative properties across a range of spatial and temporal scales. However, the multiscale nature of these interactions presents significant challenges for their accurate representation in a range of atmospheric models. In this study, we analyze these processes using data from the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Eastern North Atlantic (ENA) site. 29 cases of stratocumulus cloud conditions spanning 676 hours were identified from 7 years of data. The cloud and drizzle macro- and microphysical properties were retrieved by combining data from vertically pointing cloud radar, lidars and radiometers. Profiles of radiative fluxes were calculated by using radiosonde reported thermodynamic profiles and cloud properties as an input to the Rapid Radiative Transfer Model (RRTM). On average the cloud top height was 1.3 km with clouds 361 m thick and cloud base rain rate of 2.62 mm day-1. The radiative cooling at the cloud top was –65.22 W m-2 yielding updraft velocity at closest level to cloud base of 0.40 m s-1. The average cloud optical depth was 14.57 and cloud droplet number concentrations of 85 cm-3. We specifically focus on understanding the factors modulating boundary layer coupling, cloud base rain rate, and liquid water path through the extreme gradient-boosted (XGBoost) machine learning (ML) model framework. The models were developed using hourly and minute data to capture the adjustment timescales. The SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis revealed cloud top height (CTH), updraft velocity closest to cloud base, and liquid water path (LWP) largely determined the decoupling at hour resolution, while at minute resolution decoupling was determined by LWP, CTH, and latent heat flux. Similarly for cloud base rain rate, concentrations of cloud particles, cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and droplets had the greatest effect at hourly timescales while cloud-top radiational cooling, lifting condensation level (LCL), and CTH had the greatest effect at minute resolution. These results are useful for scale-aware cloud parameterizations aimed at simulating aerosol-cloud-precipitation-turbulence processes at a range of model resolutions. Caption for attached figure: (top) KAZR reflectivity (shades) and ceilometer cloud base height (black dots) from 20161115 to 20161117, (middle) visible satellite imagery, and (bottom) satellite LWP. The satellite snapshots are for 20161115 10 UTC, 20161115 15 UTC, 20161116 10 UTC, and 20161116 15 UTC. The local time is 2 hours behind UTC. ENA ARM site shown as red star.

498464.title: COGENT: Continuous Graph Emulators with Neural Ordinary Differential Equations for Long-Term Flood Forecasting
498464.authors: Zesheng Liu, Lehigh University, Bethlehem, PA; and M. Rahnemoonfar
498464.abstract: Accurate and timely flood prediction is essential for hydrologic risk assessment, emergency planning, and rapid evaluation of rainfall scenarios. However, physics-based hydrodynamic models, such as ANUGA, can be computationally expensive when many scenarios or long forecast horizons must be evaluated. Deep-learning surrogates can accelerate physics-based flood simulations, but many rely on single-step prediction. Long-horizon forecasting therefore requires recursive rollout, through which prediction errors can compound over time. We present COGENT, a continuous graph neural emulator trained on simulations generated by the physics-based ANUGA hydrodynamic model. COGENT operates directly on ANUGA's native triangular mesh. A graph encoder captures spatial interactions among mesh nodes, while a temporal encoder summarizes recent flood evolution from historical stage, momentum, and rainfall inputs. The resulting history context initializes and conditions a graph Neural Ordinary Differential Equation, while the prescribed future rainfall sequence is supplied throughout the continuous rollout. A residual decoder maps the continuous latent trajectory to future water stage and momentum states. This formulation avoids recursive feedback of predicted physical states and supports prediction at arbitrary forecast times. We evaluate COGENT using 20 rainfall-driven ANUGA simulations, each spanning 12 hours at 10-minute resolution, with peak rainfall intensities from 20 to 80 mm/h. Sixteen simulations are used for training, two for validation, and two for testing. In full-rollout evaluation, the first eight states are known and the next 65 are forecast while history lengths from one to eight are explored. With three historical states, COGENT reduces aggregate RMSE from 0.740 for a single-step autoregressive GNN to 0.120, an 83.8% reduction. RMSE decreases by 84.1% for depth, 81.1% for x-momentum, and 78.3% for y-momentum. Qualitative comparisons show that COGENT captures the dominant spatial patterns of flood propagation throughout the rollout. These results demonstrate an accurate and temporally flexible AI approach for long-horizon flood prediction on unstructured meshes, supporting rapid hydrologic forecasting and flood-risk assessment.

498465.title: Air Pollution Inequality Across Race, Ethnicity, and Historical Redlining Grades in a 2010 Contiguous United States Census Block Sample
498465.authors: Mohsen Nikfarjam, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and E. Nikfarjam
498465.abstract: Ambient nitrogen dioxide and fine particulate matter concentrations vary across communities, yet aggregate improvement can conceal unequal exposure. We evaluated associations between modeled residential outdoor concentrations, race and ethnicity, and historical Home Owners' Loan Corporation mortgage security grades in a large 2010 sample of census blocks spanning the contiguous United States. We linked 2010 population counts by race and ethnicity from IPUMS NHGIS to annual average CACES empirical geographic regression estimates at census block centroids. We used the spatial increment data product of Wang et al. to partition each modeled concentration into long range, mid range, neighborhood, and near source components. Historical grades were assigned only to block centroids inside digitized Mapping Inequality polygons. We calculated population weighted mean exposures by demographic group and grade, together with disparity ratios and weighted inequality measures. The current pipeline uses complete case inner joins across four concentration files and two census files, retaining 3,080,166 block identifiers representing 156,820,030 residents in 2010. Estimates therefore describe this complete case analytical sample rather than the complete national census block population. Within the sample portion covered by historical grading maps, 2010 population weighted NO2 averaged 17.0 ppb in Grade D areas and 10.8 ppb in Grade A areas, a 58 percent relative difference. Population weighted exposure also differed by race and ethnicity within every grade. These findings are descriptive associations and do not identify an effect of historical redlining. The concentration fields are model predictions rather than monitor observations. Their prediction error was not propagated into the disparity statistics, and intervals from the present workflow do not account for dependence among nearby blocks. The four concentration components represent distance scales, not emission sectors. Before estimating change from 2000 to 2010, we will harmonize 2000 demographics to the 2010 census geography with a validated crosswalk and repeat the analysis using the full eligible block universe. We will also use spatially adjusted uncertainty and test whether distance scale patterns agree with source specific inventories. These steps are needed to distinguish robust exposure inequities from artifacts of geographic change and complete case selection. Keywords include air quality, environmental justice, nitrogen dioxide, fine particulate matter, historical redlining, spatial decomposition, population weighted exposure, and census blocks.

498466.title: Intercomparison of AERONET Aerosol Optical Depth with Surface Concentrations of PM2.5 in Austin, Texas in 2024-2025
498466.authors: Josiah Alexander Guajardo, St. Edward's University, Austin, TX; St. Edward's University, Austin, TX; and P. J. Walter and P. Savala
498466.abstract: Aerosols are fine solid or liquid particles suspended in a gas, such as air, typically ranging in size between a few nanometers to 100 micrometers in diameter. We used NASA’s AERONET data collected from an instrument located at St. Edward’s University in Austin, TX, which tracks changes in the size distribution of aerosol particles and properties related to their composition, specifically analyzing Aerosol Optical Depth (referred to as AOD) in comparison to surface concentrations of PM2.5. Fine particulate matter (referred to as PM2.5) is an air pollutant regulated by the Environmental Protection Agency and consists of any small airborne aerosol particles with diameters smaller than 2.5 micrometers. We have carried out an initial investigation of the data from five PM2.5 monitors in the greater Austin area, showing the PM2.5 concentrations for these monitors over 2024 and 2025. From this investigation, we observed the highest concentrations just after midnight on 1 January due to fireworks, as well as high PM2.5 concentrations during annual Saharan dust events. We analyzed the AERONET data, and compared these AERONET observations with PM2.5 surface monitors and found moderate correlations between AOD and surface PM2.5 concentrations across different monitors in the Austin region. Overall, these findings will help us better characterize annual events and seasonal changes in air quality in Austin.

498471.title: Coming at This from a New Angle: Incorporating Incidence-Angle Dependence into Lightning-Derived D-Region Electron Density Profiles
498471.authors: Ty Stromberg, Air Force Institute of Technology, Riverside, OH; Air Force Institute of Technology, Riverside, OH; and B. T. McClung and D. Emmons
498471.abstract: Previous work by Lay and Shao (2011) and Lay et al. (2014) demonstrated that D-region electron density can be probed using lightning-generated VLF waveforms, and Smith et al. (2025) expanded this approach to model D-region electron density profiles (EDPs) using VLF radio emissions originating from lightning flashes. This method, however, treats emissions as a single geometric path and reduces oblique-incidence to a correction using a static application of the Secant Law. Because radio wave propagation speed varies with incidence angle, waveforms that arrive from different directions relative to the same ionospheric patch should hold additional, angle dependent information about the local electron density structure. By introducing this relationship, the proposed method aims to move towards a better resolved EDP estimation to improve accuracy at the altitudes FIRI (Friedrich et al., 2018) identifies as the hardest to model. This work strives to increase the information gain from each individual lightning waveform and build upon Smith et al. (2025) in pursuit of higher resolution and angle aware D-region remote sensing.

498472.title: Spatiotemporal Variability Across North America of Limited Visibility Occurrences and the Linked Weather
498472.authors: MaryLi Nielsen, Hobart and William Smith Colleges, Geneva, NY
498472.abstract: A reduction in visibility can be caused by a variety of weather conditions and has a substantial impact on travel, regardless of the form of transportation. This study examined the spatiotemporal variation of visibility and the weather associated with the occurrences of limited visibility across the United States and Canada. Surface hourly weather station data was obtained from the National Center for Environmental Information (NCEI) for 127 stations during the years of 1980-1995. Limited visibility, with potential for large impacts, was defined as having a horizontal distance ≤ 2000 meters. Limited visibility hours occurred most frequently along western and eastern coastal locations, as well as across Alaska and northern Canada. Fog, rain, snow, and blowing snow were found to be the primary weather contributors to limited visibility. Fog was the most prominent weather associated with limited visibility across most of the United States and Canada, except in northeastern Canada and the Intermountain West, where heavy snowfall was a notable contributor. The winter and summer seasons had the most and least limited visibility hours, respectively. Additional details about this research will be shared during the conference.

498473.title: Characterizing Atmospheric Environments Favorable for Mountain Wave-Associated Turbulence Near Mount Washington
498473.authors: Aspen R Medvec, Plymouth State University, Southbury, CT; and E. G. Hoffman and J. Broccolo
498473.abstract: Mountain waves (MWs) occur when strong winds blow perpendicular to a mountain range causing air to rise and then sink in a stable layer on the leeward side. When MWs break, they can generate turbulence at the bottom of wave crests. This is a common issue pilots experience at general cruising altitudes. Most studies which investigate mountain wave-turbulence interactions focus on the upper-level flow domain and avoid impacts near the surface. The goal of this study was to determine to what extent can near surface observations and reanalysis derived vertical profiles characterize atmospheric environments favorable for mountain wave-associated turbulence near Mount Washington. For the cold season of October 2025 to March 2026, hourly METAR data from the summit, hourly data from the Auto Road Vertical Profile stations, hourly data from the Cog Railway Vertical Profile stations, and ERA5 data extracted from the Copernicus Climate Data Store was used to characterize atmospheric environments favorable for MWs. Lenticular observations extracted from METAR data were used to identify MW days. Bulk Richardson calculations were completed to get a first order estimate of turbulence potential. Surface data was compared to vertically derived profiles to determine if similarities in dynamic behavior were present during MW events. This comparison showed that near surface observations alone were insufficient for fully characterizing MW associated turbulence potential. While this study could have been completed solely using reanalysis data, surface observations still provided a useful background to better help understand how the lower levels behaved during these events. When both types of data were combined, it provided a more complete characterization of environments favorable for MW associated turbulence.

498475.title: Intercomparison of Pandora and Airborne Observations During the 2023 STAQS/AEROMMA Campaigns in the NYC Region
498475.authors: Mayukh Intesar Islam, St. Edward's University, Austin, TX; and P. J. Walter, P. Savala, P. Peterson, and C. Tyler
498475.abstract: The 2023 NASA Synergistic TEMPO Air Quality Science (STAQS) and NOAA Atmospheric Emissions and Reactions Observed from Megacities to Marine Areas (AEROMMA) campaigns included airborne observations from a number of sites. In this study we performed an intercomparison of ground-based Pandora Direct Sun measurements with airborne observations of nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and formaldehyde (HCHO) for the region including NYC and the Long Island Sound. Geostationary Coastal and Air Pollution Events Airborne Simulator (GCAS) vertical column observations within narrow spatial and temporal windows of overpasses of Pandora sites were averaged to create GCAS-Pandora matched data pairs across four across four NYC region flight dates (July 26, July 28, August 5 and August 9, 2023). Preliminary results show strong agreement between GCAS and Pandora NO2 column amounts and no correlation between similar observations for HCHO. We will also perform a comparison of MAX DOAS observations at the Yale Coastal Field Station with vertically integrated in situ observations from onboard the DC8 aircraft.

498476.title: The Role of Native Plants and Vegetation in Urban Climate Change and Urban Heat Island Effect Reduction
498476.authors: Hannah Cavender, The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK
498476.abstract: The expansion and rapid growth of urban areas and large cities have resulted in significant changes to land use and land cover, including the widespread degradation of land and ecosystems. Urban growth and urban sprawl have altered land-surface characteristics across large areas. As these urban areas expand, they lead to a major loss of vegetation and native plants due to natural land being replaced with highly developed land. Urban areas often experience higher air temperatures than the surrounding rural areas due to the buildings and other surfaces absorbing and retaining heat, due to its low albedo, along with the reduction in plants and vegetation limiting the cooling effects they offer. Vegetation plays an important role in reducing air temperatures through shading, reducing human exposure to these localized increases in air temperatures, and also contribute to carbon sinks, reducing the amount of carbon in the atmosphere. Native plants and vegetation are adapted to the climate and environmental conditions where they naturally occur. They support the local ecosystems and biodiversity, and may require fewer resources and upkeep, such as water, especially in areas with already limited resources. This study aims to determine whether reintroducing native plants and vegetation into urban areas that are experiencing major land-use change can help mitigate climate change impacts and reduce higher temperatures due to the urban heat island effect. Using GIS and existing literature, I will examine where the most urban growth is occurring, what plants are native to those regions, and whether these plants have potential benefits when reintroduced to urban areas where they once occurred naturally.

498477.title: How Student-Taught Lessons Affect Youth's Interest and Engagement in Atmospheric Sciences within Volusia County.
498477.authors: Alexis Lynn Peshehonoff, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University Student Chapter of the American Meteorological Society/ National Weather Association, Daytona Beach, FL; and D. Burow, W. R. John, P. Gilliard, A. B. Lanese, J. Guiglotto, A. Schoener, and N. Cover
498477.abstract: The Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University Student Chapter of the American Meteorological Society (AMS) and National Weather Association (NWA) will conduct a youth-focused atmospheric science outreach project throughout Volusia County, FL, during the Fall 2026 semester. This project aims to connect local students with weather and atmospheric science while evaluating how students of different ages respond to weather-related educational activities. Previous outreach interactions conducted by a chapter member at a local school demonstrated a clear interest in weather lessons by both students and faculty. Building upon these past interactions, the chapter will develop age-appropriate lessons focused on basic weather concepts, local severe weather, forecasting, and career opportunities in meteorology. Student and faculty responses will be requested to observe interest in atmospheric sciences both before and after the lesson to assess changes in interest, knowledge, and perceptions. Responses will then be compared across age groups to determine which ages and education levels show a higher engagement level and interest. Results from this project will help provide insight into how effective a student-led meteorological outreach is in increasing youth interest in weather and encouraging the pursuit of atmospheric sciences into the future. It also hopes to strengthen Embry-Riddle’s AMS/ NWA student community and Volusia County schools while inspiring the next generation to explore meteorology-related sciences and careers.

498478.title: Analyzing the Relationship Between Coastal Regression and Land Surface Temperature Using Satellite Remote Sensing in Peru and Guinea.
498478.authors: Serigne Fallou Diaw, NSF, Jersey City, NJ; and M. Aghailas
498478.abstract: Remote sensing provides an effective means of monitoring environmental change at spatial and temporal scales that extend beyond the capabilities of ground-based observations. Active sensors such as the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), part of the Copernicus Program, acquire day-and-night, all-weather imagery that can penetrate cloud cover. This capability makes SAR especially valuable for monitoring coastal regions in West Africa and South America, where persistent cloud cover often limits the use of optical satellite imagery. In addition, passive sensors such as the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) provide daily global measurements of Land Surface Temperature (LST), enabling the analysis of long-term thermal trends. This study explores whether increasing surface temperatures can be associated with shoreline changes along the Guinean coast of West Africa and the Peruvian coast of South America to examine. The analysis incorporates data from the NASA ARSET program, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), and the Sentinel-1 and MODIS datasets available through Google Earth Engine. Sentinel-1 SAR imagery is processed to generate median composites for shoreline extraction, while MODIS LST data are scaled and converted from Kelvin to Celsius using established correction factors to produce thermal maps. In addition, Landsat 8 Level-2 imagery is processed in Python to derive surface reflectance and land surface temperature for the Peruvian study area. Time-series, trend, and multi-correlation analyses are then performed to evaluate the relationship between surface temperature and coastal regression across the selected regions.

498479.title: Lightning Characteristics of Elevated and Surface Based Convection
498479.authors: Conrad Slad, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND
498479.abstract: Deep convection, more notably supercells, can be characterized by the vertical origin of their effective inflow layer (EIL). Surface-based supercells are commonly associated with tornadoes and hail, while elevated supercells are associated with very large hail and damaging winds. Furthermore, the EIL can also modulate the microphysical processes within deep convection such as noninductive charging in the mixed-phase region. It is our hypothesis that surface-based and elevated convection can be distinguished through lightning characteristics such as cloud-to-ground (CG) versus intracloud (IC) flash ratios, lightning polarity, and peak current. This study compiles cases of strictly surface-based and elevated storms throughout the central plains of the United States and their respective lightning characteristics using the National Lightning Detection Network (NLDN), WSR-88D radar observations, and near-storm soundings of the surrounding environment. Ultimately, this work aims to establish lighting characteristics as a diagnostic tool for determining the origin of a storm’s EIL, offering insight into the real-time shifts of different severe weather hazard types.

498483.title: Investigating the September 29, 2023, Tri-state Flooding Event: A WRF-Based Analysis of Tropical Storm Ophelia, Elevated Sea Surface Temperatures, and Their Role in Enhancing Extreme Rainfall
498483.authors: Cole Stern, SUNY, Bellmore, NY; and P. P. Papin
498483.abstract: On 29 September 2023, heavy rainfall leading to flash flooding occurred over a significant portion of the New York City metropolitan region. John F. Kennedy Airport set a new 24-hour rainfall record of 8.05 inches, most of it occurring within a 3-6 hour period. This event contributed to September 2023 being the wettest September on record across the region. During this event, flash flooding led to blocked roads, canceled flights, and the shutdown of portions of the subway. The flooding event was a result of persistent bands of rainfall driven by the interaction between a mid-latitude trough moving into the northeastern US and a moisture-rich atmosphere across the Tri-State area (NY, NJ, and CT). Several days before the heavy rainfall, Tropical Cyclone Ophelia impacted North Carolina with strong winds and heavy rainfall before subsequently moving offshore of the Mid-Atlantic. During this time, anomalously warm Sea-Surface Temperatures (SSTs) off the northeastern United States were part of a record-warm Atlantic basin. It is hypothesized that both moisture associated with Tropical Cyclone Ophelia and the nearby elevated SSTs helped enhance the rainfall that produced flash flooding. Since few case studies have examined how the combined effects of elevated SSTs and TC moisture affect flash flooding in the highly populated Tri-State area, this study provides crucial insights to improve future forecasting efforts across this region. Multiple high-resolution simulations from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model were run to help diagnose the critical factors contributing to this event. In addition to a control run that simulated the actual baseline atmospheric conditions of the event, two additional sets of simulations were conducted that modified these initial conditions. The first set of modified simulations changed the Gulf Stream SSTs, testing how increasing or decreasing SSTs would have affected the intensity of the heavy rainfall event. The second set of simulations increased and decreased the moisture field associated with the remnants of TC Ophelia to examine how its moisture affected the event. The results show that when SSTs are modified, there is a significant influence on the moisture inflow into the rainfall event, affecting both the magnitude and location of the heaviest rainfall. For instance, if SSTs were 1°C cooler - near pre-Industrial levels - rainfall totals would have been reduced by roughly 17% across the Tri-State area. In addition, the presence of TC Ophelia’s moisture was also shown to have a direct influence on the overall severity of the intense precipitation. These findings demonstrate how SST changes in a future climate could alter the intensity and spatial distribution of heavy rainfall related to flooding events in the Tri-State area, and underscore the importance of TC moisture in these deadly and costly events.

498489.title: Stratospheric Wave Reflection Events and East Pacific Blocking: Impacts on North American Temperatures and Geopotential Heights
498489.authors: Alexa Yvonne Kaley, University of North Carolina - Asheville, Asheville, NC; University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI; and A. A. L. Lang
498489.abstract: In recent years, stratospheric wave reflection events have emerged as a potential source of long-range predictability because of their links to North American cold air outbreaks. Case studies linked prior cold air outbreaks to preceding wave reflection events followed by the development of a block in the North Pacific, but this relationship has not been characterized for an extended record of wave reflection and blocking events. This research analyzes the frequency and timing of overlaps between East Pacific blocking and wave reflection events within a 10-day lag period from 1979 to 2020. We then examined the downstream impacts of the different overlaps through temperature and geopotential height anomalies in subsequent weeks. Wave reflection events and onset dates were identified using a reflection index based on the difference in standardized meridional eddy heat fluxes over Siberia and Canada. East Pacific blocking events and their characteristics were obtained from an ERA5-based blocking dataset, and daily climatological information from the database was used alongside ERA5 data to compute average temperature and geopotential height anomalies. We found that 81% of wave reflection events had East Pacific blocking within 10 days of onset, with blocking frequency increasing significantly at lag day -2 and maintaining higher frequencies through lag day 8. On average, wave reflection events with East Pacific blocking saw anomalous cold temperatures move into Canada and the United States around lag day 3 and persist for 5-8 days.
