Wave reflection events with both blocking types or omega blocks before onset had the strongest cold anomalies, whereas events without blocking did not see a similar cold anomaly, but rather a stronger warm anomaly over the northern U.S. Our findings suggest that East Pacific blocking events, specifically their type and timing, are associated with differences in the downstream surface response to wave reflection events. Further understanding the mechanisms driving these relationships and differences may improve forecast accuracy and lead time for cold air outbreaks and other extremes on subseasonal-to-seasonal timescales.

498490.title: Pyrocumulonimbus (PyroCb) Forecast Model Verification for the INSPYRE Campaign
498490.authors: Anna Tianyue Liu, Georgia Institute of Technology, Orem, UT
498490.abstract: Fire-induced or enhanced thunderstorms or pyrocumulonimbus clouds (pyroCbs), can have regional to global impacts on atmospheric conditions. PyroCbs often occur in environments that are often favorable from dry convection with fires that have good energetics. PyroCbs can create erratic fire weather conditions at the surface which can bring challenging and dangerous conditions for fire suppression efforts (Peterson et al., 2025). Deep pyroconvection can also loft smoke high up in the atmosphere, sometimes reaching the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS). Smoke particulates can interact with incoming radiation and other chemical compounds (Fromm et al., 2010). Modeling and forecasting pyroCbs remains challenging as fire-atmosphere interactions are not well observed. For this project, we will utilize the Freitas et al. (2007; 2010) 1D plume rise model (PRM), which parameterizes cloud microphysics and entrainment effects, to simulate two pyroCbs in Utah during the summer of 2026. High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) data for vertical atmospheric profiles (atmospheric soundings), fire area, and fire heat flux were used as inputs to characterize each fire. With the PRM, we distinguished the monsoonal influence of the Babylon pyroCb and the fire-driven forcing of the Cottonwood pyroCb. This study provides insight into the accuracy of a plume rise model, one that could potentially be used to forecast pyroCb events operationally.

498491.title: Analyzing Ventilation Impacts Across Quadrants of Hurricane Ian (2022) and Fausto (2026): Comparing Goddard Earth Observing System Forward Processing (GEOS-FP) Analyses to Observations
498491.authors: Lucas Riley Donahue, Georgia Institute of Technology, Melrose, MA; and J. S. Haase, N. J. Barton, B. H. Tang, and K. Loo
498491.abstract: Radial ventilation is the transport of low equivalent potential temperature (dry) air into the inner core of a tropical cyclone (TC) by vertical wind shear (VWS). This process directly weakens a TC’s intensity. It is currently challenging to collect thermodynamic observations of radial ventilation throughout the entire TC structure. In this work, we utilize dropsonde, airborne radio occultation (ARO), and analyses from the Goddard Earth Observing System Forward Processing (GEOS-FP) model to better resolve the key features associated with radial ventilation. Dropsondes provide high-resolution vertical profiles, including winds along the flight track of a weather reconnaissance aircraft, and ARO complements this by creating profiles that reach outside the flight track. An area of ventilation was observed in the northwest quadrant (approximately between upshear left and downshear left) of Hurricane Ian (2022) on 28 September 2022 when Ian was at 105 kts intensity in an unfavorable shear environment and was therefore anticipated to weaken. Similarly, ventilation was observed in the eastern quadrant of Hurricane Fausto (2026) on 27 July 2026. This is illustrated using vertical cross sections of the GEOS-FP model, observational ARO, and observational dropsonde refractivity anomaly data. However, despite the data indicating dry air entrainment and strong environmental shear, Ian strengthened until landfall at 20:35 UTC 28 September, unlike typical ventilation cases like Fausto, where the TC dissipates soon after the process is identified. We use observed and modelled values of wind speed, deep-layer shear, layer-averaged relative humidity (300-500 hPa), and refractivity anomaly in the mid-troposphere at 500 hPa – another measure of moisture content – from the GEOS-FP model to diagnose ventilation in these hurricanes. These data were then averaged for each quadrant of varying radii, oriented by the VWS direction with respect to the pressure center of the TC. This was calculated over the entire lifespan of the storm. The model was compared to Airborne Radio Occultation (ARO) and dropsonde observations within their respective quadrants to provide validation that the GEOS-FP model was accurately representing the features of the storm. The question to be investigated was whether observations from Ian indicated a favorable environment, opposite to that of the model, and whether both observations and the model consistently showed favorable conditions for weakening in Fausto. In both hurricanes, both model and observational data show high values of relative humidity and refractivity anomaly in the 100-km radius quadrant average; however, Fausto shows a sharp decrease as the radial ventilation process begins, dissipating the TC within a day after the fact. Hurricane Ian preserves the high relative humidity at a 100 km radius but shows a sharp decrease in the same data at a 200 km radius within 24 hours of landfall. A possible explanation is that the inner-core moisture content in Ian was never impacted by the dry air and accompanying strong VWS due to a “natural barrier”. This conclusion was checked with TC-Atlas, a multi-source platform used for TC structure analysis, showing outward radial winds in the Tail Doppler Radar (TDR) in the northwest (downshear left) quadrant of Ian, preventing dry air entrainment. Fausto did not indicate any barrier in TDR or model observations, so radial ventilation allowed the TC to weaken. Future work includes incorporating calculations of radial winds/ventilation from the GEOS-FP model into the analysis. Better understanding the process and calculation of radial ventilation across a TC will improve forecast guidance for TCs. Additionally, Fausto and Ian did not have sufficient flights to completely capture their storm center and RH decrease, respectively, so future work could expand this analysis to a larger event catalog within the past 6 years, specifically when ARO observations are available.

498492.title: Predicting Landslide Hazards Using Forecasted Atmospheric Rivers along the Pacific Coast
498492.authors: Thomas Francis Hernandez, The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and A. R. Selvaag, E. Bott, and X. Chen
498492.abstract: Landslides present a significant hazard in topographically diverse regions prone to soil instability, which is caused by events of extreme precipitation. Along the Pacific coast of North America, these events are frequently driven by atmospheric rivers (ARs)—intense corridors of moisture transport characterized by strong low-level winds and high water vapor content originating from the tropics and subtropics of the Pacific ocean. However, using AR forecasts alone to predict landslide events yields a low predictive skill since not all moisture transport events trigger slope failure. This study evaluates the predictability of landslides by analyzing historical numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts of ARs alongside a multi-year inventory of documented landslide events. By correlating historical forecast parameters—such as Integrated Water Vapor Transport (IVT) and duration—with terrain attributes including slope angle and soil moisture thresholds, we identify the environmental conditions required for an AR to trigger a landslide. The resulting framework enhances predictive accuracy, transforming regional AR forecasts into actionable early-warning tools for vulnerable communities that are prone to landslide hazards.

498494.title: 3D-PAWS: Depleting Costs for Dependable Technology and Data Network Expansion
498494.authors: Dorin Kim, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and E. Keefe, S. A. LaBore, L. Alcoba, A. M. Cherny, J. Bhuiyan, and K. Mohindra-Green
498494.abstract: Automatic weather stations represent a foundational piece of instrumentation in the atmospheric sciences that present a reliable way to record consistent meteorological data. The placement of weather stations and their associated networks informs local forecast accuracy, and the regional data can empower community members to make decisions regarding their recreation, health, and safety. However, the installation of an automated weather station network requires substantial up-front cost, and a traditional weather station network is not financially suitable for groups with limited resources. In this project, members of Cornell University's GeoData Student Project Team developed and created a variation of the 3D-Printed Automated Weather Stations (3D-PAWS) system first developed by COMET at the University Cooperative for Atmospheric Research (UCAR). Undergraduate students procured sensors and electrical components, printed and assembled parts, and installed a 3D-PAWS-like automated weather station entirely on their own at a cost roughly an order of magnitude lower than commercial alternatives. For validation, this station was installed next to a permanent weather station in Ithaca, NY, originally purchased from a commercial provider. Pending data verification, we plan to install more 3D-PAWS stations across the Finger Lakes region, and engage community members in finding new, viable locations for station placement. These low-cost weather stations complement GeoData's student-hosted nowcasting weather models for the Central New York region, providing additional sources of data and improved accuracy.

498495.title: Withdrawn: North Atlantic Tropical Cyclones and Rossby Wavebreaking Interactions
498495.authors: Jonathan Lin, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and K. A. Bowley
498495.abstract: The extratropical transition of tropical cyclones (TC) often causes significant changes in the mid-latitude flow. One example of substantial change in the mid-latitude flow is the initiation of Rossby wave breaking (RWB), where isentropes on a constant potential vorticity (PV) surface are irreversibly overturned and deformed. This study investigates how TC recurvature may initiate RWB, or be associated with, during the extratropical transition process. Using the revised Atlantic hurricane database (HURDAT2) and the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts fifth generation reanalysis dataset, TC recurvature events and RWB events are catalogued. Tropical cyclones that undergo recurvature and eventual extratropical transition are compared to identified RWB events to quantify how often these are coupled. Instances of coupled events are then explored to identify preferred tropospheric circulation evolutions and outcomes, including identifying differences between TCs that are coupled to cyclonic or anticyclonic RWB events.

498496.title: Examining the Morning Boundary Layer Ozone Evolution during the TRACER campaign in La Porte, Texas
498496.authors: Lashawn Lofton, Texas Southern University, houston, TX; and T. Morris, A. J. Drager, P. J. Walter, and M. P. Jensen
498496.abstract: Ground-level ozone (O3) is a regulated air pollutant that can have serious adverse effects on human health. O3 can negatively affect the respiratory system, causing severe irritation by reducing lung function and worsening any type of conditions, such as Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease. In this study, conducted within the Department of Environmental Sciences and Technologies at Brookhaven National Laboratory, we investigated the influence of atmospheric boundary layer characteristics and meteorological conditions on ozone concentrations in the La Porte, Texas region (southeast of Houston) during the Department of Energy’s (DOE) deployment of the First Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Mobile Facility (AMF1) for the October 2021 – September 2022 Tracking Aerosol Convection Interactions Experiment (TRACER) campaign. Atmospheric observations, including wind direction, temperature, relative humidity, and barometric pressure were analyzed to determine how changes in weather conditions affect ozone concentrations. We analyze atmospheric data from multiple dates and examine relationships between the vertical distribution of ozone and atmospheric characteristics. For instance, we observed cases where there was an increase in ozone throughout the first 2 km above the surface when there was an abundance of nitrogen dioxide (NO2, an ozone precursor) in the early morning and clear sky conditions. In other cases, the total ozone did not change but the vertical distribution did because of convective mixing. During the final stages of the research, we observed a relationship between NO₂ and O₃ concentrations, consistent with NO₂ serving as a precursor in ozone formation. When NO₂ concentrations were high, O₃ concentrations tended to be lower, while lower NO₂ concentrations were associated with higher O₃ concentrations. This research improves our understanding between boundary layer processes, meteorological variables, and air quality. The findings will provide valuable insight into many factors that influence ozone pollution and its potential impacts on human health while providing hands-on experiences in atmospheric data analysis and visualization. The research we have done is useful because knowing what atmospheric characteristics are and what processes take place in boundary layers sheds light on the impact atmospheric conditions have on air quality and ozone levels. This study, based on an analysis of ARM data, helps to understand the relationship between meteorological processes and the composition of the atmosphere.

498497.title: Examining the Performance of the CU GeoData Tethersonde During Lake Effect Events
498497.authors: Evelyn Keefe, Cornell University, Syracuse, NY; Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and D. Kim, S. A. LaBore, L. Alcoba, A. M. Cherny, J. Bhuiyan, and K. Mohindra-Green
498497.abstract: Lake-effect snow events play a considerable role in winter weather, having caused significant societal impact, including dozens of fatalities and immense, higher-than-forecast snowfall. Lake-effect events from the Great Lakes are well-documented and researched due to their large impacts on weather in the Northeastern and northern Midwest United States. However, lake-effect is also generated by smaller lakes outside of the Great Lakes “snowbelt”, with meaningful implications for local communities. In particular, the Finger Lakes in western New York State present a nuanced challenge, as the geographical orientation of the lakes and a general lack of observations directly preceding, during, and following lake-effect events hinders both forecasting and research. In this study, we deploy a tethersonde during lake-effect events over Cayuga Lake to investigate whether or not boundary layer events affect lake-effect events. Students in Cornell GeoData, a student-run engineering project team, have designed a tethersonde to be easily used to profile the boundary layer. In the past, we have launched our tethersonde to capture the boundary layer profile predating severe weather or general rain events. However, to validate the data that we collect to collect meaningful boundary layer data for lake effect snow, we plan to validate our instrument with a National Weather Service radiosonde. After these tests, we will deploy our tethersonde during lake-effect events on the shores of Cayuga Lake, providing real-time, continuous data that will be available for future use, including assimilation into a local lake-effect model. This instrument can be used in conjunction with other sensors deployed by CU GeoData, which has developed additional sensors to deepen our understanding of our local microclimate. By gathering lake-effect data and pioneering local field campaigns, the tethersonde uniquely allows us to conduct research and mentor future scientists simultaneously. Subsequent research should expand the network of CU GeoData sensors around Cayuga Lake to continue building towards the eventual goal of reliable regional forecasting of lake-effect snow.

498498.title: Evaluating C-Band Radar for Hail-Warning Applications Through Paired S-Band Comparisons
498498.authors: Silas Sutherland Jenkins, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; University at Albany - State University of New York, Albany, NY
498498.abstract: Operational hail-warning guidance in the United States is largely based on S-band WSR-88D radar observations, but many regions have limited low-level S-band coverage. Local C-band radars can help supplement in some of these coverage gaps, but their observations cannot be interpreted using the same thresholds and assumptions developed for S-band radar. Differences in scattering behavior, attenuation, temporal sampling, and radar beam geometry may cause hail-producing storms to appear differently across different radar bands. This project investigates how C-band radar-derived hail signatures compare with paired S-band observations near hail reports, with an initial focus on 2025 Colorado hail cases. SPC hail reports were paired with nearby CSU-CHIVO (Fort Collins, CO) C-band observations and KCYS (Cheyenne, WY) or KFTG (Denver, CO) S-band observations. Cases were selected for analysis when both C-band and S-band radars sampled the storm at nearly the same time, within an acceptable range, and at similar beam heights. Common dual-polarization variables were compared within report-centered storm windows, and statistics were sampled to evaluate differences between these simultaneous C-band and S-band observations. Initial analysis suggests that paired C-band and S-band observations often show significant differences near the same hail reports. C-band reflectivity is often lower than paired S-band reflectivity, indicating that S-band warning thresholds cannot be directly transferred to C-band observations. If consistent differences between C-band and S-band radar signatures can be identified, C-band-specific thresholds for hail warning applications may be developed. This requires understanding how reflectivity and dual-polarization variables vary between radar bands near the same hail-producing storms. Early results indicate that radar range and beam-height difference are important factors that impact these differences. Ongoing work will expand the sample of paired hail cases across the country and further evaluate how radar geometry, scan timing, and attenuation correction algorithms influence the translation of S-band operational hail-warning guidance into equivalent C-band warning guidance.

498501.title: Goucher Outreach Program for Health and Environmental Research (GOPHER)
498501.authors: Tamara Chikuta, Goucher College, Towson, MD; and J. Lawton, S. Kasparek, T. Narock, A. Houser, and R. Sarma
498501.abstract: In Baltimore, Maryland, historical disinvestment has left predominantly Black neighborhoods systematically vulnerable to compound environmental and health crises. Baltimore’s historic redlined boundaries created a stark pattern of physical segregation known colloquially as the “Black Butterfly,” whereby predominantly Black neighborhoods fan out into the east and west, divided by the predominantly White neighborhoods between them (Brown 2022). The Black Butterfly is plagued by environmental issues including urban heat islands (UHIs), a phenomenon where the presence of large buildings, roads, and lack of green spaces concentrate heat and radiate it into the air. UHIs are known to exacerbate health issues such as asthma and heat stroke. In Baltimore, recent studies have demonstrated elevated risk of heat-related asthma exacerbations in the most socially vulnerable neighborhoods (Corpuz 2026). Addressing these disparities requires actionable, community-centered interventions supported by robust neighborhood-level data. An interdisciplinary team from Goucher College spanning data science, public health, and policy analysis is partnering with local researchers and stakeholders to expand support for environmental equity across the city. Our team will leverage machine learning for advanced environmental forecasting and uncertainty quantification, data-based public policy recommendations, community outreach and engagement, and new educational opportunities in Goucher classrooms. The Baltimore Community Weather Network (BCWN) is an existing network of community-based weather instruments that collect and stream publicly available weather data throughout Baltimore City (Waugh et al., 2026). This network was established to fill the gap in measuring neighborhood-level urban weather variability and promote community engagement in mitigation strategies. We are collaborating with the BCWN, focusing on leveraging hyper-local weather data to accurately forecast UHIs and other climatic signatures with public health relevance. We are also working to identify new community partners to expand the partnership and fill important microclimate data gaps in the BCWN with new weather stations. Each weather station records temperature, humidity, and wind speed, transmitting data to a central BCWN repository. Data collected from the new and existing stations will be combined with publicly available NASA data to train machine learning models that automatically identify neighborhood-scale UHIs and predict areas where they may arise. These results will be useful for informing specific policy recommendations to ensure that the proper preventative measures are being taken by communities to reduce UHI-related health issues. The confluence of climate, technology, equity, health, and policy appears in many other contexts, both locally and globally. For example, conversations with residents in Baltimore City have revealed concerns about the sparse mature tree canopies and housing conditions that trap excess heat indoors. Baltimore has also been affected by recent air quality concerns due to the Canadian wildfires, which could be mitigated with early detection and improved policy. Additionally, vector-borne infectious diseases such as Lyme, West Nile virus, and malaria are increasing in incidence and geographical range in the United States, in no small part due to changing climate and insufficient data-driven surveillance to match. This project enables Goucher faculty, students, staff, and community partners to integrate multiple disciplines and advance environmental justice and public health for Baltimore’s marginalized communities. Our research specifically addresses the data gap between Baltimore’s existing weather surveillance network and the areas burdened by historic disinvestment, motivated by the belief that closing data gaps can help close equity gaps. This work will produce data that will be directly usable by students, community organizations, researchers, and government officials. In this presentation, we will discuss our progress from our first community engagement event with a partner elementary school, preliminary machine learning pipelines, plans for incorporating additional climate outcomes and community health data, and a review of the relevant local policy landscape. 498502.title: Classification and Climatology of Extreme Rainfall Regimes in the Ohio River Basin
498502.authors: Joycelyn Adjekum, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and X. Fan
498502.abstract: Extreme rainfall is a major contributor to flooding and other hydrologic hazards across the Ohio River Basin. Understanding how these events vary in their spatial organization, frequency, and duration is important for characterizing regional extreme rainfall and its associated hydrologic impacts. This study develops an event-based classification and climatology of extreme rainfall across the Ohio River Basin using daily 4-km PRISM precipitation data from 1981–2025. Extreme rainfall events were identified using a Peak-Associated Region (PAR) approach, which represents precipitation as spatially coherent storm objects and links precipitation areas across consecutive days to reconstruct multi-day events. Storm-total precipitation was calculated over the study period of each event and normalized by the basin-wide precipitation total to emphasize spatial rainfall patterns independent of overall event magnitude. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Ward’s hierarchical clustering was then applied to the normalized storm-total precipitation fields to objectively classify recurring spatial rainfall regimes across the basin. The climatological characteristics of the identified regimes were subsequently evaluated based on their frequency, seasonality, and duration over the 1981–2025 period. The analysis identified 521 independent extreme rainfall events across the Ohio River Basin. Of these, 418 were one-day events, while the remaining events persisted for two to four days, demonstrating that short-duration events dominate the basin’s extreme rainfall climatology while multi-day events remain an important component. Classification of the storm-total precipitation fields further distinguished recurring rainfall regimes based on differences in the spatial distribution of extreme rainfall across the basin. The climatological characteristics of these regimes provide an objective framework for understanding the spatial and temporal variability of extreme rainfall in the Ohio River Basin and for identifying recurring patterns relevant to regional flood risk.

498504.title: Reanalyzing the Charles City Tornado Family of May 15, 1968
498504.authors: Adler T Hanson, Iowa State University, West Union, IA
498504.abstract: On the afternoon and evening of May 15, 1968, a widespread outbreak of tornadoes impacted portions of the Midwest and South. The most destructive tornado of the event hit the town of Charles City, IA shortly before 5:00 PM CDT. The tornado destroyed several blocks in a north-to-south path through the heart of the community, killing 13 people in the process. According to Storm Data’s current record of the event, the tornado originated in northeastern Franklin County and progressed over 60 miles before dissipating just south of the Minnesota border in Howard County. However, both Storm Data and tornado researcher Thomas P. Grazulis indicate in their accounts that this tornado was actually a tornado family. Recently, groups and individuals have shown that the ease of access to historical and local records through the internet makes it possible to revisit past events and reveal new details in the process. Newspaper accounts from the days following the tornadoes provide a farm-by-farm account of those who were impacted. Using land ownership records from the affected counties, names of those who suffered damage can be located. By connecting these damage reports, a new picture of the path of destruction emerges. After this, photographic and written evidence allows for precise plotting of individual damage indicators in line with the original Fujita scale. As a result, it can be determined that as many as five tornadoes progressed across Butler, Floyd, and Howard Counties that evening. Of the four new identified tornadoes, two of these achieved F1 intensity, one achieved F2 intensity, and the final tornado of the family produced damage up to F4 intensity. Evidence shows that the original rating of F5 is still appropriate for the tornado that impacted Charles City. Going forward, thanks to the help of NWS La Crosse, efforts are being made to amend the record of May 15, 1968 to reflect a more accurate picture of the tornadoes that occurred that day. Further analysis of the F5 that hit the town of Oelwein, IA at roughly the same time will be pursued in the near future as well.

498505.title: Where Lightning Strikes: Terrain-Based Lightning Climatology During the North American Monsoon
498505.authors: Annicka Joy Hennigan, Student Chapter of the American Meteorological Society at MSU Denver (SCAMS), Denver, CO; and J. D. Horel
498505.abstract: Mountain convective weather can be unpredictable, making outdoor recreation vulnerable to unexpected lightning activity. This is exacerbated within the western United States, where limited radar coverage and inconsistent cell service reduce situational awareness during rapidly evolving storms. This study examines how lightning occurrences vary across landforms within the intermountain southwest, intending to identify terrain types with elevated lightning hazard. Using data from June through September during 2021-2026, corresponding with the North American Monsoon season, a terrain-based climatology can characterize spatial patterns of lightning strike density and how it evolves during seasonal change. Connecting lightning frequency to topographic features can highlight which mountain environments within the Southwestern United States experience the greatest lightning exposure and provide increased hazard awareness.

498506.title: Sensitivity of Shallow-to-Deep Convective Transitions over the Amazon to Lower- and Free-Tropospheric Humidity: A WRF Large-Eddy Simulation Study
498506.authors: Chetan Gurung, University of Maryland Baltimore County, Arbutus, MD; and X. Li, H. B. Gomes, and H. M. Barbosa
498506.abstract: Convective clouds play an important role in tropical weather and climate through the vertical redistribution of heat, moisture, and momentum. However, the shallow-to-deep (STD) convective transition remains challenging to represent in numerical models, where convective parameterizations may not fully capture the gradual evolution from shallow to deep convection. Over the Amazon, where the STD transition is an important component of the diurnal convective cycle, previous observational and modeling studies have emphasized different parts of the atmospheric moisture profile, including lower- and free-tropospheric humidity, as being important for convective development. Observational limitations in space and time, together with the use of idealized atmospheric environments in some previous modeling studies, make it difficult to isolate the relative influence of moisture at different vertical levels. This study uses real-case WRF-ARW large-eddy simulations (LES) to examine the sensitivity of the STD transition to changes in the vertical humidity profile. Starting from a baseline simulation, individual STD days are identified, and lower- and free-tropospheric humidity are independently scaled by factors of 0.8–1.1, within saturation limits, before the model is restarted for a 24-hour simulation. Composites of the perturbed simulations are then compared with the baseline. Drying the lower troposphere reduces boundary-layer relative humidity, equivalent potential temperature, and moist static energy while increasing their vertical gradients, producing conditions that are progressively less favorable for convective deepening. Object-based cloud-tracking diagnostics also show decreases in cloud frequency and cloud size as lower-tropospheric moisture is reduced. In comparison, free-tropospheric humidity perturbations produce smaller changes in convective development. These results suggest that locally generated shallow-to-deep convection over the Amazon is more sensitive to pre-convective lower-tropospheric humidity than to free-tropospheric humidity, highlighting the importance of the vertical distribution of moisture in the development of precipitating deep convection.

498508.title: From Mesoscale Weather to Turbulence above a Hilly Forested Area using Large Eddy Simulations: A Triple Decomposition Approach
498508.authors: Joran Dartevelle, von Kãrmãn Institute for fluid dynamics (VKI), 1640 Sint-Genesius-Rode, Belgium; BioDynE, University of Liege, Gembloux, Belgium; and S. Stipa, F. Lebeau, and W. Munters
498508.abstract: Eddy covariance (EC) is the most commonly used method for measuring gas and energy exchanges between the Earth’s ecosystems and the atmosphere. However, the estimated fluxes are based on assumptions of stationarity and horizontal homogeneity (Foken, 2008), which are generally called into question at night and over inhomogeneous terrain geometry (Aubinet, 2008). Although these monitoring stations are well-equipped, a significant portion of the nighttime data collected is discarded due to low-level, intermittent turbulence, drainage flows, low-level jets (LLJs), and Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities (KHIs) at the top of the stable boundary layer (SBL). The generated sub-mesoscale motions and internal gravity waves cannot be distinguished from turbulent transport using simple Reynolds decomposition and averaging, and they violate the EC assumptions. At the Integrated Carbon Observation System (ICOS) eddy covariance site in Vielsalm (a mixed forest in the Belgian Ardennes), the energy balance closure is comparable to or slightly greater than that of a similar canopy ecosystem. However, nighttime periods are systematically excluded from valid data. This motivates a reassessment grounded in fundamental principles and based on large eddy simulation (LES) of how mesoscale forcings, wave motions and turbulence coexist and interact above and within a forest canopy under stable stratification conditions. It also considers how their combined effects distort estimates of fluxes measured by the tower. We present a modeling framework based on a nested, unidirectional CERRA to Weather Research and Forcasting (WRF) model to FastEddy pipeline, focusing on nighttime periods over Vielsalm (Fig. 1a). The CERRA reanalysis initializes and laterally forces a two-domain WRF configuration (mesh sizes ranging from 3 km to 1 km, consistently using the MYNN boundary layer scheme to avoid conflicts with the innermost gray-zone domain). This domain drives FastEddy v5.0.0 (Sauer and Muñoz-Esparza, 2020), a GPU-native LES, running on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell workstation (96 GB of VRAM) at a horizontal resolution of 5.5 m over a domain of approximately 9 × 9 km² with a cubically stretched vertical grid (surface spacing ≈ 4 m). This grid spacing allows for the resolution of the upper stable boundary layer (SBL) depth from 60 to 110 m and the leading edge of the overlying LLJ. The mixed coniferous and deciduous canopy (25-30 m) is modeled using FastEddy’s two-equation canopy drag closure model (Shaw and Schumann 1992; Shaw and Patton 2003), and the base-state stability profile is anchored to a representative sounding from Vielsalm rather than to idealized default values. Two-hour integrations (one hour of setup using the time-varying cellular perturbation method, one hour of analysis) are designed to capture the formation and dissipation of KHI waves at the inversion layer, as well as the underlying turbulence regime of the canopy. The central scientific contribution is a triple decomposition designed specifically for LES fields that are themselves forced by a time-varying numerical weather prediction (NWP) boundary state, a configuration in which the classical Reynolds decomposition is not well-posed: the non-stationary mesoscale trend injected through the boundaries contaminates any fixed-window averaging operator. We decompose each simulated state variable into (i) a mesoscale component extracted as the coarsest-scale approximation of a discrete wavelet transform (DWT) using the Daubechies 4 wavelet family, removing the non-stationary trend without imposing a fixed averaging time; (ii) a submesoscale/wave component obtained from a joint Hilbert Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (HPOD) of the DWT residuals with the three components of the velocity and the potential temperature, exploiting phase coherence across velocity and scalar fields to isolate coherent wave structures like KHI billows and gravity waves; and (iii) a residual turbulent component (Fig. 1b). We establish the orthogonality properties linking the three subspaces analytically, so that variance and flux budgets computed from the decomposition remain exactly conservative. The LES is validated against a flux tower dataset located at the center of the domain, which revealed the same shear layer instability billows in the data in terms of reduced (dimensionless) frequency. A slight difference in the average velocity causes a subtle difference in frequency between the LES and the data. Submesoscale structures are also compared against the classic theoretical model of the Taylor-Goldstein equation. The roles of each component (mesoscale, submesoscale and turbulence) are examined in terms of turbulent fluxes and analysed in relation to the eddy covariance methodology, in order to gain insight and improve it. Additionally, we demonstrate the presence of streamwise vortices caused by the shear layer and topography. These result in significant spatial variability in the surface flow around the tower in the spanwise direction, which could be related to Görtler instabilities. In conclusion, we successfully produced a high-resolution simulation of the wind flow in and above a canopy over complex terrain in a real setting, using a nested approach with the Cell Perturbation Method. This enables us to present a triple decomposition, which separates the mesoscale contribution from the submesoscale and the turbulence. This data-driven decomposition, based on the HPOD, facilitates examination of transport at and around the tower location and identification of instability structures. References 1. Aubinet, M., 2008. 498510.title: Assessing the Vulnerability of Indonesian Airports to Extreme Weather Events
498510.authors: Mochammad Donny Anggoro, Newcastle University, newcastle upon tyne, United kingdom
498510.abstract: Indonesia’s archipelagic geography, comprising approximately 17,000 islands and dominated by a maritime environment, has led to a growing reliance on air transportation as the population continues to expand. In the context of climate change, which is intensifying the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, increased awareness is required among aviation stakeholders to maintain safe, efficient, and reliable air traffic operations. This study assesses the vulnerability of Indonesian airports to extreme weather events using METAR observations from 76 airports across Indonesia during the period 2015–2024. The analysis first examines the frequency of extreme weather events, followed by an assessment of their seasonal and diurnal climatological characteristics. The results show that strong wind events occur most frequently at El Tari Airport (WATT), low-visibility events at Kualanamu International Airport (WIMM), heavy rainfall events at I Gusti Ngurah Rai International Airport (WADD), and thunderstorm events at Soekarno–Hatta International Airport (WIII). Diurnally, strong winds, heavy rainfall, and thunderstorm events predominantly occur during daytime hours (12:00–18:00 local time), while low-visibility events are most frequent during the early morning period (01:00–07:00 local time). Seasonally, strong wind events peak during June–July–August (JJA), low-visibility events during September–October–November (SON), heavy rainfall and/or strong wind events during December–January–February (DJF), and thunderstorm activity during March–April–May (MAM).

498514.title: Evaluating Environmental Conditions in Manhattan's Subway Stations for Climate-Resilient Transit Planning
498514.authors: Jason Hutchinson, NSF, Yonkers, NY; and A. R. Bah, H. Norouzi, and R. Blake
498514.abstract: Subway stations in New York City create unique underground environments influenced by limited airflow, train activity, and depth below street level. These factors significantly impact heat and air quality, often diverging from surface conditions. Heat waves and other external factors exacerbate these conditions, pushing extreme temperatures into these enclosed spaces. Despite growing concerns about climate-driven heat stress, little research directly compares underground and street-level conditions across multiple NYC subway stations, leaving a gap in understanding how these environments respond to worsening surface conditions. This project addresses this gap by tracking key indicators such as air temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide (CO₂), formaldehyde (HCHO), and particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10) on subway platforms. These measurements provide insights into the heat, air quality, and thermodynamics of underground stations. By collecting data across various stations, this project aims to assist policymakers in comprehending environmental conditions that can inform the design of new stations and improvements to ventilation and cooling in existing ones.

498516.title: Planetary Boundary Layer Characteristics During Urban Heat Waves in the Washington, D.C.-Baltimore Area
498516.authors: Justin Fleming, Howard University, Washington, DC
498516.abstract: Extreme heat events are the deadliest weather-related hazard in the United States and are projected to increase in frequency, intensity, and duration. Associated impacts include dehydration, heat cramps, heat exhaustion, heat stroke, and increased cardiovascular stress, particularly in densely urbanized environments. This research focuses on the Washington DC I-95 urban corridor, a region lacking detailed comparative heat wave analysis. The study has two primary objectives: first, to compare Heat Index (HI) and surface temperature as metrics for characterizing heatwave events, and second, to identify the dominant synoptic-scale patterns associated with these events. Building on the framework of Smith et al., who compiled sixteen heatwave indices (HI01-HI16) ranging from consecutive days above the 90th percentile of mean temperature to National Weather Service Heat Index thresholds exceeding 90°F, this study defines heat waves as three or more consecutive days exceeding the 90th, 95th, and 97th percentile thresholds. Using daily maximum temperature data from four weather stations (NAK, ADW, BWI, DMH) between 1950 and 2025, results show that while Downtown Baltimore (DMH) exhibits the highest absolute summer temperatures, stations at BWI and ADW experience more frequent and intense threshold exceedance streaks, indicating that higher background temperatures do not necessarily correspond to greater persistence of extreme heat events. Furthermore, calculated Heat Index values are consistently higher than surface temperatures, with differences ranging from +5.2°F to +8°F at the 97th percentile, highlighting how elevated urban percentile thresholds may underestimate the physiological burden of extreme heat and reinforcing the importance of incorporating human-centered heat metrics into urban heat analyses. Next steps include using NARR data to analyze the synoptic conditions driving these heat events and determining whether HI more effectively captures vulnerability across specific demographics and urban neighborhoods in the region.

498520.title: Examining Low-level Saharan Dust over the Open Atlantic
498520.authors: Madison Anne Turner, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and S. W. Freeman, T. A. Gobble, K. Britton, N. M. Falk, C. A. Neumaier, M. Nieto-Caballero, R. J. Perkins, S. C. van den Heever, R. Zhou, and L. D. Grant
498520.abstract: The Saharan Air Layer (SAL) remains largely unobserved within the lower marine boundary layer (MBL) despite its impact on Earth’s radiative balance, severe weather, and cloud formation. During the summer of 2025, the Relating Atlantic Marine Convection, Ice Nuclei and Cold pools (RAM-CINC) team collected thermodynamic and cold pool data in the Atlantic Ocean MBL using small multirotor drones. Additional measurements included aerosol concentrations and size distributions, aerosol filter samples, and surface microlayer water and rainwater samples for analysis of ice-nucleating particles. During the campaign, two Saharan dust events were observed on July 8th and July 14th, 2025, providing an opportunity to measure the thermodynamic impact of the SAL on the lower MBL. The drones measured thermodynamic changes in the lower MBL during SAL days, compared to days surrounding SAL events. Average temperatures increased by approximately 3 K compared to the preceding day and the days following each dust event, suggesting that a combination of the radiative properties of SAL dust and the strong inversion at the top of the boundary layer associated with SAL contributed to warming in the lower MBL. HYSPLIT back-trajectories indicated that Saharan dust was transported downward from the free troposphere to within 250 m of the ocean surface during the measurement period. Water vapor mixing ratios showed a similar trend to temperature, increasing on both July 8th and July 14th compared to the surrounding days. These observations suggest that the SAL significantly changes the thermodynamics of the lower MBL.

498524.title: Creating C++ Code to Efficiently Compute Sounding-Derived Parameters
498524.authors: Daniel S Schwab, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN; and D. R. Chavas, D. T. Dawson II, J. M. Peters, and N. A. Goldacker
498524.abstract: Common packages for analyzing atmospheric soundings like MetPy, SHARPpy, and SounderPy, primarily use Python for non-vectorizable calculations. As a result, these packages have significant runtimes when analyzing large numbers of soundings, especially when computing common variables like CAPE, which cannot be vectorized. One solution to this is to write these algorithms in more computationally efficient languages like C++. The time benefit from using C++ instead of Python makes computation on large datasets more feasible, and also allows for more precise but computationally intensive formulas to be used (for example, the use of generalized lapse rate formulas in the CAPE calculation), as well as additional variables, such as ECAPE. This poster will compare existing Python packages to entirely C++ code, and C++ code called via Python bindings, using precise benchmarks for quantities such as runtime and memory usage. Additionally, challenges encountered with writing the C++ code, as well as code accessibility and integration into existing Python code, will also be covered.

498528.title: Detecting Atmospheric Chemical Composition and Boundary Layer Relationship: Utilizing Aircraft Measurements During Summer 2026 Sporting Events
498528.authors: Ivan Martinez Sloan, NCAS, Brandywine, MD
498528.abstract: With the planetary boundary layer being the lowermost layer of the atmosphere where most mixing and containment is, the chemicals we release may largely be contained within this layer. Certain gases such as ozone in high concentrations being so low in the atmosphere can pose a health concern in areas where it is prevalent. Understanding how the atmosphere’s structure interacts with the composition and placement of loose chemicals can help forecast, warn, or generally be aware of air quality events or concerns. The goal of this study was to examine the sources of the emissions and observe the behavior of emissions to assist decision-making processes in spreading awareness about conditions or emergencies. Our campaign studied the region across the Northeast I-95 corridor, mainly spreading from northern Virginia to Boston. Using data recorded by the instrumentation during research flights and drives in order to determine the composition of the atmosphere during the busy sports seasons of the summer (World Cup 2026 and the NBA Finals), I found that water vapor and temperature are impacted by elevated chemical (namely NOx, methane, and ethane) levels and I verified small-scale atmospheric containment of chemicals within the planetary boundary layer.

498530.title: Emulating Sub-Grid-Scale Cirrus Cloud Evolution Using Machine Learning
498530.authors: Fiona Li, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL; and J. Ko, K. K. Chandrakar, Z. Liu, J. Liu, and K. D. Lamb
498530.abstract: Cirrus clouds are thin, high‑altitude clouds made of ice crystals that cover roughly one‑third of the Earth's surface at any given time. They have a net warming effect on the climate, yet they are poorly represented in global climate models because the physical processes that govern them – such as ice crystal formation, growth, and falling – occur at scales far smaller than the models can resolve. The most accurate way to simulate these processes is with Large Eddy Simulation (LES), a high‑resolution modeling technique that resolves cloud‑scale turbulence and tracks individual "super‑droplets" (computational particles that represent many real ice crystals). However, LES is computationally expensive, making it impractical to generate enough simulations for robust climate predictions. To address this bottleneck, we built a fast, moderately accurate machine learning emulator that learns from expensive LES simulations and predicts the evolution of ice concentration in cirrus clouds. Our goal is to replace costly LES runs with a lightweight model that can be used to explore many scenarios quickly. We trained a two‑stage machine learning model using XGBoost, a tree‑based algorithm that is well‑suited for capturing non‑linear relationships. Stage 1 learns the baseline physics – ice growth, sublimation, and sedimentation – from 26 no‑wind simulations, achieving an R² of 0.855 on the validation set. Stage 2 corrects for advection (wind‑driven ice transport) using 3 with-wind simulations, boosting performance on wind scenarios to an average R² of 0.58, with a best fold of 0.71. We also used a Gaussian Mixture Model to identify 4 distinct vertical layers in the cloud (7‑11 km) based on vertical distribution and used these layer labels as a feature. To reduce data size while preserving physical signals, we aggregated the horizontal grid from 120x120 into 12×12 columns, reducing the data by 99%. The model shows moderate generalization across different microphysics setups (up to R² = 0.66), suggesting that it roughly captures robust physical relationships rather than just fitting noise. Our emulator potentially provides a fast, physics‑aware alternative to expensive LES simulations, potentially enabling better representation of cirrus clouds in climate models. This work contributes to a broader effort to use machine learning to accelerate climate science by replacing costly high‑resolution simulations with efficient emulators.

498532.title: How Does the Olentangy River Affect the Temperature and Humidity in Columbus?
498532.authors: James Cancel, The Ohio State Univ., Columbus, OH; and A. Ensign, A. Sampson, B. Zabloudil, and S. M. Quiring
498532.abstract: Major cities worldwide have been established along rivers for thousands of years. Recently, sustainable development and urban planning have recognized the climatic cooling ability and recreational opportunities of these waterways. This study investigates how the Olentangy River affects air temperature and humidity across The Ohio State University’s Columbus campus. To evaluate how the river influences the surrounding microclimate, temperature and humidity measurements will be collected at two meters above ground level (AGL) at four locations along the Olentangy riverbank. At each sampling location, measurements will be taken at varying distances from the riverbed (e.g., 5 m, 25 m, 50 m) to measure temperature and humidity. The experiment will span several days to account for variance in morning, afternoon, and evening conditions as well as variance in overarching weather conditions, including precipitation, that may impact both the microclimate and river characteristics (gage height, discharge, etc.). Analysis will account for spatial variations in land cover characteristics (i.e., albedo), atmospheric conditions, vegetation canopy, and river levels. We hypothesize that 2 m air temperature will increase, while humidity will decrease with increasing distance from the riverbank, and that the magnitude will vary depending on atmospheric conditions and the time of measurement. This analysis builds on previous research in other geographic areas by quantifying the cooling properties of the Olentangy river. These results will enable urban planners in Columbus understand the immediate microclimatic effects of urban development near the Olentangy river.

498533.title: Examining the Impacts of Surface Roughness on Tornadogenesis
498533.authors: Emma Renee Tanner, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and S. M. Quiring and J. B. Houser
498533.abstract: Approximately 1000 tornadoes impact the United States each year, resulting in substantial loss of property, life, and money. Understanding interactions between surface roughness, tornadogenesis, and thunderstorm mode is valuable for severe weather forecasting, public perception, and loss prevention. This study evaluates the impacts of surface roughness and land cover on tornadogenesis in the continental United States. This study will examine the impacts of surface roughness on the three primary storm modes: ordinary (single cell), QLCS, and supercells. Alongside surface roughness measurements, atmospheric environmental parameters including CAPE, CIN, SRH, and bulk shear will be examined. Thunderstorm development and mode will be analyzed to identify how surface roughness and environmental conditions influence tornadogenesis and to examine how these relationships vary as a function of storm mode (ordinary, QLCS and supercell). Tornadogenesis data will be extracted from the Damage Assessment Toolkit (DAT) and land cover data will be extracted from the National Landcover Database (NLCD) to determine surface roughness. Data will be collected across the continental United States from 2015-present. We anticipate that the impacts of surface roughness on tornadogenesis will vary as a function of storm mode. The results of this study will aid in improving severe weather forecasting, public perception of severe weather events, and loss prevention.

498534.title: Inclusive Climate Communications: Accessible Hurricane Tracking Maps for the Web
498534.authors: Jessica Herring, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA; and I. Vepa, I. Martincic, and B. N. Walker
498534.abstract: Climate communications (CC), broadly speaking, are defined as the depictions, representations, and dissemination of weather patterns, atmospheric conditions, and climate-related phenomena through multi-modal means, including everything from daily weather forecasts to storm tracks, to emergency weather broadcasting. Unfortunately, frequent misinterpretations of CC create a significant gap in information equity, disproportionately affecting individuals with disabilities, non-native speakers, and those with varying degrees of scientific fluency. These misunderstandings prevent people from accessing and gathering critical information needed to make high-risk, time-sensitive decisions. This project, Accessible Hurricane Tracking Maps for the Web, aims to address these challenges through secondary research, iterative design, and evaluation with diverse individuals. The work culminates in an interactive, web-based hurricane tracking map designed to prioritize accessibility and inclusivity, with the goal of making essential storm information understandable and actionable for as broad a population as possible. We evaluated a range of common climate-related information displays, including maps, graphs, charts, audio displays, broadcasting, photographs, etc., in terms of comprehension, accessibility, and the more broad criterion of “inclusivity”. Not really surprisingly, we identified considerable accessibility and inclusivity challenges. In our evaluation specifically of hurricane tracking maps, none of the maps achieved high marks on accessibility and inclusivity. Various design hurdles prevent a more universal usage of, in many cases, such vital information. To overcome such challenges, we embarked on a program of research and design to create a more accessible and inclusive hurricane tracking map, as an example of how climate communications can be rethought for a broader audience. To start, accessibility experts and accessible design literature were consulted to understand the necessary requirements for an accessible hurricane tracking map prototype. An interactive display was chosen as the prototype design, in order to leverage the ability for a customizable experience and to allow layers with varying types and levels of information to be displayed at a given time. Display layers are accessible and compatible with assistive technology, and they prioritize plain language for extended ease of use. Various features have been implemented into the tool to communicate various aspects of information related to a hurricane, including displaying: 1) the storm path, reimagined for clarity of message; 2) points of interest, including the users’ home, location, family, etc.; 3) cone of uncertainty with annotations; 4) a dynamic and progressive legend/glossary; 5) a novel “Wiki Maps” concept to elegantly provide map details via alternative text; 6) time warping and winding back the clock; 7) inclusive sensemaking explanations using AI; 8) sonification and multimodal data display; and 9) an accessible interaction framework. The Storm Path function displays the complete storm path superimposed on the area map of the location of the hurricane, including the intensity of the storm at various time points. Points of Interest allows a user to search and add specific points of reference to the map as well, like cities and addresses. The Cone of Uncertainty is also displayed, along with a plain-language definition to address the purpose of hurricane elements. The legend and glossary provide to help bridge the information gap between users and the hurricane elements for those less familiar or with a differing native language. Wiki Maps (inspired by Wikipedia) functions on this map that allows for outsourcing information; various high-level descriptions of the map add additional context and provide more visualization for specifically blind and low vision users. The Wind Back functionality allows users to visualize the storm path at various time points to see changes in the storm path. The Wind Back featured is paired with the Inclusive Sensemaking feature, which gives a plain-language description of a point-in-time of the hurricane’s path, leveraging carefully curated AI content. Sonification is also an additional modality added to the tool and provides both spoken and non-speech auditory content that can be played to display the hurricane’s path, wind speed, sea level pressure, and storm category rating. All these features can be cohesively interacted with via the Interaction Framework, consisting of a task bar that controls the layer displays and contextual information. These features have been carefully evaluated with expert users, and the results have been extremely positive. Iterations of the display have further refined various features, bringing the overall system to a polished state. We are currently collecting additional usability and accessibility data with a diverse range of users, and on a broader range of platforms, before releasing the final version for more widespread deployment. In addition to making hurricane maps accessible and inclusive, the lessons learned in this project have been applied to tornado maps, flooding maps, and other climate communications. Our hope is for these new and inclusive tools to become more commonly deployed, to ensure no one is left behind when it comes to knowing about weather and climate, and making fully-informed life-critical decisions.

498535.title: EarthCARE Hydrometeor Climatologies for Military Operations
498535.authors: Jillian Cudney, Air Force Institute of Technology, Huber Heights , OH; and M. P. King
498535.abstract: Following the successful May 2024 launch of the ESA/JAXA EarthCARE mission, synergistic retrieval algorithms that combine the Cloud Profiling Radar (CPR), Atmospheric Lidar (ATLID), Multi-Spectral Imager (MSI), and Broad-Band Radiometer (BBR) are providing new, vertically resolved measurements of clouds and aerosols. These observations enable improved characterization of hydrometeor and aerosol properties that significantly affect electromagnetic wave propagation and the aerothermal environment encountered during hypersonic flight. This study analyzes early EarthCARE data to develop climatologies of liquid water content (LWC), ice water content (IWC), and effective particle radius across altitude, latitude, and selected geographic regions, with emphasis on the statistical distributions and extreme percentiles most relevant to military operational planning.

498537.title: Visualizing and Quantifying the Differences of Instantaneous and Reconstructed Range Height Indicators with Phased Array Radar
498537.authors: Caden G Berry, Student, CIWRO, Norman, OK; and A. A. Alford and T. J. Schuur
498537.abstract: The enhanced spatiotemporal scan capabilities of Phased Array Radar (PAR) present a unique opportunity to deepen our understanding of rapidly evolving severe storm processes. In particular, nearly-instantaneous range height indicator (RHI) scans allow for vertically oriented processes to be observed without the temporal lag and storm-movement-induced spatial offset conventional radar scan patterns introduce. By leveraging the National Severe Storms Laboratory’s Advanced Technology Demonstrator (ATD) PAR, datasets from 2024-2026 are utilized to compare and quantify differences between PAR-enabled RHIs and reconstructed pseudo-RHIs available from current operational radars, the latter of which are often used as proxies for the vertical structure of storms. This presentation will display and quantify differences between instantaneous versus reconstructed RHI data interpolated to a common grid with particular attention paid to the quantitative and qualitative differences between important storm features. The analysis will highlight the expected error induced by storm motion as well as intra-radar-volume storm evolution after correction for advection.

498538.title: An Evaluation of Hurricane Helene Windblown Forest Damage Detection and Western North Carolina Eco-hydrological Impacts From Vegetation Loss
498538.authors: Liam Logan O'Donnell, NASA, Cary, NC; North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC
498538.abstract: Hurricane Helene impacted Western North Carolina as a tropical storm starting September 27, 2024 bringing record rain, flooding, and high winds, becoming one of the costliest and deadliest natural disasters in NC history. One of the most noticeable impacts was forest damage due to high winds and flooding. This project aims to improve remote sensed detection of that change using a detection algorithm employing remotely sensed estimates of vegetation health using multispectral bands from the Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) dataset to measure the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR). The algorithm incorporates Landsat 8, Landsat 9 and Sentinel-2 multispectral ensemble imaging to create a multi-year “climatology” mean for years of 2019–2024 to compare them to those of the same time periods of 2025-2026, post Helene. After validation against observations from NOAA’s Airborne Damage Assessment imagery and comparison of the USGS’ own NDVI change map for Hurricane Helene, changes in modeled field-scale evapotranspiration (ET) from NASA’s MODIS product and soil moisture (SM) estimates from the Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) mission were analyzed. Together, these datasets relate windblown forest damage with changes to the ecohydrological system of Western NC, as well as exploring long term impacts and recovery. Relative to watersheds with little to no change in vegetation loss, preliminary results show watersheds with substantial vegetation loss have substantial decrease in ET and increase in SM in the months following the hurricane. An evaluation of the disruption that Helene caused may help improve management of the Western NC mountains, to further mitigate wildfire and landslide risk, protecting the ecosystems and people that make the region so special.

498539.title: Vessel-Specific Routing Through the Northwest Passage: A Proof-of-Concept Using Satellite Sea Ice Data
498539.authors: Eric Sun, Space Science and Engineering Center, Madison, WI, Madison, WI; Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH; and Y. Liu and R. J. Dworak
498539.abstract: The retreating Arctic sea ice has prompted the consideration of the Northwest Passage, located in the Arctic, as an alternative shipping route between East Asia and Western Europe. However, the Northwest Passage presents a different challenge: navigability depends heavily on day-to-day ice conditions and the given ice class of a vessel. This work presents a proof-of-concept routing system that produces vessel-specific Northwest Passage routes from existing sea ice data and each vessel's ice class. Sea ice thickness (CryoSat-2/SMOS) is classified into WMO ice type categories and combined with sea ice concentration from AMSR2; multi-year ice cells are then corrected using NSIDC Sea Ice Age v4.1 (NSIDC-0611). These inputs are combined via the Canadian Ice Service's AIRSS ice numeral method to produce an ice-derived risk score, which is then combined with the physical distance traversed across each grid cell to compute a per-vessel, per-cell navigability cost across seven representative ice classes. A* search over this cost surface, using an extended neighborhood with a line-of-sight constraint, yields a route (or reports that none exists) for each vessel class. Because thickness-only classification fails to detect the full extent of multi-year ice, this is corrected using the U.S. National Ice Center's Arctic and Antarctic Sea Ice Charts in SIGRID-3 Format (NSIDC G10013), analyst-produced ice charts that resolve coastal-channel ice conditions that motion-tracked products cannot classify. Planned extensions include multi-day/temporal routing to account for evolving ice conditions over a transit, and vessel-draft-based depth constraints.

498540.title: An Examination of the Atmospheric Conditions associated with Lake Maracaibo, the World's Lightning Maximum
498540.authors: Michael J Otto Jr., Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL; and B. M. Muller, S. E. Strazzo, and P. Beaty
498540.abstract: In 2016, researchers using data from new satellite-borne lightning detection instruments revealed the surprising result that the world’s lightning frequency maximum occurs in a small area on the southwest side of Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela (Albrecht et al., 2016), and not in the Congo as had been previously believed. This lightning hotspot is very focused and therefore its extreme magnitude had been missed in lower resolution analyses performed by previous researchers. Interestingly it is nocturnal, with lightning most frequent at 2 am local time and in fact, corresponds to a historically documented phenomenon known for centuries as “Relampago del Catatumbo”—the Lighthouse of Catatumbo (also known in English as the Catatumbo Lightning). Lake Maracaibo is a warm tropical water body surrounded by tall mountains, and we believe it is primarily this geography that results in such a geographically concentrated maximum. In fact, advances in lightning detection technology both on the ground and in space have revealed that local nocturnal lake lightning maximums exist in other parts of the world including Tibet and over the Great Lakes of Africa. The common denominator for all these local nocturnal lightning hotspots is the presence of a relatively warm, tropical latitude lake, surrounded by tall mountains. While previous researchers have implicated the warm lake temperatures, behavior of the Caribbean and Maracaibo Nocturnal Low-Level Jets, meridional transport of Convective Available Potential Energy (CAPE), and land and mountain breeze convergence over Lake Maracaibo as drivers of the Catatumbo Lightning activity, to date there has been no comprehensive study of the mesoscale meteorological and topographical factors that would explain such a strong lightning “bulls-eye” directly over this specific location. Our study will use the 5th generation European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasting (ECMWF) reanalysis (ERA5), geostationary satellite brightness temperatures and lightning data, and numerical modeling to investigate details of the meteorological and topographical causes of this lightning frequency maximum. Results so far reveal that meteorological variables normally thought to be precursors to thunderstorm development such as CAPE, surface convergence, and moisture flux convergence, averaged for each month over a climatological period, show locally high values at the location of the lightning maximum, but not “bulls-eyes” comparable in magnitude to that of lightning flashes. In fact, there are other local maximums of equal or greater magnitude in other regional locations that are not accompanied by a coincident local maximum of lightning frequency. We conclude that these precursor variables cannot, by themselves, explain the high frequency of lightning that occurs on the southwestern flank of Lake Maracaibo. On the other hand, highly focused absolute maximums of cold clouds indicated by large magnitude minimums of average satellite brightness temperature, as well as precipitation from the ERA5 data set, corroborate that there is, in fact, a maximum frequency of thunderstorms specifically at the location of the lightning maximum. We hypothesize that this local thunderstorm and lightning hotspot is due to a confluence of triggering factors maximizing there. Our investigation will use numerical modeling to explore whether, for example, a superposition of gravity waves, or perhaps propagation or collisions of bores, triggered each night by katabatic wind flows off the ring of mountains surrounding the lake, or other factors, happen to converge most frequently at this location, creating enhanced lift, and producing this extreme lightning hotspot.

498541.title: Below the Surface: Evaluating Well Water Depth Anomalies Against SPI and SPEI Data
498541.authors: Samuel Noah Hurd, Mississippi State University, GROVE CITY, OH; Mississippi State University, Starkville, MS; and J. K. Beck and S. M. Quiring
498541.abstract: Drought is a significant climatological hazard that considerably influences environmental and human systems. Impacts of drought on groundwater resources may persist beyond the end of any given hydrological drought. Understanding these relationships is important for improving drought monitoring and identifying when drought indicators accurately represent subsurface water availability. This study evaluates groundwater variability across Ohio and its relationship with hydrological drought using the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI). Groundwater observations from monitoring wells across Ohio were evaluated from January 1st, 2003 through December 31st, 2025. Groundwater conditions were evaluated statewide, by aquifer type, region, and time, to identify spatial and temporal differences in groundwater response. The wells' standardized groundwater anomalies were then compared with SPI and SPEI across multiple accumulation timescales to determine which drought indices and timescales best represent groundwater variability. Initial results found that 3-6 month SPI and SPEI data had the highest correlation with groundwater depth anomalies. They also show that there are some regional variations. Ultimately the initial results show that decreased precipitation amounts do have a decrease in well water depth. This study can be used to better understand the impacts drought has on the groundwater supply and used to monitor the effects of drought.

498545.title: Fog-Associated Limited Visibility Hours in the United States and Canada
498545.authors: Finley Moller, Hobart and William Smith Colleges, Warwick, NY
498545.abstract: Regional atmospheric conditions and geographic features strongly influence both the frequency and location of fog across the United States and Canada. When visibility is impaired due to fog, it can cause various issues and risks for all forms of transportation. The goal of this project was to investigate the historical spatiotemporal variation of fog occurrences across the United States and Canada when horizontal visibility is at or less than 1 km. Hourly surface weather data was obtained from the National Center for Environmental Information for 127 stations, with analysis performed using IBM SPSS and ArcGIS Pro. Hourly reports of fog, regardless of the horizontal visibility, were most frequent in the Eastern region of the U.S. and Canada and least frequent along the Rocky Mountain range. When fog occurred, the Western and Rocky Mountain regions were more likely to experience visibility less than 1 km than the Eastern U.S. and Canada. The monthly spatial variation of fog with impactful visibility was found to shift from the Western U.S. in the winter to the Eastern U.S. in the summer. The lowest visibility during fog hours was found to occur at locations with low elevation or valley-like geography, such as Eugene, Oregon, Lubbock, Texas, and Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. Additional findings about the spatiotemporal variation of visibility during fog occurrences will be discussed during the conference.

498546.title: Investigating Measurement Bias Between Weighing and Tipping-Bucket Precipitation Gauges
498546.authors: Noah Harley, The Ohio State Univ., Columbus, OH; and E. Hempker, S. McCathran, J. Nye, and S. M. Quiring
498546.abstract: Precipitation measurements are vital for hydrology and water management, climate research, and model verification, and can be acquired using weighing gauges and tipping buckets. Simple to install at mesonet sites, these instruments inherently exhibit varying degrees of bias due to their different methods of data collection. Therefore, it is important to identify and quantify sources of bias to improve understanding of their measurement characteristics. Precipitation measurements will be collected at Waterman Farm on Ohio State’s campus using two types of rain gauges: an Apogee weighing gauge and three Texas Electronics tipping bucket gauges spaced evenly nearby. Data will be taken at a 5-minute temporal frequency from each rain gauge from September to November. Values from rain gauges, as well as other atmospheric variables obtained from the mesonet site over the same periods, will be compared to parse out errors and biases. It is anticipated that these comparisons will result in measurable differences in precipitation amount, with the magnitude depending on precipitation intensity and environmental conditions. The results are expected to help identify potential sources of measurement bias and determine under what conditions the two types of gauges show the greatest disagreement. This will help provide meteorologists with a better understanding of differences in precipitation measurements between two commonly used rain gauges, and potentially improve the collection of precipitation data. Accurate data will then help meteorologists with research, as well as more effectively issuing proper flood warnings to the public.

498547.title: Sensitivity of Hurricane Helene's (2024) Cloud-Top Structure to WRF Microphysics Schemes
498547.authors: Elizabeth Kline, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA; and S. E. Ringerud
498547.abstract: Hurricane Helene (2024) rapidly intensified over the Gulf of Mexico before making landfall in Florida as a Category 4 hurricane. Accurately representing rapid intensification and storm structure in numerical weather prediction models remains challenging, in part because cloud microphysical processes must be parameterized. This study evaluates the sensitivity of simulated cloud-top temperature, upper-level ice structure, outflow symmetry, and storm intensity of Hurricane Helene to the choice of microphysics scheme in the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF-ARW) model. Four commonly used microphysics schemes --Thompson, Morrison, WSM6, and Purdue-Lin -- were evaluated using otherwise consistent model configurations over a 72-hour simulation encompassing Helene’s rapid intensification and landfall. Model output was analyzed for minimum sea-level pressure, maximum 10-m wind speed, cloud-top temperature, upper-level ice hydrometeor structure, and upper-level outflow, with structural characteristics compared against available observations. All four simulations reproduced Helene’s rapid intensification, while differences in simulated minimum sea-level pressure and maximum wind speed remained relatively small among the schemes. Morrison produced the lowest minimum sea-level pressure, while Thompson produced the strongest maximum 10-m wind speed. Larger differences emerged in the simulated cloud structure. Morrison generated the largest area of very cold cloud tops, while Thompson produced a more compact area of cold cloud near the storm center. WSM6 and Purdue-Lin generally produced intermediate cloud-top structures. The representation of upper-level ice also differed among the four schemes, with Morrison, WSM6, and Purdue-Lin producing broader regions of frozen hydrometeors than Thompson, particularly within the eyewall and surrounding cloud shield. All simulations reproduced Helene’s anticyclonic upper-level outflow; however, differences were apparent in the strength and organization of the outflow. Among the evaluated simulations, WSM6 most closely resembled the observed upper-level outflow pattern. These results demonstrate that although the four microphysics schemes produced relatively similar simulations of Helene’s bulk storm intensity, their representations of cloud-top temperature, upper-level ice structure, and outflow exhibited greater variability. The results suggest that microphysics parameterization may have a stronger influence on the simulated internal and upper-level structure of a tropical cyclone than is apparent from intensity metrics alone. This case study highlights the importance of evaluating structural characteristics, in addition to traditional intensity metrics, when assessing microphysics sensitivity in tropical cyclone simulations.

498548.title: Evaluating Satellite-Derived δD as an Indicator of Moisture Source and Drought
498548.authors: Daniel He, University of Michigan, East Lansing, MI; and A. Raudzens Bailey and K. B. Heyblom
498548.abstract: Water isotope ratios act as a natural indicator of moisture origin and transport due to their sensitivity to evaporation, precipitation, and atmospheric mixing. Moisture evapotranspired from the land surface has a distinct isotopic signature compared to moisture evaporated from oceans. Thus, we expect that the heavy-to-light isotope ratio of hydrogen (δD), observable from space, should help us identify periods of enhanced moisture loss from the land resulting in or intensifying drought. Using data from the NASA Atmospheric Infrared Sounder (AIRS) record, we examine variations in atmospheric δD and water vapor concentrations (H2O) for the period of 2003 to 2019.
