We restrict the analysis to the growing season (April to October), to isolate time periods when vegetation over the contiguous US is most active, and average the data in two-week intervals. We further limit our scope to two climatologically distinct regions: the American Southeast and Southwest, characterized generally by wet and dry conditions respectively. Our analysis reveals consistent but distinct patterns in how water vapor isotope ratios vary with growing season in these regions. Specifically, we find that δD and H2O variability are strongly correlated in the Southeast, indicating that variations in moisture are primarily driven by thermodynamic processes. Conversely, independence of δD variability from H2O variability in the Southwest implies that moisture variations there are primarily associated with changes in moisture source. As a first step in evaluating the potential of isotopic data to enhance drought prediction, we correlate δD variability with various drought indicators and related metrics, such as the Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI), Evaporative Demand Drought Index (EDDI), and water balance (evaporation minus precipitation) from reanalysis. Our first results with PDSI show that there may be linkages between years of high δD and relatively wet growing seasons in the Southeast. However, given PDSI’s relatively low bi-weekly variability compared to δD, we are unable to identify any strong correlation between PDSI and subseasonal variations in isotopic data, indicating that moisture sources may vary on shorter timescales than longer-term drying tendencies. Our work provides an initial framework for testing connections between moisture-source variability and land drying, with broader implications for understanding the mechanisms behind drought.

498550.title: Chemical Variability Across Convective Storm Types: Investigating Transport Dynamics in the U.S. Midwest
498550.authors: Lauren Elizabeth Grose, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN; and N. Rose, C. B. Swenson, and M. Vermeuel
498550.abstract: Convective storms can rapidly redistribute trace gases through vertical transport and mixing while also altering atmospheric composition through storm-related chemical processes, such as lightning production of nitrogen oxides. Previous airborne and ground-based studies have documented localized changes in atmospheric composition associated with convection, but less is known about how near-surface chemistry varies with specific convective modes and structural dynamics. Examining these differences may improve our understanding of the interactions between convective dynamics, atmospheric transport, and regional air quality. In this study, we use a targeted dataset of 10 convective storm days observed in West Lafayette, Indiana, combining near-surface trace gas observations with archived radar data to examine how chemical profiles vary across distinct convective categories: quasi-linear convective systems, multicell clusters, and single-cell events. To isolate active convective periods, we apply a standardized 40 dBZ reflectivity threshold across the observational dataset. We evaluate changes in volatile organic compound and carbon dioxide concentrations before, during, and following storm passage and compare the magnitude and timing of these perturbations among storm types. We hypothesize that storm size and organizational structure are associated with trace gas fluctuations, with larger and more organized events driving more pronounced variations. Ultimately, this study will help characterize the relationship between convective storm dynamics and near-surface trace gas variability.

498551.title: Burning Deeper: Multi-Decadal Trends in Alaska's Seasonal Mean and Peak Drought Code
498551.authors: Benjamin Bown, University of Alaska - Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; IARC, Fairbanks, AK; and R. Lader
498551.abstract: High-latitude climate warming is fundamentally altering fire regimes across sub-Arctic and Arctic ecosystems. Across northern Canada and Alaska, escalating fire weather severity and severe organic soil drying are pushing wildland fires into ecosystems and sub-Arctic zones that have historically burned infrequently. During the fire season in Alaska (April 1 - Sept 30), widespread solar noon temperature increases (+0.23 to +0.33°C per decade from 1959–2025) and reduced snow cover duration are accelerating seasonal drying of deep organic soils, despite limited changes in precipitation To quantify these shifts, this study evaluates multi-decadal trends in both seasonal mean and seasonal maximum Drought Code (DC) across 5 Alaska Predictive Service Area (PSA) groups. The Drought Code, a component of the Canadian Forest Fire Danger Rating System (CFFDRS), represents moisture conditions in deep organic fuels, providing a useful indicator of the fuel conditions underlying persistent northern wildfires. Using historical gridded climate baselines, we analyze spatial and seasonal trends in DC, surface temperature, and precipitation. Results reveal statistically significant increases in Drought Code (1959–2025), where regional mean trends were +1.92 DC per decade in the Eastern Boreal region and +1.19 in the South Central region, while localized maximum trends reached up to +2.56 and +3.77 DC per decade, respectively—demonstrating that peak trends most relevant for fire management substantially exceed regional averages. Seasonal analysis highlights pronounced early-to-mid-summer soil drying. Regional case studies—including the 2004 Taylor Complex in the Interior, the 2007 Anaktuvuk River Fire on the North Slope, and the 2014 Funny River Fire in Southcentral—illustrate how Drought Code anomalies corresponded with observed fire activity, burn severity, and late-season persistence. These elevating DC trends carry cascading ecological and operational impacts. Severe organic layer drying increases vulnerability to lightning ignitions, promotes deep smoldering combustion, and strips the protective soil organic layer, exposing underlying permafrost to accelerated thaw. Furthermore, altered burn severities are triggering non-traditional vegetation trajectories, such as shrubification and repeat-fire grassification. By contextualizing climatological DC shifts with land-atmosphere interactions and operational danger rating thresholds, this analysis translates long-term climate information into an operationally relevant fire-danger metric, providing critical decision support for wildland fire management, pre-suppression resource allocation, and carbon cycle monitoring across changing northern landscapes.

498552.title: Quantifying the Impact of Forest Canopy on the Surface Energy Balance
498552.authors: Joshua Petschke, The Ohio State Univ., Columbus, OH; and A. Rose, J. Westfall, A. Yang, and S. M. Quiring
498552.abstract: Forest cover has a significant impact on the local microclimate. This varies as a function of the density, height and type of tree cover. This study examines variations in the surface energy balance and the Bowen Ratio at three stations with differing amounts of forest cover at Waterman Farm on the west side of the Ohio State University campus. These stations will be placed ten meters into the forested area, on the border between the trees and clearing, and thirty meters into the clearing. At each station, we will situate a net ratiometer or pyranometer, soil heat flux plates, CS616 water reflectometers, and ClimaVUE 50s. With this set of instruments, we can measure net radiation, ground heat flux, and sensible and latent heat fluxes. We expect the Bowen Ratio to increase with distance from the trees, as the area becomes more exposed to the sun. Therefore, we expect there to be less moisture in direct sunlight as opposed to the shade of the trees. There is also a possibility of insolation changing slightly with distance. By calculating the surface energy balance between a shaded, forested area and a sunny, clear area, as well as the transition point, we can quantify the effect of forest canopy on the local energy budget. On a larger scale, the effect of these elements may be better understood in the context of how land cover influences the microclimate.

498555.title: Influence of Land Surface and Crop Type on Atmospheric Conditions During the Summer-to-Winter Transition
498555.authors: Luciano Canestraro, The Ohio State Univ., Columbus, OH; and G. Knipe, C. Portier, L. Timpone, and S. M. Quiring
498555.abstract: Agricultural land surfaces can influence near-surface atmospheric and soil conditions through differences in vegetation, soil, and surface properties; however, how these conditions vary among crop and surface types as the growing season transitions to winter is not fully understood locally. An additional factor is how the developing super El Niño could indirectly affect crop foliage duration this season. Understanding these differences can improve knowledge of crop-atmosphere interactions and how changing environmental conditions influence agricultural systems. Field measurements will be collected at Waterman Farms from September 15 through November 15 to examine near-surface atmospheric and soil condition variations across different crop and surface types. Measurements will include soil and surface temperature, 2 m air temperature, 2 m relative humidity, soil moisture, and net radiation, with observations collected daily. Sampling locations will include available agricultural surfaces such as corn, soybeans, grass, and bare soil. Potential confounding factors, including location, soil type, irrigation, and fertilization, will be considered when comparing surface types. We expect measurable differences in temperature, moisture, radiation, and other atmospheric variables among crop and surface types. As vegetation dies off and fields are harvested, we hypothesize that these differences will diminish as the surfaces become more similar in moisture and structure. This convergence would suggest that vegetation state plays an important role in controlling local microclimatic conditions. This project will improve understanding of how vegetation and surface characteristics influence agricultural microclimates during the summer-to-winter transition. The findings may provide a foundation for future research on agricultural responses to seasonal and climate variability.

498556.title: Increasing Accuracy of Open-Access AI/ML Forecasting Models by Leveraging a Student-Run Sensor Network
498556.authors: Orion Hoch, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and A. Aravind, L. Metlitsky, E. Keefe, and D. Kim
498556.abstract: Recent advancements in AI and Machine Learning weather models have not only improved accuracy but have reduced computational requirements, putting modeling in the hands of individuals and small groups with access to the resources equivalent of a high-end personal computer. NVIDIA's Earth2Studio suite of models, and in particular StormCast, allow for an ensemble of regional and convection-allowing models with custom assimilation of surface observations. In this project, members of Cornell University's GeoData Student Project Team implemented a 3-hourly, multi-member ensemble of StomCast for the Central New York region. This ensemble is initialized from the NOAA High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) analysis plus data from a network of local automated weather stations, including stations assembled, deployed, and maintained by GeoData. In addition to real-time forecasting, hindcasts for verification against significant past weather events in the Ithaca, NY region were conducted, including difficult-to-forecast events such as severe thunderstorm outbreaks and lake-effect snow events. Notably, the entire system of hardware and automated sensors, model fine-tuning, forecast generation, data formatting, model visualization, and verification was carried out autonomously by a small group of undergraduate students. Future work includes incorporating further observations and producing a higher-resolution downscaled model to further improve forecast accuracy. This project highlights the potential for democratized weather forecasting in the AI/ML age, including the potential for student organizations to operate their own stack of forecasting technology from raw observations to model output.

498557.title: Probabilistic Near-Storm Inhibition and Spatial Distribution of Tropical Cyclogenesis
498557.authors: Md Musfike Meraz, University of Delaware, Newark, DE; and S. Wang and H. Murakami
498557.abstract: Tropical cyclone (TC) genesis is commonly interpreted through large-scale environmental controls, including sea surface temperature, mid-tropospheric humidity, vertical wind shear, and low-level vorticity. However, existing mature TCs may also influence where and when subsequent storms form by modifying the surrounding thermodynamic and dynamic environment. This study examines whether mature TCs produce a measurable spatial and temporal near-storm suppression signal using three complementary datasets: a 20-km MRI-AGCM3.2S idealized aquaplanet experiment, a real-world simulation, and September IBTrACS best-track data from 1982-2025. To increase the number of TC samples within the limited model integration, the simulations are conducted under perpetual September-like conditions, yielding 36 September-equivalent months of TC activity. New genesis in the model datasets is defined as the first point of each track, while mature TCs are defined as separate, simultaneously active storms with wind speeds of at least 34 kt. Following the logic of spatial point-pattern summary statistics, the analysis compares the nearest center-to-center distance from observed TC genesis events to existing mature TCs with the corresponding distance measured from randomly placed points at the same genesis times. This comparison asks whether genesis locations behave like arbitrary points in the domain or whether they systematically avoid the neighborhood of mature storms. The aquaplanet experiment shows a clear near-storm genesis deficit: among 1,190 observed genesis events with an eligible same-time mature TC, the observed nearest-neighbor distribution is strongly depleted at the smallest separations compared with 595,000 random samples. The deficit is strongest within 0-500 km, remains pronounced at 500-1000 km, weakens at 1000-1500 km, and transitions to an observed excess at intermediate distances. The real-world simulation and IBTrACS analysis show similar first-order behavior, with observed genesis underrepresented within approximately 0-1000 km and more frequent at intermediate separations. A forward time-lag analysis further shows that subsequent genesis is rare within 500 km of mature TC points during the following 0-24 hour but becomes more common at larger radii and longer lag windows. These suggest that the area within roughly 1500 km of a mature TC is generally unfavorable for new TC formation, likely representing a near-storm inhibition zone shaped by different dynamic and thermodynamic conditions. Beyond this near-storm region, however, the surrounding environment appears to become more favorable again, allowing new genesis to occur at intermediate distances where large-scale conditions remain supportive.

498564.title: Optimizing Ocean Observing Networks in the Tropical Pacific
498564.authors: Ira Ranjan, Plymouth State University, Plymouth, NH; and D. Amrhein, H. Kershaw, E. Milanese, A. Janney, F. Bryan, and E. Davenport
498564.abstract: Upwelling is a process where cold, nutrient rich water rises from the deep ocean to the surface. El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) modulates upwelling in the equatorial tropical Pacific region. Ocean observations of upwelling in this region are critical for forecasting ENSO variability. NOAA’s Tropical Pacific Observing System (TPOS) Equatorial Pacific Experiment - East (TEPEX-E) field campaign aims to use Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP) equipped Wave Gliders to estimate upwelling velocities. An Observing System Simulation Experiment (OSSE) evaluates proposed observing systems by simulating them using numerical models in order to maximize the impact of costly observing platforms. In this project, we create an Observing System Simulation Experiment (OSSE) workflow to evaluate Wave Glider arrangements in tropical Pacific regional Modular Ocean Model, version 6 (MOM6) configured in Community Earth System Model (CESM) using CrocoDash. New Python tools generate synthetic observation metadata reflecting a hypothetical Wave Glider arrangement and we use the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) to sample the model. Depth profiles of weekly- and area-averaged upwelling calculated from these synthetic Wave Glider observations are then compared to the model truth to evaluate the effectiveness of the arrangement. Finally, we explore several optimization routines and choices of constraints to find optimal arrangement patterns. We show that the optimal observing problem has numerous local minima in its loss function; using a regular hexagon as a first guess qualitatively improves over other choices.

498565.title: Evaluating MODIS Liquid Water Path Retrievals over Arctic Sea Ice with In-Situ and Microwave Observations from the ARCSIX Field Campaign
498565.authors: Dylan Nahsjun, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and K. S. Schmidt
498565.abstract: Low-level liquid clouds control much of the Arctic surface energy budget and the timing of sea ice melt, and liquid water path (LWP) governs their effect. Satellites provide the only record of pan-Arctic LWP, but over sea ice, the retrieval depends on surface albedo supplied as ancillary input. If that albedo is too low, the retrieval compensates with excess cloud optical thickness and LWP is biased high. Aircraft observations in the Central Arctic are rare and are the only way to validate both the albedo and its derived products. During the late spring and summer 2024 melt season, the NASA Arctic Radiation Cloud-Aerosol-Surface Interaction Experiment (ARCSIX) field campaign sampled clouds over the Arctic Ocean north of Greenland and Ellesmere Island. We derive LWP along the NASA-operated P-3 Orion flight track two ways: by integrating droplet size distributions from wing-mounted Fast Cloud Droplet Probes (FCDP) during cloud profiles, and from the G-band Vapor Radiometer (GVR) during cloud underflights. We collocate both with Level 2 cloud retrievals from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) on Terra (MOD06_L2) and Aqua (MYD06_L2). We evaluate LWP retrievals from these satellite products by comparing them with the in-situ and microwave estimates from the FCDP and GVR respectively. MODIS LWP is consistently higher than both the in-situ and the microwave estimates. The bias is consistent with the findings of an independent ARCSIX study: the observed surface albedo in the Central Arctic exceeds the values used as ancillary input to the cloud retrievals. The albedo error does not stay confined to the surface product but propagates into optical thickness and LWP. We discuss how this affects satellite estimates of Arctic cloud radiative effect and for the albedo data sets the retrievals rely on.

498568.title: Spatial Oversampling of TROPOMI NO2 Data for the Analysis of Village-Level Air Pollution Disparities Across India
498568.authors: Alexander Michael Cherny, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY
498568.abstract: India’s existing air quality monitoring network provides notably limited coverage considering the nation’s size and predominantly rural population. Satellite remote sensing data from TROPOMI bridges this gap by providing near-daily tropospheric nitrogen dioxide (NO2) observations across the entire spatial footprint of India. However, the pixel-based data format does not align with traditional administrative and statistical boundaries regularly used to organize census, demographic, and socioeconomic data. Therefore, effective analysis requires decisions to be made about how TROPOMI NO2 observations can be converted to village-level estimates. Building on the framework originally introduced in Jin et al. (2025) for oversampling NO2 to US neighborhoods, we are comparing two different oversampling techniques, area-weighted oversampling (AWO) and physics-based Gaussian oversampling (PGO) for over 600,000 villages across India. AWO assigns satellite observations to villages dependent on the area of spatial overlap, whereas PGO represents each observation as a continuous spatial sensitivity distribution that assigns a greater weight to villages closer to the center of the satellite’s field of view. We aim to determine which oversampling method better represents estimated NO2 column densities, spatial gradients, and data availability in the context of India, as village geometries and cloud patterns differ substantially from the US context the method was originally developed under. We have developed a village-level NO2 column density dataset for all of India for both the AWO and PGO methods. While the two methods display relatively similar overall spatial patterns at the macroscopic level, PGO exhibits a downward bias relative to AWO in regions with higher NO2 column density retrievals. This dataset is being paired with existing demographic and socioeconomic data to investigate potential disparities in air pollution exposure across India. Specifically, we will examine how NO2 varies between urban and rural communities, whether particular socioeconomic groups are more likely to live in areas with greater NO2, and whether communities within the vicinity of major industrial and mining corridors face disproportionate levels of NO2 exposure. These efforts aim to develop a system for using satellite remote sensing data to characterize highly-localized air pollution patterns and identify populations potentially experiencing disproportionately high NO2 burdens.

498573.title: Hydroclimatic Extreme Events in the Salt River Basin, Kentucky
498573.authors: Sanskar Adhikari, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and Z. Suriano
498573.abstract: Hydroclimatic extreme events such as extreme rainfall and flash floods pose significant threats to infrastructure and public safety throughout Kentucky because of its challenging terrain. Kentucky falls under an extremely severe precipitation risk category, meaning existing design standards are already exceeded, signaling a rapidly emerging “new normal” of more frequent and severe rainfall events. Heavy rainfall is often viewed as the primary driver of flooding; the "memory" of the land, specifically how wet the soil is before a storm, plays a critical, yet often under-analyzed, role in determining whether a storm results in a manageable rise in river levels or a catastrophic flood. Using a non-stationary Peaks-Over-Threshold (POT) approach, this study identifies extreme events by separately analyzing rainfall and streamflow data. In this study, we integrate meteorological data from PRISM (4km), streamflow records from the USGS, and soil-moisture reanalysis from ERA5-Land (9km) to create an observational climatology of extreme and compound hydroclimatic events over a 30-year period (1995-2024) in the Salt River Basin (SRB), Kentucky. By capturing these extreme event occurrences, this study aims to characterize the spatio-temporal variability and relationships among different hydroclimatic events in the Salt River Basin (SRB), Kentucky.

498574.title: Advancing Heat Health Decision Support by Correlating Weather Information to Heat-Related Impacts
498574.authors: Matthew S. Azuara, NWS, St. Johns, FL; and T. Dang
498574.abstract: Extreme heat is the leading cause of weather-related death in the United States and drives noticeable upticks in emergency department (ED) and inpatient hospital visits. While the National Weather Service already releases helpful products such as HeatRisk in an attempt to alert communities to extreme heat events, it does not currently account for nuance in specific communities that could affect the population’s susceptibility to heat events. For example, the elderly population (aged 65+) is more vulnerable to extreme heat than the general population. This project’s goal was to create a model that takes into account weather forecast data, community demographics, and real-world hospital data to predict the risk of Heat-Related Illnesses (HRIs) exceeding locally calibrated ED thresholds. These forecasts could then be repurposed for operational use to better prepare for extreme heat events and to recognize which communities may need the most resources in such events. To facilitate the project, we collected demographic data provided by the US Census Bureau, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency. We also downloaded temperature data provided by the Parameter-elevation Regressions on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM), and the number of inpatient and ED visits per day which were provided by several state departments of public health across the country. We then trained a machine learning model that analyzed these meteorological, demographic, and exposure datasets for correlations, which allowed it to predict the probability of exceeding locally defined HRI thresholds given future heat events. We transferred this model’s results to an interactive ArcGIS visualization so it could be navigated by the end user. This model’s framework could also be used to forecast for Cold-Related Illnesses (CRIs) in addition to HRIs.

498575.title: Diabatic Heating in Jet-Regime Modulation of Northern Hemisphere Storm Tracks
498575.authors: Heidi Nsiah, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA; and D. M. Straus
498575.abstract: Storm-track activity in the North Pacific (NP) declines during midwinter despite a strong upper-tropospheric jet, a phenomenon known as NP midwinter suppression. Chang (2001) found diabatic heating generates eddy available potential energy during fall and spring, but dissipates it in midwinter, based on a calendar comparison in the Pacific. Zilibotti et al. (2026) offered a different perspective on the broader jet–storm track relationship. Rather than averaging by calendar month, they grouped atmospheric states into similar ranges of jet strength and averaged within each range. This approach revealed that EKE increases with jet speed up to a threshold and then decreases, a pattern also evident in the North Atlantic (NA) when differences in timescales are accounted for. Their analysis, however, was limited to EKE and did not examine diabatic processes, leaving open whether a diabatic signature like Chang’s appears when data are organized by jet strength, and whether it holds in the Atlantic. This study extends the binning approach to diabatic heating and eddy available potential energy generation (GAPE), using ERA5 reanalysis. The approach is first applied to EKE to confirm consistency with earlier findings, before examining diabatic processes. The analysis reproduces the nonlinear EKE relationship in both basins, with EKE increasing up to a threshold jet strength before declining. This threshold occurs at a higher jet strength but lower magnitude in the North Pacific. Vertical profiles of diabatic heating show a similar structure in both basins, with strong lower-tropospheric heating, a secondary midtropospheric maximum, and weak cooling aloft. In contrast to EKE, low-level heating keeps rising after EKE declines. GAPE depends on covariance between heating and temperature anomalies rather than heating magnitude, which motivates testing whether GAPE evolves together with EKE or reflects a causative signature consistent with Chang’s (2001) seasonal reversal.

498576.title: Disappearing Teleconnections? Increased Warming and ENSO Variability May Decrease Western United States Precipitation Predictability
498576.authors: Kinsale Day, University of Wyoming, Cheyenne, WY; and S. Rahimi, C. W. Thackeray, A. Hall, L. Huang, and T. W. Aerenson
498576.abstract: The El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the dominant mode of climate variability globally, and its teleconnection exerts a strong control on precipitation patterns across the western U.S. Since ENSO modulates the predictability of the region’s weather, a change to ENSO’s teleconnectivity may have important consequences for western U.S. planning on seasonal to annual time scales. In this analysis, we mine 10 dynamically downscaled variants of the Community Earth System Model’s second Large Ensemble (CESM2-LE) for their ENSO events, quantified using the ENSO Longitude Index, across the 1865-1964 and1985-2084 periods to quantify shifts in teleconnectivity. Considering all events, CESM2-LE counterfactuals skillfully represent the ENSO-precipitation teleconnection in terms of the well-known meridional precipitation anomaly dipole across both time periods. When considering the 30- and 100-most intense events, future-era CESM2-LE simulations showcase a much larger ENSO variability compared to the historical era, with markedly stronger El Niños and La Niñas. Despite this increased variability, ENSO-induced precipitation anomalies weaken notably in the future period, pointing to a weakening in the overall teleconnection. A potential breakdown in the teleconnection strength may jeopardize an important source of Earth System predictability, posing challenges to forecasters and practitioners who make decisions on seasonal to annual time scales.

498578.title: Quantifying the Societal Burden of Tornadoes
498578.authors: Alycia T Triplett, Howard University, Washington, DC
498578.abstract: Tornadoes pose a significant threat to communities across the United States, but their impacts are not experienced equally. Socially vulnerable communities may experience disproportionate impacts from hazardous weather because of differences in preparedness, access to warning information and resources, and varying capacity for recovery. While the relationship between high-impact weather and social vulnerability is well established, there are limited decision-support resources that jointly characterize tornado climatology and social vulnerability. This research develops a county-level Tornado Burden Index (TorBI) that integrates climatological tornado risk with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) to quantify the societal burden of tornadoes. NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information Storm Events Database was used to identify tornadoes rated F/EF1 or greater from 1973–2024. Climatological tornado risk is characterized using four components: mean event frequency, mean exposure frequency, median tornado intensity, and mean tornado footprint. These components are combined with county-level social vulnerability to identify areas where tornado hazard and socioeconomic conditions may contribute to increased societal burden. Data are processed and indexed using R and visualized using ArcGIS. The TorBI is intended to provide a decision-support tool for emergency managers, meteorologists, policymakers, and other practitioners to support disaster preparedness, risk communication, and the identification of communities that may benefit from additional resources. Keywords: Tornadoes, social vulnerability, risk communication, decision support

498579.title: Optical and SAR-Derived Sea Ice Concentration Intercomparison over Alaskan Waters for Improved Operational Monitoring
498579.authors: Olivia Smith, University of Virginia, Fairfax Station, VA; and S. R. Helfrich, W. Clark, K. Mitkari, and R. C. Julian
498579.abstract: Monitoring sea ice is a fundamental aspect of numerical weather prediction, climate tracking, polar ecology, and maritime operations in the Arctic. Despite advances in remote sensing, validating and tracking Arctic sea ice remains difficult due to uncertainties arising from limited in-situ data, persistent cloud cover, seasonal polar darkness, and surface melt and snow cover. Currently, ice analysts rely on all-weather, high-resolution synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery to create generalized charts of the Arctic and Antarctic to guide mariners, however this is a time-consuming and expertise-dependent process. Combining optical sensors and SAR imagery through blending has the potential to improve both the accuracy and speed in estimating sea ice concentrations, allowing for applications in atmospheric and oceanic models and improved operational sea ice forecasting. This work aims to inform such future dataset blending by quantifying systematic differences across ice concentration ranges and seasons between two products: the NOAA Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), an infrared and optical sensor limited by cloud cover and polar darkness, and the Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI)-Automated Sea Ice Products (ASIP) SAR-derived L3 sea ice concentration product, a CNN trained on Sentinel-1 SAR imagery and ice charts providing all-weather coverage. The differences were characterized over Alaskan waters in the Beaufort, Chukchi, and Bering Seas. Comparison days spanning winter and summer seasons were selected to maximize clear-sky VIIRS coverage and capture both the melt-out and maximum ice coverage cycles of sea ice. Both products were co-registered to a common polar stereographic grid and compared across 10% concentration bins using traditional error metrics (e.g., bias, RMSE, STD) and performance diagrams (e.g., probability of detection, success rate). DMI-ASIP consistently estimated higher ice concentrations relative to VIIRS across all bins in both seasons, with mean seasonal bias lowest in the 90-100% range (summer = 1.2%, winter = 2.4%) and largest in the 10-20% range (summer = 54.5%, winter = 72.9%), consistent with known retrieval challenges along the marginal ice zone. Winter biases were significantly larger than summer across 9 of 10 bins (p < 0.01), potentially associated with differences in new-ice detection. These initial findings suggest that future blending of VIIRS and DMI-ASIP products must account for seasonal and concentration-dependent biases, particularly in the marginal ice zone, for improved operational sea ice monitoring and forecasting.

498580.title: Heatwaves Compounded with Flooding in Tampa Bay: Intensity, Frequency, and Risks
498580.authors: Lucas Nofsinger, University of South Florida, St. Petersburg, FL; Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and O. Onochie, S. Sudheer, and A. R. Enriquez
498580.abstract: Rising global temperatures and sea levels increase compound heatwaves and flooding events, threatening coastal community health and resilience. Recent studies found that compound extreme temperature-sea level probability has significantly increased for 39.12% of global coastal areas (Zhou et al., 2024). That study, however, relied on global reanalysis datasets and focused on sea levels rather than flooding. The present study provides a regional, high-resolution analysis of heatwave trends across the Tampa Bay area from 1993 to 2026. Land surface temperature (LST) is derived from 30 m Landsat C2 L2 imagery to estimate heatwaves' spatial and temporal distribution. Results indicate that LST has increased at rates of 5-10°C/era across the region. In particular, winter and spring months exhibit higher temperature increases in recent years. The warming is not spatially uniform; areas of rapid urban expansion and vegetation loss show the strongest warming signals. In addition to satellite imagery, we build a model for air temperatures based on 14 local weather stations, showing a good performance (R2 = 0.964, RMSE = 1.02°C). Results indicate mean annual heatwave frequency doubled between 1993-2007 and 2008-2023, increasing from 1.07 to 2.19 events per year (+112%). The proportion of years experiencing ≥ 3 heatwaves increased nearly fivefold, from 6.7% to 31.3%. Overlaying the temperature maps with flooding frequency maps reveals hotspots of compound temperature-flooding hazards across Tampa Bay, with shrinking wetland areas around the inside of the bay at greatest exposure. This exposure is compounded by the weakening sea-breeze cooling effect from rising ocean surface temperatures.

498583.title: Locating “Hot Spots” Along a Street in Louisville, KY, for Future Urban Planning Efforts
498583.authors: Natalie Peters, University of Louisville, Louisville, KY
498583.abstract: Pedestrians traveling along streets and sidewalks in major urban areas are frequently exposed to elevated thermal conditions that can negatively affect human health and comfort. These conditions can vary substantially across relatively small spatial scales due to differences in land cover, pavement, building structures, vegetation, shade, solar radiation, and wind. This study examines spatial variations in thermal conditions along a portion of Chestnut Street in Louisville, Kentucky, that runs through the heart of the city’s medical district. This portion of Chestnut Street is characterized by a high volume of pedestrian traffic including both medical professionals and hospital patients. The lack of green space and shade along this street further necessitates a field study with the goal of identifying areas experiencing elevated temperatures where heat mitigation activities could have the most impact. Data for this study were collected using a mobile weather station developed through a collaboration between the University of Louisville and the nonprofit LOUMED. The mobile weather station, dubbed the Louisville Urban Heat Explorer (LouHe), was equipped to measure air temperature, relative humidity, solar radiation, black globe temperature, and wind components every five seconds. During June and July 2026, LouHe was deployed along Chestnut Street one day a week to conduct three transects spanning seven blocks. A total of ten field data collection days were conducted, with low resolution and high resolution data collected during each outing. The analysis will consist of examining the data collected throughout the study, by comparing air temperature, black globe temperature, relative humidity, and solar radiation. This data will be used to calculate heat index values, which will be used to identify the intensity of the heat and to locate the areas of thermal discomfort along Chestnut Street. Identifying localized thermal hotspots along Chestnut Street can provide valuable information for understanding pedestrian heat exposure and informing future urban planning and development strategies aimed at mitigating the effects of urban heat.

498584.title: Reconciling Northeast Snowpack Site Metadata Discrepancies and Quality Control
498584.authors: Samantha Rae Durrenberger, Plymouth State University, Plymouth, NH; and J. Smith and E. P. Kelsey
498584.abstract: Reconciling Northeast Snowpack Site Metadata Discrepancies and Quality Control Samantha Durrenberger, Justin Smith, and Eric P. Kelsey School of Science and Technology, Plymouth State University Hundreds of snowpack survey sites across the Northeast have been measuring snow depth and SWE since as early as the 1930s, giving regular observations of snow depth and SWE, a necessary aspect for operational flood risk assessment and water resource management. A homogenized snowpack database ceases to exist for the Northeastern United States for operational and research purposes. However, developing a climatological baseline of SWE for the region will inform real-time operational drought/flood risk assessments and water resource decision-making. As a part of a NOAA-National Integrative Drought Information System-funded project to create an observation-based snowpack climatology for the Northeast, this work aims to expand the existing digital record of snowpack observations by digitizing paper records, validating metadata, and reconciling missing or incomplete metadata. Paper records from multiple organizations (e.g. USGS, state agencies, hydro power companies, etc.) were digitized and homogenized to expand the current digital record. Site discrepancies such as site changes, missing and inaccurate metadata, and averaged sites were investigated and reconciled, when possible, to improve the overall data quality. Validations were conducted by reaching out to various agencies and requesting information or additional data to fix errors. In some instances, there was not enough information to confidently reconcile a site’s proper location. The results of this work help to expand this comprehensive snowpack dataset to be used for climatological and operational applications.

498585.title: Digitizing and Homogenizing Disparate Formats of Snowpack Data in the Northeastern U.S
498585.authors: Mary McGloine, Plymouth State University, Schuylerville, NY; Plymouth State University, Plymouth, NH; and E. Burke and E. P. Kelsey
498585.abstract: Digitizing historic snowpack data and SWE is imperative for creating a comprehensive snowpack climatology, a necessary context for operational flood risk assessment and water resource management. A SWE climatology does not exist for the Northeast, despite hundreds of sites having data dating back several decades. Developing a climatological baseline of SWE for the region will inform real-time operational drought/flood risk assessments and water resource decision-making (e.g., hydropower companies. As a part of a NOAA-National Integrative Drought Information System-funded project to develop an observation-based daily snowpack climatology, thousands of observations from hundreds of snow course sites from across the Northeast and their corresponding data are being digitized and quality controlled. Only in the last five years has the National Weather Service developed a centralized, online snowpack observation entry form that results in a standardized dataset with complete snow course site metadata. Prior to that, snowpack observations taken by many different organizations (e.g., state agencies, private companies, US Army Corps of Engineers) were recorded on organization-specific forms, usually paper prior to 2000, that often lacked full metadata. Across the board, agencies like New York State's Department of public works, power corporations and geological surveys were collecting snowpack data for their own personal use. Streamlining data observations to a singular format for universal use allows for a climatological analysis. Documentation formats varied across agencies leading to inconsistences that were resolved when digitizing data into a common format. This digitization and homogenization of SWE data is a necessary step for its use in developing a climatological context for drought/flood risk assessment and water resource management.

498587.title: Spatiotemporal Distribution of Fog Across the United States and Canada
498587.authors: Rebekah Lopez, Hobart and William Smith Colleges, Emmaus, PA
498587.abstract: This study aimed to examine the spatiotemporal distribution of fog across the United States and Canada, seasonally and annually. Surface hourly station data from the National Centers for Environmental Information integrated database was utilized to determine fog occurrences at 127 stations from 1980-1995 using reported present weather code information. This period was chosen due to availability of fog data, as fog reports dropped substantially after 1995 corresponding to a transition from manual to automated reporting of observations. Fog hours across the United States and Canada were most frequent during the winter with 518,305 hours and least frequent in the summer with 358,116 hours. Generally across all stations, there was an increase of fog hours in the fall and winter, followed by a decrease in fog hours in the spring and summer. Fog hours during 1986-1990 decreased from the previous period, 1980-1985, with the greatest decrease in fog in Asheville, North Carolina, US. Fog hours during 1991-1995 increased from the previous period, with the greatest increase in fog in Grand Island, Nebraska, US.

498588.title: Seasonality and Physical Mechanisms of Short-Term Wind–SST Co-Oscillation Along the California Coast
498588.authors: Thamirys Cavaton Rocha, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; and B. Villas Boas
498588.abstract: Investigation of wind–SST variability on daily timescales and oceanic submesoscales O(1–10 km) has recently become possible through high-resolution coupled ocean–atmosphere models because they provide the spatial and temporal resolution needed to resolve air–sea interactions that cannot be fully captured by satellite and in situ observations alone. Although recent modeling studies have identified a global co-oscillation between wind speed and sea surface temperature (SST) on time scales of a few days, the duration, intensity, seasonality, and physical drivers of this variability remain poorly understood. This raises several key questions: Does the strength of the wind–SST co-oscillation vary with season? How does it differ among geographic regions? Which physical processes control the observed variability? Do coastal upwelling systems exhibit stronger coupling than regions dominated by high eddy kinetic energy? Addressing these questions is essential for understanding the mechanisms governing short-term air–sea interactions and improving their representation in coupled models used for weather and climate prediction. Here, we present a characterization of the duration, strength, and physical drivers of wind–SST feedbacks along the California coast. We quantify the seasonality of this variability using lag-correlation analysis and estimate the relative contributions of coastal upwelling and surface heat fluxes. To accomplish this, we use observations from National Data Buoy Center (NDBC) buoys to evaluate simulations from the coupled MITgcm–GEOS model. Then, the model output is used to generate lag-correlation maps and diagnose the dominant physical processes responsible for the observed variability. Understanding how the wind–SST co-oscillation varies with season and geographic location, and identifying the mechanisms that control it, may help explain uncertainties in bulk air–sea flux estimates and inform improved parameterizations in coupled weather and climate models.

498590.title: Interning in Instrumentation: The Valuable Experience that can be Gained from Hands-On Training
498590.authors: Ethan Mason, Valparaiso University, La Grange Highlands, IL; and K. L. Grimme and L. Blind-Doskocil
498590.abstract: Figuring out how to get involved outside the classroom is often one of the greatest questions faced by meteorology and atmospheric science majors as undergraduates. For students who want experience in the field, participating in opportunities relating to instrumentation provides a great way to gain skills. Valparaiso University’s Meteorology Program offers an Instrumentation Internship, where interns assist in performing routine maintenance on instrumentation and leading weather balloon launches. Through the internship, students learn how to work with meteorological instrumentation and build skills in data collection, collecting experience that may be limited or hard to come by in a classroom setting. Most importantly, instrumentation interns are simultaneously able to mentor others and gain valuable field experience and expertise. The main qualifications for this program are having a strong work ethic and a willingness to get creative when problems arise. Therefore, opportunities in instrumentation are a great place to start for undergraduates wanting to gain unique experience in the field, regardless of past experience and qualifications. During the 2025-2026 academic year, Valparaiso University participated in the Coordinated University Sounding Program for Atmospheric River Reconnaissance (CUSP-ARR). As part of CUSP-ARR, the instrumentation interns led three weather balloon launches throughout the day during multiple intensive observation periods (IOPs). Leading balloon launches for the CUSP-ARR project required an ability to work through harsh conditions in a timely manner, as launches occurred at set times, regardless of the present weather. The most educational launches were harsh, wintertime IOPs, when temperatures were well below zero degrees Fahrenheit or during snow and wind that made getting radiosondes into the air significantly more challenging. These launches helped interns develop valuable teamwork and leadership skills that can be put forth in other areas within and outside the field. The skills gained by the interns from their participation in CUSP-ARR is just one example of the many ways that instrumentation opportunities can be beneficial for undergraduates.

498591.title: From Warnings to Words: An Undergraduate Perspective on Coding Tornado Emergencies
498591.authors: Madisynne Gura, Valparaiso University, Shorewood, IL; and L. Blind-Doskocil, E. C. Wolff IV, and J. E. Trujillo-Falcón
498591.abstract: Tornado emergencies (TOREs) are the highest level tornado warnings the National Weather Service (NWS) can issue, reserved for rare situations where a violent tornado is ongoing. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with NWS forecasters over the last year to understand their decision-making process when issuing TOREs. As of August 2026, 11 virtual interviews had been conducted, mostly with forecasters from previously Central and Southern Regions. To analyze the content in each interview, Phronetic Iterative Qualitative Data Analysis (PIQDA) was conducted. After each interview, the data is organized and the transcription process begins - the transcript generated by Zoom is corrected for accuracy, which requires multiple hours of slowly listening to the interview audio, ensuring words and grammar align in the transcript. A critical aspect of the transcription process is adding in physical gestures such as eye contact and hand gestures, while also noting any pauses, stutters, emphasis on certain words, etc.; these vocal and physical cues may not be apparent from the transcript alone but can give insights into possible emotions or ideas revealed in the interview. Once the transcribing process is complete, first-cycle coding is conducted for each transcribed interview. This involves evaluating all the data and collecting words/phrases together to capture the centralized themes. Lessons learned about organizing the data and first-cycle coding for PIQDA from the undergraduate student perspective will be shared, along with some initial results from the interviews with forecasters.

498592.title: Diabatic Heating in Organized Convection Across Model Resolutions During the July 4, 2025 Central Texas Floods.
498592.authors: James Maddox Meador, Penn State University, University Park, PA; NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. Lojko, K. Werner, and W. Wang
498592.abstract: Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) simulations initialized at 0000 UTC on July 4, 2025 were performed at 60 km, 60–15 km, and 60–3 km horizontal resolutions to investigate the July 4–5, 2025 Central Texas floods. Diabatic potential vorticity (PV) tendencies and radar reflectivity fields were analyzed throughout the evolution of an organized convective storm episode associated with the heavy rainfall. All simulations captured the organization of the system at approximately 0900 UTC. Additionally, convective storms were more intense in the 60–3 km simulation compared to the coarser simulations. However, all simulations produced a distinct diabatic PV tendency structure. In particular, a region of strong negative PV tendency developed in the lower troposphere. The structure in the 60–3 km simulation was also tilted compared to those in the 60–15 km and 60 km simulations. This differed from the expected PV tendency structure within deep moist convection, which features a region of positive PV tendency in the lower troposphere associated with diabatic heating and a region of negative PV tendency in the upper troposphere. We suspect that this PV signature was associated with intense melting processes, which were further analyzed through radar reflectivity. We discuss the potential implications for the dynamics of the storm.

498593.title: From Local Classrooms to National Alerts: Forecasting Unsafe Indoor PM2.5 via TEMPO Derived Products
498593.authors: Mykhaylo Severinov, Lucy Family Institute for Data & Society, Notre Dame, IN; University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN; and K. Almeida, C. Smith, J. Ciliberti, S. Ghorbany, M. Hu, W. McGillis, M. Sisk, and C. Wang
498593.abstract: This work introduces a dual-layer encoder to decoder attention architecture (InDEPT-PM) specialized for predicting indoor PM2.5 without any direct input from on the ground monitoring networks. Circumventing this requirement through the use of NASA’s soon to be released TEMPO PM2.5 product (September 2026) allows for indoor PM2.5 forecasting across the entire continental United States (CONAS) without any limitation by expensive ground monitoring stations. Through a specialized 4-stage training approach, sufficient accuracy is then developed to provide an 18 hours lead time for when intervention strategies to reduce PM2.5 exposure should be implemented. Specifically, the approach detailed below provides interventional coverage across 80% of all hours above the WHO’s 15 μg/m3 threshold for public K-12 educational facilities. These were chosen as an intervention target due to the increased lung to body mass ratio present in children and the increased value of intervention at an early life stage. To our knowledge this is the first system to provide accurate indoor PM2.5 forecasts without the direct use of on the ground monitoring stations. While our approach is currently limited to CONUS, rapid advancements in satellite technology makes it reasonable to expand this to a global scale in the near future. The hope is that this approach can be used to inspire interventions in other areas where high PM2.5 due to rapid industrialization is met with limited investment in monitoring infrastructure. In the USA, we show that temporal targeting of interventions to high PM2.5 events such as wildfire (only 3.5% of all exposure to elevated PM2.5) can have as much impact as blanketed interventions that require constant usage. The system proposed here enables that targeted intervention requiring the use of only a singular low-cost indoor PM2.5 sensor for forecasting.

498594.title: Kilometer-Scale Variability in the Simulated Tornadic Environment during the 2 March 2012 Kentucky Tornado Outbreak
498594.authors: Alexander Honeycutt, Western Kentucky Univ., Bowling Green, KY
498594.abstract: The 2 March 2012 tornado outbreak produced several significant, long-track tornadoes across Kentucky, including supercells that moved into complex terrain of the Appalachian Plateau. This study uses 1-km Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations to examine the fine-scale variability present in the low-level environment encountered by these supercells. The main emphasis of this study is to diagnose boundary-layer circulation and terrain-modified flow along footprints of supercell and tornado tracks. Nearby radar observations are used in support of such diagnoses. As the supercells progressed across eastern Kentucky, the simulated thermodynamic environment remained modestly unstable, with surface-based CAPE generally around 1000-1500 J/kg. While the low-level kinematic environment became increasingly favorable and conducive of long-track significant tornadoes. Lifted condensation level heights also decreased from around 700-750m to nearly 500-550m. Localized maxima developed in 0–1-km bulk shear, storm-relative helicity (SRH), and effective-layer significant tornado parameter (STP). These fields exhibited substantial spatial variability over relatively short distances rather than a uniformly favorable inflow environment. A prominent simulated feature was a series of southwest-northeast oriented waves/bands in 0 –1-km bulk shear. Similar banding also occurred in vertical velocity between 250 and 500 m AGL, with alternating regions of ascent and decent. These regions broadly correspond to changes in the low-level wind field. Vertical cross sections revealed retreated horizontal wind perturbations that extend through much of lowest kilometer and beyond, with successive perturbation bands separated by 7-10 km. Comparable spatial patterns are also evident in SRH and effective-layer STP, indicating that the circulations influenced multiple tornado-related parameters. The characteristics are consistent with an organized boundary-layer wave/roll like circulation, although additional diagnostics are needed to determine its exact dynamical origin. As these circulations encounter the increasingly dissected terrain of eastern Kentucky, changes in orientation occur. These terrain-related blocking, channeling, and lifting potentially modify the near-surface wind field which contributed to more localized changes in low-level shear and SRH. This simulation suggests that the tornadic supercells encountered a more heterogeneous near-storm environment than earlier analysis has shown. These results also show the value of kilometer-scale model resolution for resolving localized variations in the near-storm environment that may be poorly represented at coarser resolutions.

498595.title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of NOAA Weather-Station Data Gaps During Major Hurricane
498595.authors: Tsetan Tashi, CUNY CREST Institute, The City College of New York, new york, NY; and Y. Awan and N. Y. krakauer
498595.abstract: Hurricanes can disrupt weather-station reporting when reliable observations are most needed for forecasting and emergency response. This project investigates whether machine learning can identify NOAA stations likely to stop reporting during major hurricanes and extreme-rainfall events. Global Historical Climatology Network-Daily (GHCN-Daily) observations were combined with HURDAT2 hurricane tracks for Katrina (2005), Sandy (2012), Harvey (2017), Florence (2018), Laura (2020), and Ida (2021). Each station-storm record included the station's prior reporting reliability, elevation, rainfall, distance from the hurricane track, and storm conditions. A station was classified as failed when it missed at least two expected reporting days during an event. Logistic Regression and Random Forest classifiers were evaluated using storm-grouped training and testing, which kept complete storms together. Logistic Regression detected a larger proportion of failed stations, achieving 62.3% recall, but it also produced 4,352 false warnings. Random Forest performed better overall, achieving 85.1% accuracy, 29.2% failure precision, a 36.0% failure-class F1-score, and a 75.7% ROC-AUC; therefore, it was selected to generate the final probability maps. Observed failure rates ranged from 5.6% for Katrina and Laura to 16.3% for Florence. Sandy also had a high failure rate of 15.0%, while Harvey showed the largest difference between observed and predicted failures. These findings indicate that storm exposure and prior station reliability provide useful information for identifying reporting-failure risk, while also demonstrating the limitations of the current model. Failure cases were uncommon, and the dataset did not include infrastructure characteristics such as backup power, communication systems, maintenance history, or direct physical damage. Machine learning could support targeted inspections, backup equipment placement, and temporary observation coverage before extreme events; however, its predictions should complement, rather than replace, operational judgment until the model is further refined.

498596.title: Evaluating Extreme Inland Rainfall Mechanisms during Hurricane Helene (2024) Using Operational HAFS
498596.authors: Etsub Tallmadge, NCAS-M Howard Univeristy, Washington, DC; and F. Hsiao and S. Chiao
498596.abstract: On September 22, 2024, a low-pressure system formed over western Caribbean islands that would intensify as it moved through the Gulf, ultimately becoming Hurricane Helene. After landfall, the storm began to weaken as predicted, except when it moved over southern North Carolina near the Appalachian Mountains and briefly intensified. The storm momentarily intensified, dumping a record-breaking amount of rainfall, costing the region an estimated 53.6 billion dollars in damages and leading to a verified 107 fatalities. Hurricane Helene’s impact on North Carolina was unexpected and left unanswered questions about how forecasting was insufficient to account for intensified conditions. Prior studies have suggested several mechanisms contributing to Helene’s extreme inland rainfall. For instance, wind profiles of Hurricane Helene were observed and analyzed to better understand the increase in precipitation as the storm passed over the Appalachian Mountains. The analysis led the study to directly associate the higher wind speeds with higher precipitation, but there is still a question of what other factors contributed to the intensification of the storm. In addition, the preexisting rain event significantly increased soil moisture before Helene arrived. In general, previous studies suggested that strong winds over an already saturated surface may have enhanced surface evaporation and near-surface moisture availability, supplementing the larger-scale tropical moisture supply and contributing to sustained heavy rainfall over the southern Appalachians. This study further evaluates whether operational Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) output can be used to diagnose these proposed mechanisms. Forecasts from multiple HAFS initialization times will be analyzed for Helene’s track and intensity, precipitation distribution, low- and mid-level wind fields, atmospheric moisture transport, and surface moisture-related processes as the storm progressed inland. This study will focus on the relationship among pre-existing wet-soil conditions, strong near-surface winds, moisture transport, 850–500 hPa wind shifting due to topographic effects, and the location of heavy precipitation. The study will assess the consistency of these features in operational HAFS forecasts and determine how effectively the model represents the processes associated with extreme inland precipitation from landfalling tropical cyclones.

498597.title: Hydrological Whiplash Across Alaskan River Basins and Associated Ecohydrological Variability
498597.authors: Samantha Lynn Scheve, NASA, Washington, DC; Saint Louis University, Saint Louis, MO
498597.abstract: Climate whiplash is defined as the rapid shift between opposing extremes (e.g., anomalously dry and wet), and hydrological whiplash is specifically characterized by anomalously low-flow and high-flow seasons. Although a widely studied phenomenon in the Continental United States, whiplash events have been under researched in the Alaska region where Earth system changes are altering streamflow, snowpack, glaciers, and permafrost, with implications for ecosystems, water resources, and downstream communities. This study aims to address this research gap by identifying occurrences of hydrological whiplash at 25 Alaskan watershed basins and examining associated evapotranspiration (ET) variability and potential drivers. This study analyses daily mean discharge data from 25 US Geological Survey stream gauge locations from May 16 through September 30 from 1990–2025. Whiplash events were identified as yearly averaged transitions between dry (driest 15% of timeseries) and wet (wettest 30% of timeseries) streamflow seasons using a z-score analysis. Following identification of these events, evapotranspiration (ET) over the same months for years 2000-2025 for each watershed was further analyzed using Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) data. A corresponding z-score analysis was performed to identify the ET extremes and characterize ET behavior alongside the identified whiplash events. Preliminary analysis identified 80 hydrological whiplash events across the 25 Alaskan river basins, with variability in event frequency among watersheds, suggesting differences in regional hydrological response to both climate and vegetation variability. Examining the relationship between streamflow and ET anomalies for individual events revealed variability between the two variables. For example, watersheds with considerable glacier coverage exhibited positive streamflow-ET anomaly relationships, suggesting that additional inputs such as glacier melt may influence watershed behavior. Ongoing analysis will investigate atmospheric and cryospheric influences on these relationships, including the role of temperature and precipitation conditions associated with hydrological whiplash events. Together, these findings will improve understanding of hydrological extremes in Alaska and provide insight into how high-latitude watersheds may respond to Earth system changes.

498599.title: Calculating Hailstone Fall Velocity and Measurement Uncertainty from a Mobile Hail Camera Deployed During ICECHIP
498599.authors: Anya M. Brenholt, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and T. D. Kurtz and A. D. Kennedy
498599.abstract: The Open Snowflake Camera for Research and Education, OSCRE, is an in-situ, high-speed hydrometeor imager. In collaboration with the Atmospheric and Environmental Research (AER) and Janus Research Group, OSCRE’s original design was modified to build a mobile hail camera for the In-situ Collaborative Experiment for the Collection of Hail In the Plains (ICECHIP). With a frame rate > 400 frames per second and a resolution of <1mm, four camera systems were deployed to identify the size, shape, and fall speeds of hailstones. These properties are important to understand due to the impact of hail on society and past work that has been focused on laboratory (controlled) experiments. In practice, the designed hail camera uses a singular camera aimed at an LED backlight to image the shadows of passing hailstones. By using a hailstone centroid through the consecutive images, the fall velocity can be calculated by identifying the horizontal and vertical velocities over two-frame pairs and then taking the average of consecutive pairs to identify an average velocity. Due to the optical design of the instrument, however, uncertainty arises due to fore/aft position of the hailstone within the sampling volume. This work will identify the uncertainty of size and velocity measurements by conducting lab experiments with the instrumentation. The experiment design focused on operating the hail cameras indoors in an area with a 3rd story balcony where proxies for hailstones could be safely dropped. Three different sizes of spherical ice cubes were used in place of the hailstones: 19.9 mm (80 count), 25.4 mm (96 count), and 41 mm (20 count), totaling 196 dropped ice cubes. Besides recording size and velocities with the camera, the fore/aft displacement of the synthetic hailstones was recorded. This presentation will describe the outcomes of this experiment and identify the uncertainty associated with the instrument.

498600.title: Atmospheric and Environmental Drivers that Contribute to Peak Streamflow at the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest in New Hampshire
498600.authors: Izzy Collins, Plymouth State University, Plymouth, NH; and E. P. Kelsey, M. Green, and A. Bailey
498600.abstract: High streamflow events can produce substantial flooding across New England, yet the meteorological and hydrologic conditions that lead to the largest catchment responses are complex. The Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest (HBEF), located in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, provides uniquely long hydrometeorological records for investigating high flow events in small, forested catchments. Streamflow response depends not only on the magnitude and characteristics of a precipitation event, but also on the antecedent conditions of the catchment. Understanding the interaction between these atmospheric, hydrologic, and pedologic factors is important for determining why some storm events produce noticeably greater streamflow responses than others. This study examines the atmospheric and antecedent watershed conditions associated with peak streamflow events in Watershed 3 (W3), a south-facing watershed at HBEF, to better understand the factors that contribute to peak flows and potentially improve the anticipation of flood-producing conditions. Long-term instantaneous streamflow observations from W3 are used to identify and characterize high flow events based on volumetric streamflow output for each event. For identified high flow events, precipitation characteristics and antecedent watershed conditions, including soil moisture and seasonal influences such as snowmelt, will be examined to characterize the hydrologic state of the watershed before and during each event. Atmospheric conditions associated with high flow events will be analyzed using reanalysis data. Particular attention will be given to storm type and moisture transport, including the magnitude and direction of integrated vapor transport. The occurrence and characteristics of atmospheric rivers will also be examined to assess their role in producing high flow events at HBEF. Together, these analyses will provide an assessment of the meteorological and hydrologic conditions that favor extreme streamflow responses at HBEF and their potential relevance to flooding across New England.

498603.title: Quantifying CMIP6 Soil Moisture Skill Across Hydroclimatic Regimes
498603.authors: Brayden Mikulski, Mississippi State University, Starkville, MS; Mississippi State University, Starkville, MS; and J. K. Beck and S. M. Quiring
498603.abstract: Soil moisture has a vital role in land—atmosphere interactions: influencing severe weather, impacting wildfire activity, and indicating hydroclimatic extremes. Increasing numbers of global climate models use soil moisture to assess environmental responses to climate change. However, model results showcase spatial and temporal variability, yielding differences in individual and mean model comparison to observations. This study compares the accuracy of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project – Phase 6 (CMIP6) models against the North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS) model across the 10 Level 1 ecoregions in the Contiguous United States (CONUS). More specifically, we compare the seasonality and severity of hydroclimatic events in each region. Preliminary results reveal model overestimation of soil moisture in dry regions with seasonal underestimations in plains and forested regions. Findings will highlight and quantify individual and mean model performance in each region, wet or dry biases associated with each model, and seasonal accuracy.

498604.title: A Sensitivity Case Study Using WRF Model of the 16-21 November,2022 Lake Effect Snow Event in Buffalo, NY
498604.authors: Aidyn Bruns, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and M. Voth and E. A. McMahon
498604.abstract: Lake-effect snow (LES) is notorious for causing isolated high snowfall totals within snowbands across the Great Lakes region. Because the heaviest snowfall is localized and influenced by many environmental factors, predicting LES events is difficult, and these predictions can vary dramatically from real observations. The Buffalo, NY lake-effect snowstorm of 16-21 November, 2022, was one of these instances where the forecast greatly underestimated the duration and total snowfall. The forecast predicted a maximum of 36-48” of snow in the Buffalo Metropolitan area; however, the snowfall totals reached 84”, and the event lasted two days longer than predicted. A discrepancy of this magnitude has significant impacts on daily life and hinders emergency management efforts. Improved lake-effect snow forecasts ensure proper measures can be taken to prepare for these events. Reviewing Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model observations from the Buffalo, NY event in 2022 can increase understanding of how the models forecasted this event and what parameters negatively affected the outcome. This study aims to determine the WRF model sensitivities to various parameter adjustments that aid in lake-effect snow development. Parameters being tested include the 850 mb temperature, 1000-850 mb wind direction, and 850-700 mb wind shear. We altered these parameters to mimic the storm's environment in order to identify potential model faults.

498605.title: Climatology of Supercell-Squall Line Mergers Across the United States from 2013-2024
498605.authors: Kaitlyn Ivey, Ohio University, Athens, OH; and D. V. Blount
498605.abstract: Supercell–squall line mergers are a complex form of storm interaction that can quickly change storm structure and severe weather potential. While supercells and squall lines have been studied extensively on their own, much less is known about how often these storms interact, where these mergers occur, and how the storms change during and after the interaction. These mergers are important because they can be associated with changes in storm intensity, including the development of stronger damaging winds, bowing structures, and changes in embedded rotation. Previous research has focused on a small set of individual cases or idealized simulations, making it difficult to understand how common these interactions are across the United States. This study will develop a climatology of documented supercell–squall line mergers across the United States from 2013 through 2024. Merger events will be identified using archived NEXRAD radar observations along with the Storm Prediction Center Severe Weather Event Archive. For each event, the date, location, timing, storm characteristics, and associated severe weather reports will be documented. The resulting dataset will be used to examine where and when mergers occur, including geographic and seasonal patterns and potential diurnal trends. Merger events will also be categorized based on whether the interaction occurs north or south of the apex of the squall line’s bowing segment. Radar observations will be used to subjectively identify the apex and document storm structure before, during, and after the merger, including changes in the strength and organization of the convective line, bowing structures, embedded rotation, and severe weather reports. This climatology will provide a broader observational look at how frequently supercell–squall line mergers occur and how their location within a bowing segment may relate to storm evolution and severe weather activity. The resulting dataset will also provide a foundation for future research into the environmental and storm-scale processes that contribute to supercell–squall line mergers.

498606.title: In Search of Future Fires: Nebraska's Fire Weather Sensitivity to Fuel Type
498606.authors: Andreas Michael Udby, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and R. D. Dixon and E. Hunt
498606.abstract: Anthropogenic climate change has contributed to a growing trend in wildfire activity across North America, including in regions that have not historically experienced large-scale fires, such as Nebraska. Until the early 2020s, the western section of Nebraska experienced a high-frequency, low-intensity fire regime. In recent years, however, wildfires have burned faster and longer than first responders have traditionally encountered. In March 2026, the Morrill fire set a new state record for acreage burned and occurred outside Nebraska’s traditional fire season of April to November. Nebraska’s recent State Climate Report highlighted shortcomings in the state’s ability to accurately forecast wildfire risk for longer timescales. Given recent fire seasons, it is apparent that this gap in Nebraska’s emergency preparedness represents a time-sensitive and important challenge for the state. In order to see Nebraska’s projected wildfire risk, we use statistically downscaled climate projections from LOCA (Localized Constructed Analogs) version 2, which is applied to model output from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6). This dataset provides daily maximum temperature, total precipitation, and relative humidity at 6 km resolution across Nebraska through 2100 for several emissions scenarios. This output is then processed through a Python version of the Canadian Fire Weather Index (CFWI) System, to show how much Nebraska’s risk of wildfire is projected to change. Traditionally, the CFWI is computed assuming a standard mature pine forest. However, the 2025 update to the CFWI algorithm has optional code and indexes for grassland fuels, known as the Grassland Fire Weather Index (GFWI). Since Nebraska is 46% grasslands and contains the largest grassland ecosystem in North America, this brings about a unique opportunity to explore how sensitive projections of fire risk across the state are to the representation of fuel type. Using the same inputs from the downscaled models, we create three separate forecasts of fire weather risk: 1) one using the traditional pre-2025 CFWI, which was tuned for pine forests, 2) one using the new GFWI, and 3) one using a GIS ground cover flag to identify which index is more appropriate for each grid square. We explore the sensitivity of these choices to fire weather vulnerability during the historical period, which will allow us to compare the model output to observational datasets and determine the added-value of the GFWI algorithm. We will also see how sensitive projected fire weather vulnerability is to our choice of algorithm, which will provide useful information to decision-makers, stakeholders, and communities vulnerable to wildfire-related hazards.

498608.title: Mesoscale Effects of Cold Pooling on Tornadogenesis in the Southeastern United States During the 5 April 2022 Severe Weather Outbreak
498608.authors: Aidan Corley, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and C. Gaske, E. Joyce, J. Dunning, and A. W. Lyza
498608.abstract: A pair of long-tracked supercells followed by a quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) were observed by the Propagation, Evolution and Rotation in Linear Storms (PERiLS) field team during the morning of April 5th, 2022. The southern supercell would go on to produce an EF-2 tornado, while the northern supercell remained nontornadic. Observations from this field campaign include dewpoint, temperature, and pressure recorded by NSSL Probe 1 and Probe 2 Mobile Mesonet trucks, radiosondes taken by both the probe teams and local National Weather Service (NWS) stations, and WSR-88D doppler radar data. This presentation uses the thermodynamic observations from this event to draw conclusions on whether the cold pools of nontornadic supercells significantly differ from tornadic supercells in the southeastern United States. Preliminary results show the nontornadic supercell featured a minimal cold pool relative to observed tornadic supercells.

498609.title: Investigating Emission Sources in Korea using Airborne Observations using Ethane from Aerodyne’s Tunable Infrared Laser Direct Absorption Spectrometer during ASIA-AQ
498609.authors: Victoria Wright, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and J. P. DiGangi, G. S. Diskin, Y. Choi, J. A. Miech, J. Crounse, P. O. Wennberg, K. Ball, Y. R. Lee, E. C. Apel, R. S. Hornbrook, A. Hills, B. Roozitalab, D. Jeong, A. Wisthaler, W. Wojnowski, and D. A. Caulton
498609.abstract: Ethane observations are useful tracers of emission sources. Ethane is often used to identify oil and natural gas related (ONG) sources of methane, a major greenhouse gas with one of the greatest contributions to global warming.
