Due to the recent increasing temperatures around the world, identifying and quantifying methane-emitting sources is critical to combatting climate change. Ethane is also a useful biomass burning (BB) tracer. Human exposure to BB is increasing and the hazardous air pollutants they release are known to be associated with respiratory and all-cause mortality. However, BB and ONG sources co-exist in Southeast Asia and each source’s prevalence varies from country to country. Thus, in this region, it should not be assumed that is an accurate tracer of both sources on its own and instead should be traced and attributed itself. The 2024 Airborne and Satellite Investigation of Asian Air Quality (ASIA-AQ) combined ground and airborne-based measurements with satellite data and air quality models to investigate emissions over the Philippines, South Korea, Thailand, and Taiwan during February and March of 2024. NASA’s DC-8 aircraft housed twenty-eight instruments during the campaign, including an Aerodyne tunable infrared laser direct absorption spectroscopy ethane analyzer (E-TILDAS) and NASA’s Differential Absorption Carbon monOxide Measurement (DACOM) which also reports methane. This work combines in situ airborne 1Hz ethane measurements from E-TILDAS with measurements from various instruments, also on the DC-8, to identify and attribute emission sources in Southeast Asia, a region where such studies have rarely been conducted. Ethane observations from this field study give us insight into ONG and BB emissions in this region and improve the global emissions inventory. This study will focus on investigating ethane emissions and the prevalence of their sources in Korea.

498610.title: Tree-Based Machine Learning for Dynamic Line Rating Using HRRR and Utility Field Measurements
498610.authors: Leah Crespo, Georgia Institute of Techology, Atlanta, GA; and J. Grot, L. Graber, Z. Jin, Z. Zheng, and S. Wilkie
498610.abstract: Tree-Based Machine Learning for Dynamic Line Rating Using HRRR and Utility Field Measurements Leah Crespo1, Jenna Grot1, Zhong Zheng2, Steven Wilkie2, Lukas Graber1, and Zhiyang Jin1 School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, 30332 New York Power Authority, White Plains, NY, 10601 Growing electricity demand, renewable energy integration, and transmission congestion are increasing the need to utilize existing transmission infrastructure more effectively. Dynamic line rating (DLR) can increase the usable capacity of overhead transmission lines by determining conductor ampacity from actual or forecast meteorological conditions rather than conservative static assumptions. However, conventional DLR implementations often rely on dedicated line-mounted sensors, which can increase deployment and maintenance costs. This study investigates whether numerical weather prediction data, enhanced using tree-based machine learning, can support a scalable DLR approach with reduced dependence on field sensors. In collaboration with the New York Power Authority (NYPA), meteorological measurements from transmission-line monitoring sensors are compared with NOAA High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) data. Ambient temperature, wind speed, wind direction, solar irradiance, and particularly the wind component perpendicular to the conductor are evaluated because of their influence on conductor heat transfer and line rating. The comparison indicates that HRRR represents ambient temperature relatively well, whereas wind-related parameters exhibit greater discrepancies, particularly under low-wind conditions where convective cooling is limited and accurate wind estimation becomes especially important for DLR. To improve HRRR-derived wind estimates, tree-based machine-learning approaches, i.e. LSBoost and LightGBM, are investigated using paired HRRR and NYPA field measurements. Preliminary results indicate that tree-based models substantially reduce the errors in HRRR-derived wind estimates and improve the systematic bias observed in the original HRRR predictions. The quantile-regression (LightGBM) formulation further provides calibrated P10–P90 uncertainty bounds around the corrected wind estimate, complementing the point-estimate correction from LSBoost with a measure of prediction confidence. These results suggest that tree-based machine learning can compensate for systematic and location-specific discrepancies between numerical weather prediction and field-observed conditions. This work combines numerical weather prediction, utility field measurements, tree-based machine learning, and transmission-line thermal modeling to explore a sensor-reduced approach to DLR. Ongoing work focuses on improving model performance under low-wind conditions, quantifying the resulting improvement in line-rating accuracy, and evaluating the transferability of the approach across transmission-line locations.

498611.title: GRA2PES Downscaling for Use in WRF-Chem
498611.authors: Liam Kieran Sheji, SUNY Albany, Albany, NY; University at Albany, SUNY, Albany, NY; and C. Loughner, C. H. Lu, J. Freedman, and B. C. McDonald
498611.abstract: The GReenhouse gas And Air Pollutant Emissions System (GRA2PES), developed by the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory (CSL), bridges the gap between greenhouse gas inventories and air quality inventories. GRA2PES provides these emissions at 4 × 4 km resolution across the contiguous United States, with annual, monthly, day-of-week, and diurnal temporal information. GRA2PES is actively used in the Unified Forecast System with Chemistry (UFS-Chem), while growing applications of high-resolution chemical models have created a need for emissions at finer spatial scales. However, a generalized pathway for downscaling GRA2PES for high-resolution modeling applications has not yet been established. Here, we present a framework for downscaling GRA2PES emissions directly to a user-supplied Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) domain using higher-resolution spatial surrogates while conserving emissions from the parent inventory. This approach lets users apply GRA2PES to the resolution and geographic extent of individual WRF domains for direct use in regional and urban chemical modeling applications.

498612.title: Assessing the Impact of Saharan Dust on Aviation Visibility and Flight Operations In The Eastern Caribbean: 2020 Godzilla Dust Outbreak
498612.authors: Janiea Marshall, CIMH, Bridgetown , 01, Barbados; and A. Sealy and R. Chewitt-Lucas
498612.abstract: Saharan dust is a mixture of sand and dust originating from the Sahara Desert and the Sahel. Saharan dust events are large plumes of minerals lifted off the Desert and transported by winds from Africa, across the Atlantic. These Trans-Atlantic dust plumes frequently impair regional air quality and atmospheric visibility throughout the Caribbean and Atlantic region, creating operational and safety issues for civil aviation. This research assesses how severe dust events affect aviation visibility and flight activities in the Eastern Caribbean, using the significant June 2020 Godzilla dust event as the primary case study. Firstly, Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) data from NASA’s AERONET network was examined together with surface meteorological information including METARs, SPECIs, and visibility observations obtained from the Caribbean Institute for Meteorology and Hydrology (CIMH), to measure the length and intensity of visibility deterioration. Furthermore, upper-air soundings were constructed to analyse the vertical profile and altitude of the Saharan Air Layer (SAL) relative to surface observations. Results show a direct correlation between peak AOD levels and prolonged drops in airport visibility below standard Visual Flight Rules (VFR) thresholds in Jamaica where visibility dropped below 5 km for 25 consecutive hours. Lastly, previous research papers within the same scope of study were used to provide comparative analyses for the initial results. In the future, this research can be further explored to provide more in-depth correlations between dust and other extreme aerosol events and aviation operations and aircraft safety in the Caribbean, using more statistical methods.

498614.title: Comparing cloud top vertical velocities in automated and manually tracked nascent convective cells in Southeast Texas
498614.authors: Jessica J. Burghardt-Scriven, Texas A&M University, Dripping Springs, TX
498614.abstract: 2027 AMS Conference Abstract Title: Comparing cloud top vertical velocities in automated and manually tracked nascent convective cells in Southeast Texas Authors: Jessica J.B. Scriven, Christopher J. Nowotarski, Milind Sharma, Anita D. Rapp, Sarah D. Brooks Previous research on deep convection intensity has focused on aspects of the near-storm environment on convective evolution. However, the influence of initial properties of nascent clouds (while convection initiation is ongoing), like cloud top cooling rate and cloud area, on later convective evolution has remained relatively unexplored. Furthermore, the variability of these variables between different convective initiation mechanisms, and the potential for using merged, automated radar and satellite tracking for individual convective cells have remained relatively unexplored. This research project attempts to both map satellite attributes of nascent cells to different initiation mechanisms and determine any notable relationships, and to assess the capability of automated tracking software for the tracking of individual nascent convective cells. The Summer 2022 Department of Energy TRACER project observations over the coastal Texas region are used as a foundation for data analysis due to the readily available sample of isolated deep convective cells and the relative lack of synoptic-scale influencing factors such as frontal boundaries (the goal of this project being to create such a database and provide a foundation for various future research on convective cells given the consistent conditions in the area of study). Overall, we aim to determine how cloudtop cooling rates mapped to each nascent cell initiation mechanism vary in their resulting effects on cloudtop vertical velocity, and also to assess the impact of automated tracking for individual cells to determine the worthiness of manual verification. In order to track individual nascent cells and their relevant thermodynamic variables, specialised software was utilised, using the Python Flexible Object Tracker applied to NEXRAD reflectivity as a foundation for identifying and tracking individual cells. At its earliest point, each radar-tracked cell was then matched to clouds tracked even further back in time using GOES-13 Channel 13 brightness temperatures and Channel 02 reflectance values to create individual profiles backtracked from initial radar echo. Within each satellite tracked cloud, minimum and average brightness temperature as well as cloud area were calculated. The results of the automated tracking algorithm were manually reviewed and classified to identify the initiation mechanism of each cell (e.g., sea-breeze front, outflow boundary, boundary layer turbulence) , and changes were made to cell track and/or area as needed., After manual track editing was complete, time series of cloud top temperature and cloud area are compared with the unedited automated results to assess the importance of manually verifying cell tracking, since the process of manual editing is rather time-consuming and would be desirable to avoid if unnecessary. In addition to an in depth discussion of the motivation and method for this work, results will be presented describing the frequency of cells initiated by each mechanisms, how cloud top cooling rates, estimated vertical velocity, and cell area vary by initiation mechanisms, and how much manual editing of cell tracks changes these results compared to a purely automated approach. Various additional parameters of these convective cells will also be assessed for any other potential noteworthy links to the aforementioned primary focus; any of these additional variables of interest will be included in the combined results. This potential additional research may also serve as a bridgehead for future research on this topic, in the case that some additional variables are worth extra investigation.

498615.title: Improving Public Response to Warnings through Terminology (Flash Floods and Destructive Severe)
498615.authors: Caleb Ross Pennington, OU SoM, Norman, OK; and J. Hall and A. Paoletti
498615.abstract: Weather warnings notify the public of a weather situation that poses a threat to life and property. Understanding the information of a warning is crucial for a larger majority of people to take protective actions. Getting more people to listen to warning messages in a short amount of time is also paramount, especially when there is little time to act. Using previously existing survey data, we aim to answer the question of how different wording in a warning prompts people to act in the moment. Our project focuses on Severe Thunderstorm Warnings and Flash Flood Warnings using two surveys done in 2022 and 2024 respectively. These surveys measure how much the public trusts certain sources and how concerned people would be based on different warning texts provided. These surveys show us how the public perceives different levels of warnings and how different information affects individuals during an event. Once we understand the best terminology for prompting action, we can tailor information properly to external sources and quickly reach bigger public groups that may not directly receive a warning. Prompting more people to take protective/precautionary actions through these methods will reduce harm done to people and maintain the trust of media outlets built-up over time.

498616.title: Sensitivity of Soil Moisture in CONUS to ENSO Amplitude
498616.authors: Benjamin Usher, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; and S. Larson and A. L. Griffin
498616.abstract: Soil moisture has a significant impact on wildfires, floods, and crop yield, thus making seasonal predictability valuable. The El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is attributed to a significant portion of the annual soil moisture predictability as a result of altered seasonal precipitation patterns, especially over CONUS. Currently consensus has not been reached on how climate change will impact ENSO, but some research argues that increased global air and sea temperatures will result in an increase in ENSO amplitude. The impact of higher amplitude ENSO cycles presents a significant area of uncertainty in future changes in precipitation patterns, thus with implications for seasonal predictability of soil moisture. To address this issue, we analyze 4 idealized Community Earth System Model version 2 (CESM2) simulations, each with a different amplitude ENSO cycle, to quantify the impact of ENSO amplitude on soil moisture. These include one simulation where ENSO is absent (No-ENSO) and three with different amplitudes of ENSO (low , moderate, and high). This approach allows for large sample sizes of even extreme ENSO events. The No-Enso run was used as the baseline for soil moisture variability unforced by ENSO. Seasons were quantified as El Nino or La Nina based on the DJF Nino 3.4 index preceding it, with an emphasis on Spring and Summer months, when implications for reduced soil moisture include amplifying heat waves and the likelihood of drought. Soil moisture has highly limited observational data, thus motivating this model experiment approach rather than analyzing historical data. Analysis of these model simulations indicates that soil moisture does not respond inversely between phases with this asymmetric relationship becoming more prevalent for the higher amplitude simulation. This suggests a higher amplitude ENSO cycle alone will result in an overall shift in mean annual soil moisture. Results under various amplitude El Nino events aligned with expected precipitation patterns in the US southeast southern California and soil moisture was amplified across the spring and became more widespread in the summer, especially in the Great Plains. With La Nina, anomalous soil moisture lows appear in the US south west in the spring. This low region strengthens and grows into the lower Great Plains during the summer, mirroring the pattern from El Nino but much more intensely. This could be an indication of La Nina amplifying the Southwest Monsoon, which future work should consider. Notably, more intense La Nina events did not have equally intense increases in soil moisture. This result suggests that soil type and regional geology plays a significant role in soil moisture variability. These results provide insight into what regions are more preconditioned for severe droughts if ENSO intensity increases.

498618.title: Assessing the Relationship Between Pre-Storm Soil Moisture Conditions and Tornadogenesis
498618.authors: Marissa Bugos, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and J. K. Beck, S. M. Quiring, and J. B. Houser
498618.abstract: Soil moisture is a critical variable in many land-atmosphere interactions, many of which influence day-to-day weather, including severe weather. Previous work has shown that wetter than normal soil moisture conditions occur during the time leading up to tornadogenesis. This work will identify the conditions when this relationship is strongest. Using North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS) soil moisture percentiles and tornado records from 2015-2018, this work investigates variations in the relationship between soil moisture and tornado formation to quantify how the relationship between soil moisture and tornadogenesis varies as a function of season, region, tornado strength, track length, and storm mode. This is a case study that analyzes these variables in specific storm events. Preliminary analysis has shown that soil is wetter than usual in the hours leading up to tornadogenesis at 5, 20, and 50 cm depths, especially in EF3+ tornadoes. Wetter soil is also prevalent in tornadoes with track lengths of over 40 miles. Understanding how tornadoes form is integral to increasing warning time to the public. Additionally, knowing where the relationship between soil moisture and tornadogenesis is strongest can aide in the prediction of severe weather.

498619.title: "Deep Convective Cloud Probabilities as Sport Strategies in Southern Africa"
498619.authors: Jazz Slappey, University of Miami, Decatur, GA
498619.abstract: Situated in south central Africa, which can also be considered the central continent of the world, the Democratic Republic of the Congo is a hub for captivating weather patterns that occur across the globe. With Africa located closely between regions in the Western Hemisphere and Eastern Hemisphere, the contingencies over time, in say a year, were a call to deeper examination. This research here looks closely at the formation of deep convection cells and future possibilities of these cells onto more in the Congo basin. The atmosphere is unstable due to the sun heating the ground, the ground heating the air, air rising, then radiative cooling where heat goes to space as longwave radiation. Latent heat release is increased by anvil longwave trapping outgoing heat and clouds have a cooling effect. Also, the diurnal cycle plays a role as these interactions have a short memory and are reset daily. So, deep convection occurs as a way to lower the center of gravity of the atmosphere. All motions are constrained to obey mass continuity and Newton's laws. The spatial arrangement of storms all serve a function with different strategies to accomplish that function. There's a rate in which potential energy converts to kinetic and the bigger that rate, the more efficient conversion and gravity rewards by growing strategies. This research helps to understand which pattern extracts energy from unstable atmosphere most efficiently by studying competition/interaction with two strategies. Additionally, the thunderstorms that deep convective cloud cells produce are crucial because of the risk associated. To name a few, these include lightning, soil moisture, and ground scarring. Understanding the conditional probability of these cells onto one another impacts the forecasts and ultimately the response. What the public can always look back on is when they received critical information, so this understanding matters in the timeline especially as weather patterns change according to the climatology. Drawing from chaos theory that as two weather systems may appear alike, but there may be differences in their initiations or any other detail; thus, their final outcomes are likely to not be the same (two sides like a game). Also, drawing from the phenomena that in a world of competitors and cooperators, everyone turns into competitors even if they don’t want to. Lastly, drawing from the aforementioned Hot Hand Fallacy that nearby convection is favored as one location has cells appear. Keep in mind: existing clouds modify the environment by moisture convergence, cold pools, diurnal cycle, vertical motion and gravity waves; all of which are represented in our conditional probability code. (Ex: if kernel radius= 10km, cold pools influence convection up to 10km away) When rain evaporates it requires latent heat, so air cools and the cold pools spread at surface leaving to the lifting of warm air (gust front lifting). More convection means more thunderstorms as the collisions of cold pools increase, so organized storm convection systems dominate. All these factor into triggering nearby clouds and the kernel captures the net effect. There are 2 kinds of players (orange and green) Probability kernels which consist of asymmetry, speed, and amplitude. 4 different kernels with green-orange, green-green, orange-green, and orange-orange. It’s a mix of self-influence/inhibition and cross influence/inhibition. So, how do we establish the boundaries for the simulation? Is there a salary cap? Are there superteams? Are any teams tanking in hopes of future gain? How do we create rules while keeping the convective cells organized? Each isolated storm isn't orange or green, but the system as a whole shows which strategy has the most influence. This understanding will develop because knowing how storms organize trickles into understanding of soil moisture sensitivity and climatological differences in regions, to name a few.

498620.title: Estimating PM2.5 Emissions from the 2025 Palisades Fire Using Satellite Data
498620.authors: Trinity M Abraham, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL; and H. Holmes and S. Dahal
498620.abstract: Wildfire smoke events contribute to the presence of gaseous pollutants and aerosols in the atmosphere, degrading air quality and adversely affecting human health. Thus, estimating fire emissions is critical not only for forecasting air quality but also for ensuring public health and safety. In January 2025, wildfires devastated Southern California, resulting in detrimental impacts on the environment as well as Los Angeles communities, with surface PM2.5 concentrations reaching as high as 300 µg/m3. The Palisades Fire burned over 23,000 acres, destroying thousands of homes and businesses in the area. The severity of this fire event accentuates the necessity for high temporal resolution (i.e., sub-daily) estimates of fire emissions. This study combines observations from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) and Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI), from polar-orbiting and geostationary satellites, respectively, to estimate hourly fire radiative power (FRP). Geostationary satellites, such as GOES-18, offer continuous monitoring of a specific region; however, they have higher uncertainties when detecting FRP. Polar-orbiting satellites such as VIIRS provide more accurate FRP measurements, but with limited temporal coverage. Daytime VIIRS FRP observations were utilized to calibrate the more frequent GOES-18 FRP measurements to apply the strengths of both satellite systems. GOES-18 and VIIRS observations were collocated within a temporal window of ± 3 minutes, and a relationship between these measurements was developed for the fire. The relationship between these values was applied to the GOES-18 time series to generate hourly VIIRS calibrated FRP estimates. This approach combines the VIIRS FRP with the continuous coverage of GOES-18, overcoming the limitations of both satellites. Fire radiative power represents the observed rate of emitted radiative energy by a fire at a specific time, with higher FRP values indicating greater amounts of burned biomass and heavier smoke production. Using the hourly FRP, empirical scaling equations were used to estimate the PM2.5 emissions for the Palisades Fire, preparing fire emissions for use as inputs to an atmospheric model that can simulate wildfire smoke transport. Hourly fire emissions allow changes to be monitored throughout the duration of the fire, rather than relying on the limited VIIRS overpass observations.

498622.title: Assessing the impacts of estuarine dynamics on water level measurement accuracy
498622.authors: Dahlia Barranco, University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA; and L. Heilman and R. Heitsenrether
498622.abstract: Estuaries are coastal environments characterized by the mixing of freshwater and saltwater, where tide-driven transport results in regular salt intrusion, impacting the density of the water column. This study aims to evaluate the variations observed among different water level measurement technologies utilized by NOAA’s National Water Level Observation Network (NWLON), particularly in estuaries. These differences result from how different sensors account for variable density and measure water level. The Center for Operational Oceanographic Products and Services (CO-OPS), a program office of NOAA's National Ocean Service, maintains the NWLON. CO-OPS provides reliable oceanographic and meteorological observations, reporting water levels and delivering tidal predictions for the Great Lakes and U.S. coastlines. This real-time data informs flooding outlooks and other forecasts to protect coastal communities and commerce. To investigate these differences, we deployed a subsurface bottom platform alongside a NOAA tide gauge along the Elizabeth River, a tributary of the Chesapeake Bay, located near Norfolk, Virginia. The bottom platform was equipped with an Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler plus two pressure-temperature sensors, one of which also measured conductivity, while another conductivity-temperature-depth sensor was deployed at a shallower depth. This instrument array was intentionally designed to complement the tide station's operational radar and pressure water level sensors. This instrumentation also captures additional water properties that contribute to reported water level measurements. Initial analyses utilize the collected observations to illustrate the different methods of measuring water level and varying water properties that affect reported water levels to reevaluate future studies. Results will inform our understanding of estuarine and coastal tidal dynamics, improving water level measurements where density varies spatiotemporally, ultimately supporting the reliability of NWLON water levels.

498623.title: From Laboratory Sparks to Natural Lightning: Quantifying Ultraviolet Emissions and Hydroxyl Production
498623.authors: Cheyanne Williams, Penn State University, Dumont, NJ
498623.abstract: Lightning is a potentially significant source of hydroxyl (OH) radicals, which are the primary mechanism for oxidizing and removing atmospheric pollutants. Quantifying ultraviolet (UV) radiation emitted by lightning provides insight into its OH radical production. However, quantifying UV radiation produced by individual lightning flashes is difficult due to a lack of observations. In this study, a Python-based image analysis program is developed and applied to UV and visible-light emissions from laboratory tesla-coil sparks observed with a UV camera. The resulting UV-to-visible emission relationship is then applied to satellite observations of natural lightning to estimate UV radiation and OH produced during lightning flashes. These estimates provide a first step towards improving our understanding of the lightning emission spectrum as well as further constraining lightning's role in atmospheric chemistry.

498624.title: Long-term Variation of the Urban Heat Island Effect at Dallas, Texas, and Chicago, Illinois
498624.authors: Justin Keith Robinson, North Carolina A&T State Uni., GREENSBORO, NC; and J. Zhang
498624.abstract: The Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect makes urban areas significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas, which has caused significant socio-economic and health impacts, particularly for vulnerable populations such as elderly adults, young children, and low-income families. In this study we perform a long-term climatology study of the UHI effect in the urban areas of Dallas, Texas, and Chicago, Illinois, using the climate data of PRISM (Parameter-elevation Regressions on Independent Slopes Model) with the following objectives: 1) analyze the long-term variation of the UHI effect in the selected two urban areas; and 2) quantitively compare the UHI effect during daytime and nighttime, during normal and extreme heat events, and at different geographical locations. The study methods involve using PRISM daily minimum and maximum temperatures at a 4 km resolution for the period 1980-2025, and Google Earth to map the study areas with land-use classes of urban, suburban, or rural. The UHI effect is measured by the average temperature difference between the urban and rural grids. The preliminary study results indicate that the UHI effect increases in both daytime and nighttime, though the nighttime UHI is much stronger and increases at a greater rate. Further investigation into whether this increasing trend in the UHI effect is attributable to climate change or urban expansion, and a comparison of UHI effects during typical extreme heat events and across different geographical locations, are ongoing.

498629.title: Development of an Improved Cloud Ceiling Diagnostic Algorithm
498629.authors: Donna Jade Ritter, Metropolitan State University of Denver, Denver, CO; and X. Sun and J. B. Olson
498629.abstract: Cloud ceiling forecasts are critical for aviation operations and weather forecasting, especially for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the National Weather Service (NWS). This study presents the implementation and evaluation of an improved cloud ceiling diagnostic algorithm using output from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model. The diagnostic utilizes optical depth, cloud and ice effective radii, cloud fraction, and mixing ratio to identify cloud ceiling conditions. The algorithm was evaluated against the Unified Post Processor (UPP) cloud ceiling product to assess its ability to reproduce and improve modeled conditions. Satellite observations were also used as a source of verification to evaluate the representation of cloud cover. The goal is to develop a diagnostic that more closely aligns with observed and operational ceilometer data while providing a foundation for continued refinement. This work provides a framework for physics model developers to identify limitations and improve cloud ceiling models in numerical weather prediction models, supporting improved forecasts for aviation and operational usage.

498630.title: Arctic Cyclone- Structure and Evolution: Accuracy of Wind Nudging Only Compared to Temperature and Wind Nudging
498630.authors: Trevor Tom, University of Washington, Renton, WA; and A. Jacobs and C. Bitz
498630.abstract: Arctic cyclones have large impacts on sea-ice redistribution and are hazardous to communities in the region because of the strong winds, precipitation, and sea-ice breakup. However, we are wondering how wind only nudging compares to wind and temperature nudging. Therefore, we examined two case studies of Arctic cyclones to determine if wind nudging alone is sufficient to accurately simulate Arctic cyclones or if wind and temperature nudging is required for accurate simulation. One case occurred in January 2022 as the strongest storm in the ERA5 (European Centre for Medium-Range Forecasts (ECMWF) Reanalysis 5) record while the other was a strong summer cyclone in July 2022. In addition, we used these case studies to determine if seasonality influences model performance compared to ERA5. To examine them, we evaluated data from ERA5 and from the Community Atmosphere Model (CAM). We analyzed plots from both cases to find differences between thermodynamic and dynamic evolutions to understand how nudging affects those processes separately. We expect adding temperature should better capture the thermodynamic evolution of the storms, meaning wind nudging alone is less accurate than temperature and wind nudging. Further, we anticipate seasonality influences model performance since stronger summer temperature gradients between land and open ocean may enhance early-stage thermodynamically driven cyclogenesis. Our research demonstrates the differences between both forms of nudging and how they change the simulations. Accurately simulating Arctic cyclones is important for understanding their structure and evolution and provides a baseline for future studies to understand the impact on sea-ice redistribution.

498631.title: Validation of Radar-defined Hydrometeor Classification via the Radar Columns and Aircraft Timeseries (RadCAT) Product
498631.authors: Bryce Ronald Rickbeil, Argonne National Laboratory, Lemont, IL; University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and J. R. O'Brien
498631.abstract: The understanding of atmospheric processes, specifically convective storm processes, is crucial for day-to-day life as these events impact people and property across the world. The Mid-latitude Continental Convective Clouds Experiment (MC3E) was a campaign hosted by the Department of Energy’s (DOE) Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Southern Great Plains (SGP) facility from April 22 – June 6, 2011, as a collaboration between the DOE and NASA. This campaign was focused on better understanding convective storm dynamics by utilizing a collection of ground-based and aircraft-based observations to explore mesoscale convective systems (MCS). The 20 May 2011 MC3E case has had significant attention from the scientific community to test agreements between observed radar reflectivity’s and in-situ aircraft observations of hydrometeor characteristics. However, the methods used for these comparisons are not openly available for the larger scientific community, limiting analysis of convective storm processes within recent and future campaigns. The Radar Columns and Aircraft Time-series (RadCAT) product was developed as an open-source method for spatiotemporally syncing radar and in-situ aircraft observations. Utilizing the Python ARM Radar Toolkit (Py-ART) and CSU Radar Tools, validation of radar defined hydrometeor classification with RadCAT is conducted. Exploration of periods identified by the C-band Scanning ARM Precipitation Radar, 2nd Generation (CSAPR2) as hail are explored, with particle images from the High Volume Precipitation Spectrometer (HVPS-3) indicating these regions are a collection of small graupel and melting large aggregates. Additionally, these hail identified periods indicate the potential to use RadCAT to explore the electrical structure of trailing stratiform MCS, as large chained aggregates are identified within the HVPS-3 images just above the radar observed melting layer.

498633.title: Comparing Classical Baroclinic Instability Models Across Physical and Numerical Parameter Regimes
498633.authors: Tim Eric August, Student, CHURCHVILLE, PA; and W. G. Blumberg
498633.abstract: Classical baroclinic instability models provide fundamental frameworks for understanding atmospheric and oceanic dynamics and serve as benchmarks for more complex numerical models. Although modern research increasingly relies on complex numerical simulations, classical models provide controlled benchmarks for evaluating and interpreting those simulations by isolating fundamental physical interactions. In this work, we derive the governing equations and dispersion relations for the classical Eady, Charney, Phillips, and N-Layer baroclinic instability models. Where analytical solutions are unavailable, we develop finite-difference numerical eigenvalue solutions to examine the effects of the planetary vorticity gradient (β) and the vertical discretization on phase speeds, growth rates, and convergence. We find that the planetary vorticity gradient alters the wavenumber cutoffs associated with unstable phase speeds and growth rates. In addition, increasing the vertical resolution reveals the emergence of Green modes (1960). The N-Layer model converges to the continuously stratified phase speed and growth rate solutions at second order. Furthermore, the numerical error shows a dependence on the planetary vorticity gradient: smaller values produce greater accuracy on coarse grids, whereas larger values require finer grids to resolve the associated potential vorticity gradients.

498635.title: Evaluating UHR ASCAT for Tropical Cyclone Intensity and Wind Field Structure
498635.authors: Samantha Fuchs, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and S. Walters and J. Carstens
498635.abstract: Satellites can give a high-resolution view of tropical cyclone (TC) surface wind fields, which can inform best track estimates of intensity and size. This study investigates how well the Ultra-High-Resolution Advanced Scatterometer (UHR ASCAT) product can be used to estimate tropical cyclone maximum wind speeds, comparing retrievals to global best track intensity data from the International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS). We develop an automated processing framework using UHR ASCAT wind fields published by NOAA STAR. The procedure applies quality control to remove retrievals affected by land and identifies usable satellite passes based on the availability of wind data surrounding the linearly-interpolated TC center. Specifically, a pass is considered to be good for analysis when wind data are present throughout a circle extending 1.5 times the radius of maximum wind (RMW) from the interpolated TC center. Then the UHR ASCAT maximum wind speeds get compared to the IBTrACS maximum sustained winds, and this comparison is used to measure the intensity bias. The analysis looks at how UHR ASCAT–IBTrACS intensity differences change as a function of IBTrACS TC intensity, and with the time mismatch between the satellite observation and the best track record. The latter analysis investigates if UHR ASCAT or other satellite remote sensing tools can identify episodes of rapid intensity change. Additionally, extra structural variables like the radius of maximum wind, minimum central pressure, and radius of tropical storm-force winds will be checked as possible drivers for variability in the ASCAT intensity bias. The results will help judge how useful UHR ASCAT is as a comprehensive observation platform for tropical cyclone intensity and wind field structure.

498636.title: Upper-Level Evolution and Mesoscale Forcing During the 24-25 January 2026 Oklahoma Winter Storm
498636.authors: Charles Durbin, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and S. Cavallo
498636.abstract: From 23 to 25 January 2026, a high-impact winter storm produced heavy snowfall, sleet, and dangerous cold conditions across the southern Great Plains (SGP). The storm developed within a strongly baroclinic environment ahead of an amplifying midlevel trough with a strong subtropical moisture source. Previous studies have shown that tropopause polar vortices (TPVs) are often associated with extreme cold air outbreaks (CAOs); however, it is less common for such CAOs to occur in conjunction with widespread precipitation. This study investigates how the evolution of a TPV and associated jet streak, as well as frontogenetic forcings, produced synoptic- and meso-scale forcings culminating in this high-impact event. European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts Reanalysis Version 5 (ERA5)data are employed in this study to analyze basic atmospheric conditions and to compute synoptic- and meso-scale forcings for this event. NOAA HYSPLIT backward trajectories are used to trace the airmass origin and characteristics. It is shown that a TPV interacting with both the subtropical and polar jet streams as it approached the SGP was an important feature that led to the generation of a jet streak resulting in broad synoptic-scale ascent over the region of interest due to low-level thermal advection. The presence of a high-amplitude trough with an additional TPV embedded north of the region was also important in providing ample conditions for an extreme cold air outbreak to occur in the SGP. As the trough moved eastward and southward and intersected the Gulf Coast, strong 850-hPa frontogenesis developed over a rich source of subtropical moisture to produce localized regions of heavy winter precipitation. These results establish a coherent temporal and spatial association between TPVs, its interactions with jet streams, and frontogenesis to result in an unusual and impactful winter weather event. Future studies will be needed to further isolate the exact role of each component.

498638.title: Negative Differential Backscatter Phase in Characterization of Hailstorms
498638.authors: Rylan Lopez, University of Oklahoma, School of Meteorology, Austin, TX; and J. Ho, G. Zhang, J. T. Carlin, J. Gao, V. N. Mahale, A. V. Raaijmakers, S. Kotturi, P. McCrone, P. Bukovcic, and M. Johnson
498638.abstract: ABSTRACT: Differential phase (ΦDP) and its range derivative, specific differential phase (KDP), contain information about precipitation microphysics and have been used in quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE), particularly where traditional Z-R relationships fail. Measured ΦDP is composed of the differential propagation phase (φDP), differential backscattering phase (δ), and measurement error (ε). Most existing KDP estimators were developed based on the assumption of Rayleigh scattering, under which δ is negligible and ε can be substantially reduced through smoothing. However, this assumption does not hold when hail or melting snow are present, even in S-band radar measurements. Hail and melting snow can scatter S-band radar signals in a non-Rayleigh scattering regime, which can induce a nonzero δ and cause a localized departure from the otherwise monotonically increasing ΦDP field. Recent advances in KDP estimation algorithms show that this δ should not be neglected, both due to its tendency to contaminate operational KDP estimates and because it may provide useful information for characterizing storms. Negative δ signatures appear as localized dips in the raw ΦDP field, and are often colocated with moderate to strong reflectivity (Z) and low correlation coefficient (ρHV). Most existing least-squares-fit (LSF) KDP estimators, including the operationally used algorithms on NEXRAD, do not account for or estimate δ. In operational KDP fields, this appears as negative and positive couplets along the radar beam where KDP is being first underestimated, and then overestimated to correct for the previous underestimation. In this work, we utilize a classification-based linear programming (LP) method with physical constraints to separately estimate both KDP and δ. This estimation algorithm has been developed to be compatible with currently operational systems should this become an option. We analyze several cases in which negative values of δ are present, and establish relationships between the present hydrometeors and the δ signature. We find that large hail of approximately 5 cm (~2 inches) or greater in diameter tends to be moderately to strongly correlated with negative δ signatures. In addition, we see this negative δ in cases of melting snow where ZDR is enhanced, and ρHV is reduced. Our finding suggests that this signature may be important and useful in severe weather detection, potentially addressing part of the challenge of estimating hail size from polarimetric radar variables. The isolation of the δ contribution can additionally improve KDP estimation and, consequently, QPE and storm characterization.

498640.title: Assessing the Relationship of Large-Scale Weather Regimes and Teleconnections on Peak Energy Load in the United States
498640.authors: William Thomas Beasley III, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and C. G. Berry, Student, L. Ryan, and J. Wagstaff
498640.abstract: Assessing the Relationship of Large-Scale Weather Regimes and Teleconnections on Peak Energy Load in the United States Cold air outbreaks (CAOs), which are periods (3-7+ days) of extremely cold temperatures, are associated with unusually high energy loads in the United States every winter. However, accurately predicting the timing, location, and severity of CAOs remains challenging, limiting the ability to anticipate periods of elevated peak energy load. Such elevated peak load can potentially lead to blackouts and other infrastructure issues, raising the socioeconomic costs of CAOs. Previous studies have linked variability in the Northern Hemisphere stratospheric polar vortex and North American weather regime behavior to wintertime temperature patterns across the central United States. However, the relationship between these factors and making long-range predictions of peak energy load in the central United States has not been explicitly investigated. This study examines to predict periods of elevated peak energy demand in the central United States during CAOs from 1 to 5 weeks ahead of time using large-scale teleconnection patterns. We make use of a standardized index of polar vortex strength, weather regime patterns, Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) load data, and ERA5 reanalysis data, to analyze the relationships between these variables. Composite maps for 2-meter temperature anomalies, mid-tropospheric geopotential heights, and jet stream winds are first computed with lead time of 1 to 5 weeks to see statistically if there are significant relationships. We then evaluate whether polar vortex and weather regime behaviors can provide useful predictive information for CAOs and extreme peak load events using a standard linear regression model and a simple neural network. The results between the two are compared and forecast skill is quantified. Overall, this research will identify the potential for long lead prediction of peak energy load during the winter, allowing for better preparation for these events.

498641.title: Spatio-Temporal Analysis of Tornadic Activity Trends and Exposure for Public K-12 Schools in Georgia, 1950-2024
498641.authors: Treja Jaslynn Smalls, University of Georgia, Athens, GA; and J. M. Shepherd
498641.abstract: Tornado activity is becoming increasingly concentrated over eastern U.S. and exposure growth has amplified tornado disaster potential. Georgia has experienced substantial population growth over recent decades, home to over 11 million people. The state's location in the southeastern U.S. introduces a unique type of tornado vulnerability due to its dense tree cover, nocturnal tornado threat, and population density. This region experiences a disproportionate amount of tornado deaths despite producing fewer overall tornadoes than the Midwestern U.S. Education facilities such as K-12 schools are often included in hazard mitigation and emergency planning efforts, though research on their long-term exposure to tornado hazard are limited. The large concentration of students and staff in addition to being distributed across diverse environments highlight a need for this analysis. This study will investigate the spatiotemporal trends of tornadoes across Georgia over an ~75 period from 1950-2024. This study will utilize the Severe Weather (SVRGIS) Database (1950-2024) to assess statewide tornado climatology and identify localized trends by region over this span of decades through ArcGIS. Analysis of tornado counts and track trends will occur on a county-level, and statistically significant regional hotspot shifts will be observed using Kernel Density Estimation and Getis-ord Gi* and will be aggregated by decade to examine temporal variability. To assess exposure of K-12 schools to historical tornado hazard, data from the National Center for Educational Statistics will be used to geocode all 2025 K-12 locations and overlay them with tornado hazard surfaces. Proximity analyses, path intersections, and hazard extraction will occur. County-level exposure metrics will be developed and compared across benchmark years for decadal trend observation. Preliminary results analyzing the total tornado count from 1950-2024 show spatial clustering in the west-central portion of Georgia, and Southwest Georgia for weaker (EF0-EF1) tornadoes. Strong (EF2-EF3) tornado occurrences, are less concentrated than its weaker counterparts with greater variability in its locations spanning most of Georgia. Violent (EF4-EF5) tornadoes are rarer and much more localized to eastern coastal Georgia, northwestern near the Tennessee border, and on the middle Alabama border, indicating singular events. Laurens, Colquitt, and Early county lead the state in total tornado counts with 19-23 tornadoes each and there are 20 counties located in eastern central Georgia who have seen the least amount of tornadoes over the years in the 0-4 total tornadoes each category. These upcoming spatial models will provide highly localized, actionable baselines for regional emergency planning.

498643.title: Heavy Rain Events and Rapid Permafrost Thaw in Northern Alaska
498643.authors: Gracyn D Nehring, Metropolitan State University of Denver, Denver, CO; SUNY, Buffalo, NY
498643.abstract: Alaskan permafrost is threatened not only by increasing global surface temperatures, but also by increasing rain events. With northern latitudes experiencing Arctic amplification, non-frozen precipitation is contributing to rapid permafrost melt during the warmer months. Thawing permafrost results in both immediate and long-term hazards. Ground instability threatens infrastructure while recently thawed soil releases trapped greenhouse gases. Both in-situ and remote sensed data were used to visualize changes in soil and air temperature near Toolik Lake from 2016-2026. Preliminary, interferometric synthetic aperture radar (inSAR) imagery was used to monitor major changes in the active layer of permafrost as heavy rain events permeate the soil, helping scientists identify areas of ground subsidence.

498645.title: The Eye from Above: Tracking Three Decades of Eastern U.S. Deep Convection Using GOES-East Satellites
498645.authors: Patrick Jeremiah Newman, University of Massachusetts Lowell, Woburn, MA
498645.abstract: Leveraging the GOES Fundamental Climate Data Record (GOES-FCDR) provides a nearly continuous dataset for calculating climatological trends. This project presents a climatological analysis of mid-latitude continental deep convective systems utilizing 4km, 11 µm infrared channel data from successive generations of operational GOES-East satellites over the Eastern CONUS, focusing on the meteorological spring and summer months (March-August) from 1995 to 2024. With many earlier studies focused on the evolution of tornadic trends, this study isolates large-scale continental deep convective systems, such as Mesoscale Convective Systems (MCSs). By employing the Tracking and Object-Based Analysis of Clouds (tobac) Python package alongside custom spatial filtering, we successfully detect localized cold-core cloud features, their surrounding structural cloud shields, and linked storm trajectories. Tracking parameters and thresholds include ≤215 K for identifying convective brightness temperature cold core features, as well as an areal extent of at least 960 km2 for broader storm characteristics. These parameters allow us to track the most mature and intense phases of convective activity, thereby allowing for an evaluation of monthly climatological metrics, including track location densities, maximum areal footprint, track persistence and length, and core brightness temperature intensities. To evaluate long-term spatial variations, filtered storm trajectories are aggregated into multi-year spatial plots. These distributions, alongside temporal time series of system counts and structural behavior, highlight changes to the convective season. Ultimately, this tracking framework establishes a baseline for understanding how large-scale continental deep convective storm structure and frequency has fluctuated across the Eastern United States over a 30-year climate record.

498646.title: Assessing Near-Surface Weather and Air Quality Simulations in the California Central Valley using WRF
498646.authors: Malia Pasillas-Pablo, California State University, Stanislaus, Turlock, CA; and J. Cervantes-Duran, W. To, and J. D. Mirocha
498646.abstract: This work examines how well the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model can simulate near-surface meteorology and air pollution in California’s Central Valley (CCV). The first objective of the project is to evaluate WRF’s ability to simulate near-surface meteorology and to examine the role of Land Cover/Land Use (LCLU) maps, which influence surface energy exchange. Meteorological analysis is based on comparisons between WRF-simulated weather conditions and observations from the California Irrigation Management Information System. Simulations using LCLU maps from 2010 have shown significant discrepancies in atmospheric moisture, with model accuracy generally decreasing with increasing distance from the San Joaquin Delta. This presentation will show how updated LCLU and irrigation maps impact WRF simulations across the region. The second objective is to better understand and model air quality within the CCV using WRF with Chemistry (WRF-Chem) and by comparing simulation results with ground-based observations from NASA’s Aerosol Robotic Network (AERONET) and Pandora instruments. Combining these efforts will improve our understanding and predictive capabilities for near-surface weather and air-quality parameters that affect both agricultural productivity and human health and well-being within this key agricultural region. This work is an undergraduate research project in the Department of Physics and Physical Sciences at California State University, Stanislaus, in collaboration with NASA Ames Research Center and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.

498648.title: Midwest Extremes: Quantifying 26 Years of Excessive Heat Events and Demographic Risk
498648.authors: Nasir Grant, OEMS, Jacksonville, FL; Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL; and M. Costa and A. Boreham
498648.abstract: This study investigates the spatial and statistical relationships between population change and exposure to Excessive Heat Events (EHEs) across the 12 states of the Midwest Census Region. With only using hourly Meteorological Terminal Aviation Routine Weather Reports (METARs) from 82 Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) stations between 2000 and 2025, paired with the United States Census API data of population between 2000 and 2020, this research analyzed Compound Annual Growth Rates (CAGRs) with EHEs and heat waves. Statistical regression metrics showed that population growth alone is a poor linear predictor of EHE and heat wave counts. Although spatial interpolation maps showed a geographical risk gradient, most noticeable in the southwestern Midwest, including Kansas and Missouri, and least noticeable toward the northeast. Surprisingly, the stations in cities with the largest populations did not experience the same number of EHEs, which voids the argument that infrastructure and asphalt cause greater EHE exposure. Overall, this study concludes that geographic climatology is more dominant than demographic shifts in determining EHE exposure in the Midwest, underscoring the importance of geography over population change (CAGRs).

498649.title: From Warning to Shelter: Improving Tornado Preparedness in Schools
498649.authors: Ciara Audrey Longo, Millersville University, Millersville, PA; Millersville University, East Stroudsburg, PA; and S. Hammaker and A. Shive
498649.abstract: Severe weather warnings are effective only when the people receiving them understand the threat, know where to go, and can act quickly. Schools present a particular preparedness challenge because large numbers of students and staff must receive warning information, move rapidly to designated shelter locations, and remain protected within buildings that vary substantially in age, construction, layout, and available refuge space. This project examines how meteorological information, building-specific shelter assessment, and emergency planning can be integrated to improve tornado preparedness in primary and secondary schools. The project will use the National Weather Service Severe Weather Preparedness Guide for Schools as its primary framework. The NWS recommends that each school develop a plan appropriate to its individual building and circumstances, identify interior shelter locations on the lowest practical level, maximize the number of walls between occupants and the exterior, avoid windows and large-span rooms such as gymnasiums and auditoriums, consider the configuration of interior hallways, provide reliable and redundant methods for receiving and communicating warnings, and regularly practice and evaluate the school severe-weather action plan. FEMA guidance for identifying the best available refuge areas in existing buildings will provide an additional basis for evaluating shelter locations. Working with select local primary and secondary schools, we will develop and apply a standardized severe-weather preparedness assessment. The assessment will begin with a review of each school's existing emergency action plan, warning and notification procedures, building floor plans, designated tornado shelter areas, and procedures for students, staff, buses, after-school activities, and individuals with mobility or other accessibility needs. Students will then conduct a guided building walkthrough with appropriate school personnel to evaluate designated shelter locations. Factors will include distance from exterior walls and windows, number of intervening walls, location within the building, corridor geometry and exterior openings, proximity to large-span roofs, shelter capacity, accessibility, and potential hazards from glass or debris. The meteorological component of the project will examine how schools receive and interpret severe weather information. Particular attention will be given to understanding the distinction among outlooks, watches, and warnings; monitoring National Weather Service products; maintaining redundant warning sources; and translating a tornado warning into an immediate protective action. Interviews with school administrators, facilities personnel, emergency-management personnel, or other designated staff will identify differences in preparedness practices, perceived vulnerabilities, and barriers to improving severe-weather procedures. Each participating school will receive a baseline preparedness assessment based on a common rubric. In collaboration with school personnel and, where possible, local emergency management and the National Weather Service, the student team will then recommend practical improvements. These may include revised shelter locations, updated shelter maps, clearer warning and communication procedures, improved signage, alternative routes, staff responsibilities, and modifications to severe weather drills. Where building characteristics present vulnerabilities that cannot be addressed procedurally, the project will identify the need for professional engineering evaluation or longer-term mitigation rather than attempting to prescribe structural solutions. A subsequent drill or tabletop exercise will be used, where feasible, to evaluate the revised plan. Measurable outcomes will include shelter travel time, shelter capacity, number and type of preparedness deficiencies identified, changes implemented following the initial assessment, and changes in the school's overall preparedness score. Results from participating schools will be aggregated to identify common strengths, recurring vulnerabilities, and practical interventions that can be transferred to other schools. The final product will be both a research assessment and a community-engagement model demonstrating how meteorology students can translate weather information into protective action. Results will focus on the assessment methodology, participating-school results, representative preparedness improvements, and a replicable school severe-weather assessment framework. Ultimately, the project seeks to strengthen collaboration among schools, meteorologists, emergency managers, and the National Weather Service while helping schools move beyond simply conducting a tornado drill toward developing, practicing, and continually improving comprehensive severe-weather emergency action plans.

498651.title: Influence of ENSO Teleconnection on Surface Ozone in Baltimore-Washington Region
498651.authors: Kaliyah Simone Bennett-Reynoso, University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC), Atmospheric Physics, Crofton, MD; and J. A. Richards, D. Parada, J. Gordon, and B. Demoz
498651.abstract: The El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) teleconnection has global effects on synoptic setups dependent on its phase. These different setups can have an impact on air quality and in particular on ozone production near the surface. Previous research has found effects of the teleconnection on surface ozone in both Houston Texas and the Northern Front Range Metropolitan Area of Colorado but little to no research has been done to explore the Eastern United States. In this study we take ozone surface monitors and historical ozonesonde records from the Baltimore-Washington Region of Maryland examine the influence of the El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) teleconnection on air quality within the region. Utilizing 30 years of surface ozone observations from continuous ambient monitoring stations run by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), we evaluated these large-scale influences and their relationship to exceedances of the 70 ppbv National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS) for ozone. Linear regression fits to the daily peak 8-hour average concentrations for each county revealed an increasing trend throughout the selected period. Utilizing the Oceanic Nino Index (ONI) index to distinguish El Nino, La Nina, and neutral phases of ENSO, and removing an overall increasing trend in ozone exceedances revealed a higher amount of ozone exceedances in the warm season (May, June and July) during both El Nino and La Nina phases in comparison to the neutral phase across all counties within the region. We perform statistical analyses to further explore this finding and examine how meteorological conditions associated with these phases would encourage this enhancement.

498657.title: High Ozone Warnings for Environmental Justice Communities - A Localized Two-Stage Machine Learning Framework
498657.authors: Divyansh Kumar, Montgomery Blair High School (STEM Magnet Program), Silver Spring, MD
498657.abstract: Environmental justice (EJ) communities often experience disproportionate air pollution burdens, yet regional ozone forecasts can mask neighborhood scale differences in air quality and health risk. This limitation is especially consequential on Code Orange or higher days, defined here as days when the daily maximum 8 hour average ozone concentration (MDA8) reaches at least 71 ppb. This study develops a localized, two stage machine learning framework intended to improve advance identification of these health relevant events at four monitoring locations near EJ communities in the Washington, D.C., metropolitan region. Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Regression, and a CNN–bidirectional LSTM with attention were trained using March–October data from 2017–2019 and 2022 and independently tested on 2023. Models predicted ozone one hour ahead using meteorological, temporal, and lagged ozone variables. Two input configurations were evaluated: a 1-hour window (H1) and a rolling 24-hour window (H24). Hyperparameters were selected through Bayesian optimization with five-fold time-series cross-validation. For each target day, hourly predictions were used to calculate MDA8 ozone, AQI, and color category. The best performing model varied by site: XGBoost H1 performed best at McMillan, XGBoost H24 at Prince George’s Equestrian Center, and Random Forest H24 at HU-Beltsville and Rockville. These models achieved R² values of 0.71–0.86 and improved agreement with observed AQI color categories by 8–24 percentage points compared with the official regional forecast. H24 performed slightly better at three of four sites. Despite strong average performance, rare Code Orange+ events remained difficult to predict. Only 2–8 such days occurred at each site in 2023, and none were correctly identified. A refined analysis therefore focused on XGBoost and Random Forest and incorporated additional transport and atmospheric variables, including upwind ozone, shortwave radiation, cloud cover, boundary-layer height, 10-m wind speed, and ventilation index. Elevated ozone observations were given greater weights during model fitting. The refined framework used two stages. Stage 1 predicted hourly ozone concentrations, with XGBoost H24 providing the strongest overall performance. However, it correctly identified only 1 of 20 Code Orange+ site-days. Stage 2 used an XGBoost classifier to estimate the probability that hourly ozone would reach at least 60 ppb, providing earlier indication of potentially elevated MDA8 conditions. Rolling 8-hour probabilities were combined with a development calibrated plausibility threshold based on Stage 1 MDA8 predictions. An AND gate issued a warning only when both components indicated elevated risk. The classifier alone detected 13 events with H1 and 14 with H24 but produced 86 and 108 false alarms, respectively. The AND gate detected 7 of 20 events with H1 while reducing false alarms by 87%, and 9 of 20 events with H24 while reducing false alarms by 81%. Thus, H1 provided greater precision, whereas H24 provided greater sensitivity. These results show that strong overall concentration prediction performance can obscure poor performance on rare, health relevant ozone episodes. Combining concentration regression with event focused classification increased Code Orange+ detection from 1 of 20 site-days to 7–9 of 20 while removing more than 80% of classifier false alarms. The approach provides a pathway toward localized high ozone warning systems designed around the events of greatest public health consequence.

498658.title: Puget Sound Convergence Zone event's impact on snowfall totals at Stevens Pass Ski Resort.
498658.authors: Ian James Hamrick, Metropolitan State University of Denver, Denver, CO
498658.abstract: The Puget Sound Convergence Zone (PSCZ) is a narrow band of enhanced precipitation that forms when winds split around the Olympic Mountains and converge over the Puget Sound in western Washington. This project will examine how PSCZ events influence snowfall totals at Stevens Pass Ski Resort in the central Cascades. To accomplish this, the research will look at PSCZ events from the past 20–25 years using radar data, surface observations, and data from the National Water and Climate Center. These events will be compared with snowfall measurements from Stevens Pass to determine how often PSCZ events produce snow at the resort, how much snow they transport, and whether winters with more PSCZ events tend to have higher snowfall totals. The goal of this research is to understand whether PSCZ events play a role in snowfall production at Stevens Pass. This information may improve short‑term winter weather forecasting and support operational planning for ski areas and mountain travel in western Washington.

498663.title: Withdrawn: Evaluating TDS Height Utility for Tornado Emergency Issuance
498663.authors: Elijah Conklin, Valparaiso University, Valparaiso, IN; and L. Blind-Doskocil, E. C. Wolff IV, and J. Goodnight
498663.abstract: In 2014, the NWS formalized the tornado emergency (TORE) as a distinct product to be used as the highest level of tornado warning. In subsequent years, the NWS Warning Decision Training Division (WDTD) developed a set of guidelines to be used by forecasters when considering whether to issue a TORE. Previous research by Wolff et al. (2026) found that the rotational velocity (VROT) and/or significant tornado parameter (STP) guidance were not met in the majority of TORE cases from 2014-2023, but this study did not investigate the guidance related to tornadic debris signature (TDS) height. A TDS is an area of low correlation coefficient on radar, collocated with high reflectivity and a velocity couplet, that indicates the presence of debris being lofted by the tornado to the radar beam height. The WDTD guidance lists the TDS height threshold for an EF2+ tornado as 8,000-10,000 feet, but research on TDS height and its relation to tornado intensity is limited. To test the utility of TDS height for TORE issuance and whether this can be used as a predictive measure for tornado intensity, the 89 TOREs investigated in Wolff et al. (2026) will be analyzed from the 15 minutes preceding TORE issuance time until 15 minutes after the warning’s expiration. TDS height at each elevation angle of the nearest radar with a correlation coefficient threshold of 0.8 or less will be recorded, along with VROT and mesocyclone width. The radar data will then be matched with damage points in the Damage Assessment Toolkit (DAT) to examine the time offset between TDS height and maximum damage.

498665.title: Creating and Applying a Geospatial Model of Snow-Filled Crevices in the Northeastern United States
498665.authors: Reid Buchanan, SUNY Oneonta, Oneonta, NY; SUNY Oneonta, West Hartford, CT; and C. Karmosky
498665.abstract: The purpose of this project is to establish snow-filled crevices as a distinct sub-category of ice caves, map currently known ice caves and related features in the northeastern United States, and create a geospatial model to identify areas that can support snow-filled crevices. Snow-filled crevices are cracks in the ground that fill with snow in winter and retain ice into the summer months. Even after they melt out, they maintain an internal temperature significantly lower than the outside. There are at present two known snow-filled crevices in the northeastern United States: the Petersburg Snow Hole in the Taconic Mountains and the Crevice at Ice Cave Mountain in the Adirondack Mountains. Temperature, snowfall, and bedrock geology data were gathered to create a geospatial model that highlights areas in the northeastern United States that are most likely to support snow-filled crevices. Minimum thresholds were established for average annual temperature and snowfall based on data from the Snow Hole and Ice Cave Mountain. It is hypothesized that snow-filled crevices can only exist in non-porous rocks, so the bedrock geology data were selected based on that criteria. At present, the model covers New York and Vermont, but it may be expanded in the future to include other areas of the northeastern United States.

498668.title: Project MELD: Misovortex Evolution and Landspout Dynamics
498668.authors: Steven Ralph Daniel Lenz, MSU Denver, Aurora, CO
498668.abstract: Landspouts are a common phenomenon during mesoscale driven severe weather episodes, particularly in the High Plains with topographically influenced areas of surface vorticity. Though we have an understanding about where landspouts come from and how landspouts develop, the specific microscale influences / triggers behind misovorticies strengthening into landspouts are still not very clear. Surface boundary characteristics, storm interactions, forcing mechanisms, topography, and background atmospheric parameters have to work together in very specific ways to allow misovorticies to mature into landspouts, and the steps between a misovortex becoming a landspout are still not properly understood, especially in cases where mature misovorticies on thunderstorms don't become landspouts while weak surface boundaries with only cumulus clouds sometimes do. The purpose of Project MELD is to find out these missing steps, and the purpose of this first presentation is to share possible clues taken from several years of observing storms as well as unanswered questions subject for a possible field research campaign in the future.

498670.title: Refining a Reconstructed Temperature Record of a Taconic Mountains Snow Filled Crevice to Account for Radiational Cooling
498670.authors: Sofia Gould, SUNY Oneonta, Oneonta, NY; and C. Karmosky
498670.abstract: The Petersburg Snow Hole in Petersburg, NY is a crevice in the ground located in the Taconic mountains that retains its winter snowpack into mid-summer. A recent study was done on this site to determine whether the geologic environment and air temperatures could support permafrost by reconstructing a temperature record of the area, but the model performed poorly on radiational cooling nights. This study aims to address this limitation by creating monthly predictive temperature models for nights where radiational cooling does, and doesn’t occur. Data from three NOAA COOP stations were compared to Snow Hole data as well as data from a nearby station at WIlliams College in Williamstown, MA to create the temperature models much like the previous study. Skew-T diagrams from Albany at 1200 UTC were also analyzed for every day that there was temperature data from the Snow Hole to determine which nights had radiational cooling and which nights did not. The nights with and without radiational cooling had separate multiple linear regressions performed on them to create a temperature model for each month based on the temperatures at the 4 stations as they related to the Snow Hole. The models for radiational cooling nights performed slightly better than the models for non radiational cooling nights. This is most likely due to the higher number of radiational cooling nights, meaning more data to base the equation on. This study is essential for the understanding of snow filled crevices and how they are able to trap cold air, and provides a more detailed model for predicting temperature at the Snow Hole.

498673.title: Toward a Transferable Observability-Aware Framework for State-Scale Boundary-Layer Climatology: Maryland as a Testbed
498673.authors: Christopher "Chuck" C. Baker Jr., University of Maryland, College Park, MD; University of Maryland College Park, College Park, MD; NOAA Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR), Boulder, CO; University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and P. Stratton, X. Ren, and X. Z. Liang
498673.abstract: Planetary boundary layer height (PBLH) is often treated as a directly comparable quantity across observing systems, although wind profilers, radio acoustic sounding systems (RASS), ceilometers, radiosondes and aircraft profiles respond to different physical properties and sample different temporal, vertical and horizontal volumes. These distinctions become especially important in Maryland, where coastal advection, inland and urban forcing, complex terrain, stable and residual layers and vertical shear can produce multiple lower-tropospheric boundaries. Maryland’s compact coastal-to-highland environmental gradients and heterogeneous mix of fixed and moving observations provide a demanding testbed for a state-scale framework intended to extend beyond a single observing network. Using Maryland as the initial testbed, this study develops an observability-aware framework for interpreting boundary-layer structure and climatology, designed for adaptation to other state- and regional-scale observing networks. We hypothesize that atmospheric regime organizes lower-tropospheric layer architecture, which then determines when heterogeneous diagnostics converge on one dominant boundary and when they identify physically distinct layers. The framework is built around wind-profiler observations from Beltsville, Piney Run and Horn Point spanning 2013 through July 2026. RASS, ceilometers, radiosondes and airport-centered AMDAR profiles provide conditional thermodynamic, aerosol and kinematic constraints, while ASOS/AWOS and Maryland Mesonet observations characterize surface state and regime context. Initial archive reconciliation shows substantial differences in usable wind and RASS support among the three profiler sites and nonuniform overlap among platforms, supporting a nested pairwise observational design. The analysis constructs the largest scientifically admissible sample for each platform pair. Matching rules account for time offset, altitude above ground level versus mean sea level, fixed versus drifting or slanted profiles, aircraft flight leg and trajectory, retrieval eligibility and the physical boundary represented by each diagnostic. Atmospheric states are classified first by stability and boundary-layer phase and by flow and advection. Cloud, precipitation, aerosol structure, shear and terrain coupling are incorporated where observational support permits. Regime-conditioned observability is then evaluated using boundary-height differences, detection or non-detection, transition timing, robust spread and uncertainty. Transferability will be evaluated by separating general platform roles, matching logic and regime dimensions from site-specific geometry, environmental setting and data availability, then testing relationships across held-out sites, seasons and years. Finally, a baseline profiler climatology will be compared with state-conditioned and pairwise platform climatologies to determine whether observability materially changes diurnal, seasonal or site-level conclusions. The resulting synthesis will report a common boundary where diagnostics are physically comparable and retain multiple labeled boundaries or an indeterminate state under partitioned conditions. By distinguishing general observability logic from Maryland-specific sampling and environmental constraints, the framework provides a physically explicit basis for boundary-layer climatology, air-quality interpretation, observing-network design and model evaluation, while establishing a method whose applicability can later be evaluated in other heterogeneous observing networks.

498674.title: Evaluating Performance and Dynamical Consistency of AI Models in Predicting a Late 2025 Atmospheric River
498674.authors: Matt Case, University at Albany, Albany, NY
498674.abstract: Global AI weather forecasting models have been shown to outperform traditional weather models. However, it remains unclear how these models predict regional severe weather and whether they learn and capture the correct dynamics. The goal of this study is to evaluate the performance and dynamical consistency of two AI models, AIFS and AIFS-CRPS, in predicting the high-impact atmospheric river event that affected the U.S West Coast in late December 2025. By comparing with the ERA5 reanalysis, we assess how well the models predict precipitation and the associated dynamical processes in California at different lead times.
