Preliminary results indicate that notable differences emerge in key dynamic features, such as moisture transport, vorticity, and upper-level jet, with increasing lead times. However, the precipitation forecast errors are consistent with errors in the predicted dynamical processes. These results provide a comprehensive assessment of the AI models and help improve confidence in AI predictions.

498676.title: Longevity of Tornado Season and the Shift of Tornado Alley in the United States
498676.authors: Samantha Jo McAllister, Metropolitan State University of Denver, Denver, CO
498676.abstract: Does Climate Change impact the longevity of tornado season and the shift in tornado alley? Due to the increased air and water temperatures in the Gulf, along with the changes in ENSO, how does the data from 20-30 years ago, differ to today's trends with climate change? Within the last 30 years, the surface water temperatures in the gulf have increased as well as the surface air temperatures. By looking at the shifts in both the winter and summer months, the observations of mid-latitude patterns, and comparing storm reports between the Great Plains region and the Mississippi River Valley, that data can help to determine how climate change has made an impact, if any, on the tornado season and the areas hardest hit by tornadoes.

498677.title: Impact of the Saharan Air Layer on Diurnal Convection and Lightning Activity over Western Puerto Rico
498677.authors: Yadiel Torres González, Student, Mayagüez, PR; and B. Wolding
498677.abstract: Saharan Air Layer (SAL) events transport dust across the Atlantic Ocean directly to Puerto Rico. In Puerto Rico, the regional mid-summer drought occurs between June and July, which coincides with the peak of Saharan dust concentrations over the island in July. This led us to investigate the effects of the SAL on rainfall and lightning activity across western Puerto Rico. We utilized the NCAR supercomputer, Derecho, to analyze multi-sensor data using Jupyter notebooks, combining observations from GOES satellites, MERRA-2 reanalysis, and weather radar. Our results showed that the SAL significantly reduces both rainfall rates and lightning flashes over western Puerto Rico, but it does not alter the timing of when peak afternoon convection occurs. Looking at the thermodynamic profiles, the SAL significantly reduces the available moisture at mid-levels while slightly increasing temperatures aloft. This creates a thermal capping inversion that enhances convective inhibition (CIN). We will research the effects of the SAL on our local weather, which will help us to better understand these events and to improve regional weather and climate models.

498678.title: The Relationship Between Gulf SSTs and Increased Cool-Season Tornados in Oklahoma
498678.authors: Amelia Flahie, University of Oklahoma, Holt, MI
498678.abstract: Occurrences of tornados in the state of Oklahoma between October and February have significantly increased within the last five years. Between 1950 and 2019, the annual average number of tornados in the cool-season time period was 5.10. Between 2020-2024, the annual cool-season tornado count jumped to 22.6. In addition, sea surface temperatures (SSTs) in the Gulf of Mexico/Gulf of America since 2020 are roughly 0.5℃ to 1.5℃ higher than they were between 1991-2020. This research will focus on a possible connection between cool-season Oklahoma tornados and warmer-than-normal SSTs. Elevated sea surface temperatures increase evaporative potential, which can result in higher boundary-layer dew points within the marine layer. When the more-moist marine layer is advected northward into the Southern Plains, greater atmospheric instability is realized (Li 2026), resulting in a favorable environment for tornados. This research will investigate overall trends in SSTs, tornado occurrences, and boundary layer dew points and how they are correlated. It will also demonstrate several case studies featuring cool-season Oklahoma tornado events in the 2020s to establish the link between elevated Gulf of Mexico/Gulf of America SSTs and cool-season Oklahoma tornados. These cool-season tornados also are more likely to be nocturnal (Ashley 2007), which means there is an enhanced risk to public safety. A better understanding of the causes of the increase in cool-season Oklahoma tornados can improve severe weather forecasting and help inform operational forecasters, public safety officials, and the general public about probability and risk of tornados at a time of year when they are less common.

498679.title: Leveraging SUNY Oneonta as a Living Laboratory to Better Understand Local and Regional Climate Change and Variability
498679.authors: Emma Panzarella, SUNY Oneonta, Cooperstown, NY; and A. Hannigan
498679.abstract: Since 1983, the SUNY Oneonta Earth & Atmospheric Sciences Department has maintained a daily record of weather variables including temperature, dewpoint, pressure, wind, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, and solar radiation. These observations were recently used to develop a 30-year climate normal record for Oneonta NY, providing a long-term baseline of average local climate conditions. This project aims to enhance that dataset with the addition of a temperature-moisture profile of the SUNY Oneonta campus. The current HOBO RX3000 weather station atop the Perna Science Building provides a continuous record of weather conditions at one location on campus. However, this region experiences elevation-dependent weather hazards, particularly in the winter months, some of which cannot be fully captured by the primary weather station. The addition of HOBO RXW-THC-900 wireless sensors at other locations will allow for a more thorough examination of spatial and temporal variations in temperature and humidity. By observing and analyzing such patterns, fine-scale variability of these elements across the Oneonta region can be better characterized. To achieve this, five wireless sensors — each with a transmission range of 1500ft— will be installed across campus, collecting temperature, dewpoint, and relative humidity data at 5-minute intervals. Preliminary locations were determined for these sensors in collaboration with SUNY Oneonta Athletics. The sites identified align with high-use athletic fields, which will allow for easy access to near-field conditions, and coincidentally, form an ideal range of elevations for profiling. Sensor placement was constrained by physical obstructions that interfered with line of sight between sensors and the main station. The acquisition of HOBO RXW-RPTR-900 repeaters was necessary in combatting several signal and connectivity issues. Once the network is fully operational, the athletics department will be able to use a customized online dashboard, updated in real time, to inform decision making. An additional dashboard will also be available to the public, further advancing the goal of making Oneonta climate and weather data accessible to more people. While designed to investigate temperature and humidity patterns across the SUNY Oneonta campus, this micronet can support a range of applications beyond the scope of this study.

498680.title: Elevated Risk? Quantifying Drought in Alpine Environments Under Climate Change
498680.authors: Brayden Mikulski, Mississippi State University, Starkville, MS; and J. K. Beck
498680.abstract: Climate change is projected to change precipitation patterns that will result in shifts in hydroclimatic extremes. These changes will influence the timing, frequency, severity, spatial extent, and duration of droughts. Understanding these changes in drought characteristics are important for predicting environmental events such as wildfires as well as agricultural yield. Most research has been focused on investigating soil moisture and drought impacts with respect to elevation at regional scales. This study aims to create ensembles for alpine environments and project future soil moisture conditions. This will be evaluated across multiple warming scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5) at various elevations in the Contiguous United States (CONUS). Results will shed light on how drought frequency, severity, and duration will change in mountainous and flatter regions. Outcomes of this project will improve methods for preparing for drought on a national scale.

498684.title: The Case Study of the June 3rd Supercell
498684.authors: Erick Drayton, SUNY, New York, NY
498684.abstract: This summer, I spent two weeks storm chasing in the Midwest of the United States. I'm specifically focusing the day June 3rd when we were in South Dakota. There were multiple cells popping up but failed to become super cellular. Eventually, a cell found a favorable environment. My research is covering that cell from the moment it appeared on the radar to the minute it began to weaken. The reason I chose this topic is because I find it so interesting that so many cells failed while this one cell in particular thrived.

498685.title: Comparison of Boundary Layer Environments in Proximity to Storms during the Evening Transition
498685.authors: Michael McCarthy, Millersville University, Millersville, PA; and W. G. Blumberg, M. Muller, M. Cokain, J. Biondo, P. Corman, A. Jones, and B. White
498685.abstract: The evening transition (ET) period has notable effects on the boundary layer of the atmosphere. However, still much is unknown about what occurs during this timeframe. Studies (Blumberg 2018, Coffer and Parker 2015) show that the increased low-level shear associated with the nocturnal low-level jet (NLLJ), along with an increase of moisture around sunset, can help to make the boundary layer more favorable for storm development or storm prolongation. During May 2026, members of Project TILTTING-BL (Thermodynamic Investigation into LCL Thresholds for Tornadogenesis in the Northeast and Great Plains – Boundary Layer), an undergraduate research initiative at Millersville University of Pennsylvania, deployed to the Great Plains to study how the evening transition affects the boundary layer in proximity to thunderstorms. Throughout the deployment, data collection commenced across several Intensive Observing Periods (IOPs) in which the team performed frequent windsonde launches and near-surface observations. Windsondes were launched in the near field of storms both before and after the evening transition to observe changes in the kinematic and thermodynamic profile. These changes were compared with existing documented data of the evening transition based off their Sunset Relative Time (SRT), a metric showing what changes can be expected in parameters (such as moisture, wind, shear, etc.) at times based on their proximity to the ET.

498687.title: How Possible Is It? Investigating Influences that Affected the Issuance of Tornado Possible Tags in Severe Thunderstorm Warnings on April 18th, 2019
498687.authors: Gabriel Slade, Mississippi State University, Starkville, MS; and J. R. Reed
498687.abstract: How Possible Is It? Investigating Influences that Affected the Issuance of Tornado Possible Tags in Severe Thunderstorm Warnings on April 18th, 2019 Severe thunderstorm warnings sometimes include a tornado possible tag (TORTAG) to indicate the potential for tornado development within a thunderstorm. The TORTAG is issued when forecaster confidence is not high enough to issue a tornado warning. The issuance of the TORTAG in severe thunderstorm warnings remains highly subjective to forecaster interpretation and tolerance of environmental conditions within and near a storm. Both forecaster confidence and environmental conditions that typically differentiate a TORTAG severe thunderstorm warning from a tornado warning remain poorly documented. To better understand the environmental factors that may contribute to the issuance of TORTAG severe thunderstorm warnings, data from a severe weather episode on April 18, 2019 in the Deep South was collected. Using a combination of radar observations, interviews with National Weather Service forecasters, storm-scale velocity data, warning polygon data, and environmental data, we will perform quantitative analyses and develop statistical visualizations of severe weather data, storm-scale characteristics, and warning polygon data to answer three questions. 1.) For two storms at an equal distance from the radar, how did shared distance influence the operational decision to include TORTAG? 2.) How did the specific storm-scale velocity signatures of storms correspond to the operational decision to issue a TORTAG during the event? 3.) How did the environmental conditions during the April 18, 2019 event correspond to the operational decision to issue a TORTAG? Preliminary analysis has identified variations in storm-scale characteristics and environmental conditions among storms during the April 18, 2019 event. Quantitative and statistical analyses will further examine the relationships between these factors and operational warning decisions. The results of this study will be beneficial to anyone who issues or communicates the hazards associated with TORTAG severe thunderstorm warnings.

498688.title: The Linearity of Precipitation Trends in Response to Evaporation Anomalies
498688.authors: Timothy James Considine IV, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and T. W. Aerenson, D. McCoy, and D. Caulton
498688.abstract: Accurately modeling precipitation remains a critical challenge in climate science due to the complex dynamics of the hydrologic cycle. This study investigates the linearity of global precipitation trends by establishing direct, causal links between evaporation source regions and their corresponding precipitation fields. We employ the WAM2layers moisture tracking model to construct a comprehensive global map that routes moisture from specific evaporation sources to its ultimate precipitation destinations. Using the evaporation field to estimate global precipitation validates well in most regions. To evaluate the nature of these relationships, we systematically perturb the evaporation rates within source regions to estimate the subsequent changes in downwind precipitation. The difference between the actual precipitation pattern and that derived from mapping evaporation to downwind precipitation indicates non-linearity in the response of downwind precipitation to evaporation anomalies. This work provides critical insights into moisture transport dynamics, and how it ultimately sets precipitation across the globe.

498689.title: Flood Events in the United States: Flood-Related Fatalities
498689.authors: Sam Rose Huckstep, Southern Illinois University Edwardsville, Edwardsville, IL
498689.abstract: Flooding is the leading cause of death from atmospheric hazards and studies have shown that there has been a rise in fatal floods over the last several years. While there are still some years with fewer floods, these events are becoming more frequent due to the potential association with global warming. The purpose of this study is to analyze demographic, spatial, and temporal patterns of flash flood-related deaths in the United States for the years 1996-2025. Following earlier studies such as Ashley and Ashley (2008), Storm Events data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NCEI 2025) was gathered for the years 1996-2025. The Storm Events dataset contains records on flood related fatalities, locations, and times. Statistical analysis was completed in Excel to look at distributions of age, gender, and seasonal timing. Spatial patterns of deaths are examined using maps created in ArcGIS Pro. The results of this study will allow for a better understanding of flood fatality patterns in the United States. The goal of the research is to better understand how flood fatality patterns have changed over time. The results of this research will hopefully improve preparedness and response to these events by allowing for a better understanding regarding flash flood-related deaths in the United States.

498690.title: Radiosonde Return and Reusability Evaluation for Enhanced Rapid High Altitude Weather Observations
498690.authors: Laura Maria Tra, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK; and B. Walker and J. Jacob
498690.abstract: Radiosondes attached to weather balloons are sent into the atmosphere to measure the variations of pressure, temperature, humidity, and wind speed and direction. Generally, radiosondes are not recovered after gathering data, resulting in a negative environmental impact caused by abandoning radiosondes and allowing them to degrade, an issue that is exacerbated by the need to conduct periodic launches with multiple radiosondes to investigate changing weather patterns. To address this environmental issue, this project investigates recoverability and reusability of radiosondes. By attaching a Graw radiosonde to a Meteoglider produced by Meteomatics, data can be collected on the descent as well as the ascent. With a programmed autopilot, the glider can be returned to a previously set location on the ground for simple recovery of the glider and the radiosonde. Additionally, gliders give radiosondes an increased flight range, enabling this technology to be used to gather data that was previously inaccessible, such as atmospheric measurements from severe storm fronts. However, because radiosondes are designed for single use, the reliability of data collected on the descent and on subsequent flights of a previously flown radiosonde is evaluated by comparison with other atmospheric measurements collected simultaneously. A camera is attached to the tail of the glider to gather images from the flights.

498692.title: Do Corporate Climate-Risk Disclosures Reflect Physical Flood Exposure?
498692.authors: Ruixuan Ding, The Ohio State Univ., Columbus, OH; and S. M. Quiring
498692.abstract: Climate-related flood risks show increasing challenges to corporate infrastructure, supply chains, and long-term economic resilience. At the same time, companies are under growing pressure to disclose physical climate risks through voluntary reporting frameworks such as the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP). However, it remains unclear whether corporate climate-risk disclosures align with the actual spatial distribution of physical flood exposure. In this study, we investigate the relationship between corporate climate-risk attention and flood exposure across the United States using CDP disclosures from 2013 to 2024. We apply Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modeling to quantify the proportion of disclosure text related to physical climate risks and combine these results with facility-level flood exposure assessments derived from reported corporate site locations and flood hazard layers. We then evaluate temporal and spatial patterns of alignment and mismatch between disclosure attention and physical flood exposure. Our preliminary results indicate that reported corporate flood exposure increased substantially over time, largely driven by expanding participation in CDP reporting and increased disclosure of facility locations. In contrast, climate-risk attention exhibited strong temporal variability, with elevated disclosure attention during 2017–2020 followed by declining attention after 2020. Spatial evaluations indicate persistent regions where companies have relatively high flood exposure but low climate-risk attention, particularly in various coastal and metropolitan areas. These findings indicate that the company's attention to physical climate risks is only partially aligned with actual flood exposure patterns.The study highlights potential blind spots in corporate climate-risk awareness and adaptation planning.

498693.title: The Construction and Utilization of a Mobile Mesonet for Project TILTTING-BL
498693.authors: Melanie Jones, Millersville University, Millersville, PA; and C. A. Longo, I. J. Gray, A. J. Guillaume, A. C. Haberman Sr., B. H. Nornhold, D. D. Reynolds, K. S. Rooney, J. F. Zwolinski, S. M. Waugh, and W. G. Blumberg
498693.abstract: Real-time ground weather observations are a crucial part of in-situ severe weather research. Originally founded in 2021, Project TILTTING-BL (Thermodynamic Investigation of LCL Thresholds during Tornadogenesis and its Influence in the Northeast and Great Plains – Boundary Layer) is an undergraduate research initiative at Millersville University of Pennsylvania. The project, initially researching LCL heights, underwent its first deployment to the Great Plains during the spring of 2024 with its first iteration of a Mobile Mesonet – an anemometer and GPS mounted on a PVC rack. After the project shifted its research goals to focus on changes in the near-storm boundary layer during the evening transition, it was determined that a more substantial Mobile Mesonet was required. In preparation for the spring 2026 deployment, the project developed its second Mobile Mesonet, upgrading to a sturdier aluminum rack and incorporating new instrumentation such as pressure, temperature, dewpoint temperature, and humidity sensors. A substantial addition to the new Mobile Mesonet was the U-Tube, an aspirated device that houses the temperature and humidity sensors, designed by Dr. Sean Waugh of the National Severe Storms Laboratory. The U-Tube was constructed with help from Dr. Waugh, with the main intent of its construction being a desire to capture data without solar radiation errors and “wet bulb” cooling, ensuring the evening transition could be properly documented. To test accuracy of results, the data from the Mobile Mesonet is being compared to data from the Oklahoma Mesonet with preliminary results showing that temperature readings aligned with the Oklahoma Mesonet.

498695.title: Dual-Pol Radar Analysis of the 2026 North American Blizzard, "Winter Storm Hernando"
498695.authors: Lauren Grace Tushar, Millersville University of Pennsylvania, Austin, PA; and N. Morris
498695.abstract: This study investigates the usage of radar and the utility of specific radar products during the bombogenesis intensification of the 2026 North American Blizzard. The blizzard was a major winter weather event that formed off the coast of North Carolina on February 21, 2026, and impacted much of the northeast during the February 23-24, 2026, period. As the system moved up the East Coast, it rapidly intensified into a bomb cyclone, creating widespread blizzard conditions that were characterized by heavy snowfall and strong, damaging wind gusts. The most severe impacts were on February 23, when snowfall rates and wind speeds peaked, particularly across Rhode Island and Massachusetts. A mixture of qualitative and visualization methods was used within this study to gain an understanding of the application of radar products and imagery, and their importance on the prediction of the system and its impacts, as well as the tracking of transition periods throughout the duration of the event. An investigation into the origin of the low-pressure system that would later undergo bombogenesis as it moved off the East Coast and into the Atlantic was conducted. As the system moved into the northeast, the focus of the study shifted to the KBOX radar in Massachusetts. Radar data from the period of February 22-24, 2026, with a focus on products such as base reflectivity, base velocity, base spectrum width, echo top, correlation coefficient, differential reflectivity, and specific differential phase products were examined. This focus also included the use and applications of derived products during this winter weather event verified with ground-based observations and the Storm Prediction Center’s estimates of snowfall totals to validate the accuracy of the findings. Based on an assessment of S-band radar products, benefits and shortcomings were identified that would be beneficial in the short-term prediction and lifecycle of winter weather events. This study found that radar products were especially beneficial with ground-based tracking of the system as it moved up the East Coast, enabling for detection of where the heaviest and lightest snowfall was occurring, as well as any areas of convection developing within the system. This was achieved through the usage of base reflectivity, spectrum width, and correlation coefficient products to identify the intensity, size, and movement of precipitation. Monitoring of convective pockets aided with the understanding of the system’s movement based on velocity and shear effects, in addition to the locations of hail formation. Radar systems in general have helped with determining the impacts of blizzards through enhanced understandings of the variation in wet and dry snowfall, and total snowfall accumulation. This was partially done through the application of the hydrometeor classification (HC) derived product, and to some extent, through accumulation products such as the digital accumulation array (DAA) and digital storm total accumulation (DSA). There were several limitations during this event due to range folding which was especially prevalent in the base reflectivity, base velocity, and spectrum width products. In addition, the KBOX radar experienced beam blockage, and at times, specific tilts were not available. The derived products – HC, DAA, and DSA – were also not reliable. The HC product showed persistent graupel around the radar, which, based on surface observations and skew-T profiles, was inaccurate. It also showed constant dry snow, although various products suggested the occurrence of wet snow. Based on previous studies, DAA and DSA are not reliable in snow due to radar calibration settings and non-Rayleigh scattering. This study noted the same, as they severely underestimated the in-situ snowfall, as well as the total accumulated snowfall. As an example, when ground-based observations had rates of 3 inches/hour, radar had around 0.6-0.8 inches/hour. The upgrade of dual-pol technology has proved to provide more accurate information and therefore a better understanding of winter weather. In addition, the proposed improvements as part of the next upgrade to the radar network along with gap-filling radars promise to provide more accurate information for short-term predictions and validations.

498696.title: Ozone Production Regimes and Compound Meteorological Extremes over U.S. Nonattainment Areas: Insights from TROPOMI and TEMPO
498696.authors: Yohan Yang, Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey, New Brunswick, NJ; and D. Chatterjee, Y. Wang, Y. Li, and X. Jin
498696.abstract: Ozone (O3) near the surface is a secondary air pollutant that poses risks to human health and the environment. Over the US, the most densely populated and industrialized regions continue to experience ozone exceedances despite substantial emission reductions over recent decades. Whether these exceedances are driven by emissions or meteorological extremes such as stagnation and heat waves remains difficult to separate, yet critical for targeting the right emission controls. Here, we use sun-synchronous TROPOMI and geostationary TEMPO observations, to diagnose changes of ozone precursors as well as the ozone production regimes on exceedance days. We then assess how stagnation events and heat waves modulate these regimes and contribute to the ozone exceedances over the study period. TROPOMI NO2 and HCHO columns are broadly elevated on exceedance days across U.S. nonattainment areas, with larger increases in urban cores and more modest increases in surrounding suburban areas along the East Coast. HCHO/NO2 column ratios similarly increased across most regions, though the magnitude varies by location. On exceedance days, ozone production is predominantly NOx-limited, with the strongest signal concentrated in urban centers. In terms of meteorological co-occurrence, stagnation accounts for 59% of exceedance days along the West Coast, while most other regions show exceedances occurring without concurrent stagnation or heat waves. The Northeast is a notable exception in exceedance days, stagnation alone (12%), heat waves alone (23%), and their combination (8%) together account for roughly 40% of exceedance days over 2020-2023.

498697.title: Withdrawn: Seasonal Prediction Skill and Predictability of Physical and Biogeochemical Variables in the Caribbean
498697.authors: Milo Haniel Soto Pérez, GFDL, Aguada, PR
498697.abstract: Seasonal ocean forecasts can provide valuable information for marine resource management, fisheries, conservation, and blue economy planning in the Caribbean. Their usefulness, however, depends on the ability of forecasting systems to represent both physical ocean conditions and the biogeochemical processes that support marine ecosystems. This study evaluates seasonal prediction skill and predictability of physical and biogeochemical variables across Caribbean Sea ecoregions using the high-resolution MOM6-COBALT-NWA12 forecasting system. Retrospective 12-month forecasts initialized quarterly and spanning 1994–2023 were analyzed for sea surface temperature, sea surface salinity, bottom temperature, nitrate, phosphate, bottom oxygen, surface chlorophyll, and net primary production. Forecast performance and predictability were quantified across multiple lead times using the detrended anomaly correlation coefficient (ACC). Physical variables were additionally evaluated against available observational datasets to characterize forecast skill, while comparisons with corresponding model analyses were used to assess predictability. Results reveal substantial differences in seasonal prediction skill and predictability among variables and forecast lead times. Physical variables generally retain useful skill over longer lead times, whereas biogeochemical variables exhibit greater spatial and temporal variability. Detrended analyses further demonstrate that long-term trends can substantially influence conventional skill estimates, highlighting the importance of separating trend-related agreement from interannual predictability. These results improve understanding of physical and marine ecosystem predictability in the Caribbean and help identify where seasonal forecasting systems provide useful predictive information, supporting continued development of ocean and biogeochemical prediction capabilities for ecosystem management, conservation, and NOAA’s environmental prediction mission.

498699.title: Evaluating Performance and Dynamical Consistency of AI Models in Predicting the March 10-12, 2026 Severe Weather Outbreak
498699.authors: Michael John Miller, University at Albany, Albany, NY; and Z. Wu and R. Lazear
498699.abstract: While global AI-based weather forecasting models are rapidly transforming the field of weather prediction, it remains unclear how well they predict regional extreme weather and represent the correct dynamics. In this study, we evaluate how well the AI models predict the high-impact March 10-12, 2026 severe weather outbreak in the continental US and the associated dynamical processes across various lead times. We assess predictions of the deterministic and ensemble AI models developed by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) and compare them with ERA5 reanalysis. The results show that the prediction errors increase with lead times for surface variables. We further examined what dynamical process the AI models incorrectly predicted and how this affected the surface predictions of the event. While the AI models generally capture the dynamics of the severe weather outbreak, they may have performed better in certain regions impacted by the storm than in others. The results provide a comprehensive dynamical analysis for global AI models and help improve our confidence in AI predictions for regional extreme events.

498700.title: Do Block Level Air Pollution Data Represent Where People Work? A Geographic Coverage Assessment
498700.authors: Mohsen Nikfarjam, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and E. Nikfarjam
498700.abstract: Environmental studies increasingly connect where people live with where they work, but block level air pollution products may not represent both sets of locations equally well. We assessed the geographic support obtained when 2010 census block NO2 and PM2.5 model predictions were linked to version 7.5 Census Bureau Longitudinal Employer Household Dynamics Origin Destination Employment Statistics. The pollution files contain 6,234,988 exactly aligned block records for the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia. We streamed these records against S000 JT01 Residence Area Characteristics and Workplace Area Characteristics files using exact 15 digit block identifiers. Direct residence versus workplace comparisons were restricted to the 48 jurisdictions represented in both products because Massachusetts lacks a 2010 workplace file in this release. We measured coverage as matched primary job weight divided by total LODES primary job weight and audited the published race and ethnicity marginal sums against the all job count. All demographic sum checks passed. Residence area linkage covered 110,862,318 of 114,104,475 all job weight, or 97.16 percent. Workplace linkage covered only 70,904,544 of 114,233,027 all job weight, or 62.07 percent. Workplace coverage ranged from 44.20 percent in the District of Columbia to 84.79 percent in Vermont and differed across demographic marginals, including 57.82 percent for Asian alone job weight and 62.61 percent for White alone job weight. All workplace job weight in blocks with positive census population was covered, compared with only 1.76 percent in zero population blocks. Missingness was concentrated in urban, high job density, workplace intensive blocks, a pattern consistent with the pollution product's emphasis on residential or nonzero population centroids. A population weighted tract fallback raised all job coverage to 99.68 percent but smoothed within tract gradients and materially changed NO2 estimates. The fallback is a sensitivity analysis, not a replacement for complete block level predictions. The current workplace concentration results therefore remain diagnostic rather than nationally representative. This audit demonstrates that broad residential coverage does not guarantee valid coverage where people work, a general concern for mobility informed environmental and social vulnerability research.

498701.title: Air Pollution Inequality Across the Communities Where United States Workers Live
498701.authors: Ehsan Nikfarjam, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and M. Nikfarjam
498701.abstract: Where workers live can shape their contact with ambient air pollution, yet workforce geography is often absent from national environmental inequality assessments. We linked 2010 annual modeled NO2 and PM2.5 concentrations to the Residence Area Characteristics files in version 7.5 of the Census Bureau Longitudinal Employer Household Dynamics Origin Destination Employment Statistics. The analysis used S000 JT01 primary job counts at 2010 census blocks in the 48 jurisdictions that also have corresponding workplace files, preserving all block identifiers as 15 digit strings. We summed the published long range, mid range, neighborhood, and near source concentration components and calculated concentration means weighted by the published LODES race and ethnicity marginals. Race and ethnicity were analyzed separately because the public files do not provide their joint distribution. Exact block linkage retained 110,862,318 of 114,104,475 all job weight, or 97.16 percent. Matched weight coverage across demographic categories ranged from 96.01 to 97.28 percent. For NO2, the residence area mean weighted by Black or African American alone job counts was 23.1 percent higher than the corresponding White alone mean, and the Asian alone mean was 47.1 percent higher than the White alone mean. The Hispanic or Latino weighted NO2 mean was 38.6 percent higher than the Not Hispanic or Latino mean. PM2.5 contrasts were smaller: the Black or African American alone mean was 10.7 percent higher than the White alone mean, the Asian alone mean was 2.0 percent higher than the White alone mean, and the Hispanic or Latino mean was 0.6 percent lower than the Not Hispanic or Latino mean. These are descriptive residence area concentration patterns for primary job tabulations, not personal exposure estimates or causal effects. LODES data are administrative tabulations subject to privacy protection and nonsampling error, and the concentration fields are model predictions whose uncertainty has not been propagated. The results establish a residential workforce baseline for future analyses that distinguish the communities where people live from the places where they work.

498702.title: When Places Change but Identifiers Persist: Building Valid Environmental Comparisons Across Census Years
498702.authors: Ehsan Nikfarjam, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and M. Nikfarjam
498702.abstract: Environmental conditions change over time, but the geographic units used to measure communities also change. We conducted a reproducibility audit of a national workflow that linked 2000 and 2010 decennial census demographics, modeled NO2 and PM2.5 concentrations, and historical Home Owners' Loan Corporation polygons. The audit examined data codebooks, the production script, analytical sample counts, geographic keys, centroid construction, and newly inventoried 2000 and 2010 state, county, tract, and block group boundaries. The concentration product locates both years on 2010 census blocks, whereas the demographic inputs include an ordinary 2000 block table and an ordinary 2010 block table. The production workflow inner joined them using the same formatted 15 digit identifier but implemented no geographic crosswalk. It retained 3,080,166 identifiers representing 139,665,947 residents in the 2000 input and 156,820,030 residents in the 2010 input, far below the complete national census populations. The code also constructed point geometries at block centroids for historical grade assignment rather than rendering millions of block polygons. The boundary inventories use different year specific schemas. The unfiltered files contain 65,310 tract features for 2000 and 73,669 for 2010, with 208,672 block group features for 2000 and 219,774 for 2010, but differences in geographic universe also mean these raw counts are not measures of boundary change. A textually matching block identifier across census vintages does not establish that it represents the same physical area. Consequently, the prior 2000 to 2010 population weighted changes and same identifier temporal correlations cannot yet be interpreted as harmonized longitudinal estimates. One defensible design can allocate 2000 demographics to 2010 geography with a documented crosswalk and quantify allocation uncertainty. Another can hold 2010 demographic weights fixed for both concentration years to estimate pollution change for a fixed population distribution. These safeguards provide a foundation for valid longitudinal studies of air pollution, wildfire smoke, climate hazards, transportation access, social vulnerability, mobility, and environmental policy.

498704.title: On the Wind-Wave Forcing of Multi-scale Ocean Surface Slope Statistics
498704.authors: Junzhe Liu, LDEO, New York, NY
498704.abstract: The classic Cox and Munk (1954) wind–mean-square-slope (MSS) relation provides a foundational framework linking ocean surface roughness to wind forcing, which forms the foundation for radar remote-sensing applications over the ocean. However, relatively few studies have examined scale-dependent surface roughness, particularly in the ocean, largely due to observational challenges in resolving short-wave dynamics. In this study, we exploit advanced visible polarimetric measurements collected during the ASIT-2019 field campaign to investigate the ocean surface roughness across a wide range of spatial scales -- from long-period swell to gravity–capillary waves with wavenumbers up to approximately 700 rad m⁻¹. We investigate the mean responses to wind other environmental forcing, and we also present observations of long-wave phase-coherent modulation of gravity–capillary waves. We quantify the modulation attributed to (a) free-wave components, modulated by both airflow perturbations and hydrodynamic interactions, and to (b) bound-waves. The study contributes to the understanding of the complicated dynamics of ocean gravity–capillary wave forcing and modulation. Furthermore, the results have important implications for the modulation of Bragg waves in X-band and Ka-band radars, which can inform the development of future wind and surface current radar retrieval algorithms.

498706.title: Understanding the Environmental Characteristics of Canadian Prairie Tornadoes Using ERA5 Proximity Soundings
498706.abstract: *]:pointer-events-auto R6Vx5W_threadScrollVars scroll-mb-[calc(var(--scroll-root-safe-area-inset-bottom,0px)+var(--thread-response-height))] scroll-mt-[calc(var(--header-height)+min(200px,max(70px,20svh)))]" dir="auto" data-turn-id="request-6a8bc0a3-bfe0-83ea-8335-a47268909d41-92" data-turn-id-container="request-6a8bc0a3-bfe0-83ea-8335-a47268909d41-92" data-testid="conversation-turn-229" data-turn="assistant"> During the summer months, the Canadian Prairies experience various severe weather events, including tornadoes. Understanding the environmental conditions that favor tornado development and persistence requires detailed information on the thermodynamic and kinematic characteristics of the atmosphere near tornado initiation. Radiosonde observations provide vertical profiles of temperature, pressure, moisture, wind speed, and wind direction throughout the troposphere and are widely used to characterize severe-storm environments. However, radiosonde observations are spatially sparse and typically available only twice daily. This limitation is particularly important across the Canadian Prairies, where radiosonde stations are widely separated and no operational radiosonde station is located in Saskatchewan. To address these spatial and temporal limitations, this study uses proximity soundings derived from the ERA5 reanalysis (Hersbach et al., 2020) for observed tornado events across the Canadian Prairies. ERA5 profiles were obtained using the Python package SounderPy (Gillett, 2025), and a suite of thermodynamic and kinematic severe-weather parameters was calculated from the resulting atmospheric profiles following approaches established in previous peer-reviewed studies. ERA5 provides hourly temporal resolution and a horizontal grid spacing of approximately 0.25° × 0.25° (~31 km), enabling spatially and temporally consistent characterization of tornado environments across the region. We analyze approximately 200 observed land-based tornadoes and compare their environmental characteristics across EF intensity classes, provinces, and months. We further compare the thermodynamic and kinematic environments associated with tornadic and non-tornadic supercells across the Canadian Prairies. Preliminary results indicate that the majority of observed Prairie tornadoes are associated with supercell thunderstorms and are predominantly rated EF0–EF1. Tornado lifetimes are generally short (<30 min), while long-track tornadoes are exceptionally rare. Tornadic supercells are characterized by substantially greater low-level storm-relative helicity, with many events exceeding 0–1-km SRH of 150 m² s⁻², and lower lifting condensation level heights, frequently below 1200 m, compared with non-tornadic supercells. Comparisons with environments documented for the U.S. Great Plains further suggest that several commonly used tornado-environment parameters and classifiers may require lower threshold values to discriminate tornado potential over the Canadian Prairies. These regional differences demonstrate that thresholds developed primarily from U.S. Great Plains environments may not be directly transferable to the Canadian Prairies. The results highlight distinct thermodynamic and kinematic characteristics of Canadian Prairie tornado environments and emphasize the importance of developing regionally appropriate severe-weather forecasting guidance. These findings may contribute to improved operational tornado forecasting, severe-weather risk assessment, and climate adaptation strategies across the Canadian Prairies.

498709.title: Case Study of a Record Lightning Flash Rate Thunderstorm in Northern Florida/Southern Georgia
498709.authors: Chloe June Knight, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL
498709.abstract: Space-based lightning sensors such as the Lightning Imaging Sensor (LIS) and the Optical Transient Detector (OTD), which are predecessors of the Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM), have found thunderstorms with the highest lightning flash rates in the world to be continental Mesoscale Convective Systems (MCSs) due to their vast size, complex structure, and favorable environment for intense convection. However, recent analyses of unusually high localized lightning rates have identified a maritime thunderstorm along the Gulf coast as the top land-based case detected by GLM. Maritime thunderstorms have been underappreciated in previous studies of total lightning production, which includes both intracloud and cloud-to-ground lightning, throughout the entire thunderstorm lifecycle. This is because of their typically smaller sizes and compact structures that cause individual flashes to overlap in lightning measurements. This artificial flash merging makes it difficult for GLM to quantify lightning flash rates in the most intense thunderstorms. This study investigates the top flash rate land-based maritime thunderstorm detected by GLM, which was found in the North Florida/Southern Georgia region of the US, to better understand its development and processes enabling its extremely high flash rates. The thunderstorm occurred on March 19th, 2018, and reached its peak intensity over Tallahassee FL, expanding into Thomasville and Valdosta Georgia as it interacted with a warm front present along the Florida Panhandle and other favorable atmospheric conditions. Its high concentration of lightning distinguishes it as a Lightning Dense Thunderstorm (LDT), a type of storm typically observed in offshore regions throughout the Gulf of Mexico, the Mediterranean Sea, or east of South Africa. These maritime environments produce thunderstorms with the greatest lightning densities on Earth and produce lightning at rates that rival large MCSs. As this case occurred in an onshore location with radar coverage, it provides new insights into the environmental conditions and convective cloud processes that drive exceptionally high flash rates and improves our understanding of LDTs, specifically in the costal environments that are frequently impacted by severe weather.

498713.title: Implications of Base Cation Deposition from Increased Climate-Driven Wildfires In the United States
498713.authors: Patrick C. Campbell, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA
498713.abstract: Climate‑driven increases in wildfires are altering atmospheric deposition patterns across the United States, with implications for ecosystem acidification and critical load (CL) exceedances. Using the 2002–2021 North American Chemical Reanalysis (NACR), we quantify multi‑decadal trends in fire‑derived base cation (Ca2+, Mg2+, K⁺, Na⁺) deposition and evaluate their capacity to buffer concurrent increases in reactive nitrogen (Nr) and sulfur (S) deposition from fires. We find substantial fire‑derived enhancements in base cation deposition, often exceeding 100% near major wildfire regions, yet these increases are spatially inconsistent with Nr and S deposition maxima. Our results suggest that regions exhibiting the greatest relative increases in base cation deposition do not regularly coincide with those experiencing the largest Nr increases, thus limiting the potential for widespread acid buffering. After 2017, base cation contributions from fires rise sharply (~30 to 80%), reflecting intensifying fire activity, but combined Nr+S deposition remains overwhelmingly dominant, with increases 100 times larger than base cations due to fires. Overall, our results show that although fire‑derived base cations provide localized buffering, they do not offset the broader rise in acidifying Nr and S deposition driven by climate‑driven wildfires, reinforcing concerns about increasing CL exceedances in vulnerable western U.S. ecosystems.

498723.title: The Saharan Oscillation Index (SaOI): A Sea-Level-Pressure Teleconnection Governing Compound Dust, Particulate, and Heat Extremes over North Africa, and Its Predictability for Climate-Health Early Warning
498723.abstract: Across North Africa, extreme heat and hazardous mineral-dust loading frequently strike the same regions in the same season, yet the large-scale atmospheric mechanism coupling these hazards has remained poorly characterized, and standard global teleconnection indices capture it only weakly. Here we characterize the Saharan Oscillation Index (SaOI), a standardized sea-level-pressure dipole between the Azores High and the Saharan Low, and test whether a single circulation mode organizes co-occurring dust, particulate matter (PM10), and surface heat, and whether its ocean coupling and persistence confer predictive skill. Using 75 years (1950-2024) of ERA5 reanalysis together with Copernicus CAMS EAC4 aerosol reanalysis, we reconstruct the monthly SaOI and compute season-by-season Pearson spatial correlations against dust aerosol optical depth (DAOD550), PM10, 2-m air temperature, and sea-surface temperature (SST), assessing significance with an effective-sample-size correction (|r| ≥ 0.27, p < 0.05; coherent signals retained at |r| ≥ 0.40). The record exhibits a post-1990 regime shift toward the positive, “dusty” phase (a mean shift of roughly +0.18σ, with negative phases becoming rare after 2010). During boreal summer, positive SaOI phases coherently elevate dust and PM10 along a continuous trans-Atlantic corridor emanating from Saharan and Sahel source regions (r ≥ 0.50), driven by an intensified Azores High and strengthened northeasterly trades, while simultaneously amplifying surface heat over the Sahara–Sahel through coupling to the Saharan Heat Low (r ≥ 0.45). Peak particulate and peak thermal exposure therefore coincide in space and season, a compound heat–dust hazard governed by one atmospheric mode. Critically, SST anomalies coupled to the index emerge one to three months ahead of it, and the index’s own persistence (e-folding = 1.4 months) reinforces its predictability. These results establish the SaOI as a physically interpretable, seasonally predictable indicator of compound dust and heat extremes, offering a screening basis for climate-health early-warning systems in a chronically underserved region. We discuss its limitations, associational, grid-scale evidence requiring prospective validation against ground observations and health outcomes, and a pathway toward operational monitoring that could empower vulnerable communities to anticipate, rather than merely observe, compound environmental risk.

498724.title: Reaching for Solar Max: Linking Geomagnetic Precursors to Polar Coronal Hole Extensions
498724.authors: Cole Ian Gakos, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT; and S. W. McIntosh and R. J. Leamon
498724.abstract: We present a novel framework for forecasting the amplitude of sunspot maximum four to six years in advance using the aa index residuals as described by Feynman. We show that, when analyzed within the timescale of the unit Hale Cycle as described by McIntosh & Leamon, the rise in residuals from baseline activity levels between 0.22 and 0.82 of a unit cycle displays a strong positive correlation with the amplitude of the next sunspot cycle’s smoothed maximum. This rise in residual activity is attributed to properties of coronal holes - in particular, that arising from equatorward extensions of the polar flux systems during the declining phase of the sunspot cycle. Using coronal hole data gathered from EIT and AIA imagery spanning the declining phase of cycles 23 and 24, we find that a measure combining the area and equatorward extent of these polar-flux-system coronal holes closely tracks residual geomagnetic activity. Together, these two results suggest that the aa index residuals are an Earth-based measure of the evolution of the polar flux systems, providing a physically motivated explanation for the Feynman precursor as well as a means of forecasting the ensuing sunspot maximum before the current minimum.

498727.title: Piecewise-Linear Scheme for Solving Nonlinear Navier-Stokes Equations Using Quantum Computers for Tornado Modeling
498727.authors: Yi Zhao, Missouri Univ. of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO; and Y. C. Li, Y. Zhang, and G. Yan
498727.abstract: Mitigating the adverse impact of tornadoes on civil structures requires a deep understanding of tornado characteristics and tornado-community interaction. While Large Eddy Simulation (LES) has been used for modeling these complex tornado dynamics, conducting LES at the required spatial/temporal resolution is computationally prohibitive. This bottleneck inspired the authors to explore the possibility of using quantum computing to resolve fine-scale turbulence. A major challenge in this work is solving the non-linear Navier-Stokes equations on quantum hardware. This difficulty arises because quantum computation evolves through strictly linear unitary operations, whereas Navier-Stokes equations are inherently nonlinear. Beyond this, it is challenging to efficiently encode classical information into quantum circuits and establish effective methods for reading out the resulting states. This study will only focus on the major challenge of solving nonlinear N-S equations. To address this, the study proposes a new linearization scheme of N-S equations, which is the freeze the velocity within a certain number of time steps. A 2D flow problem that has analytical solution has been used to test this new scheme, producing very promising results, although comprehensive parameter studies need to be conducted to determine how many steps of time can be freezed to obtain accurate results. Figures 1 provides a direct visual comparison between the Quantum Matrix solution at N = 10 using the proposed scheme and the exact Taylor-Green velocity magnitude at T = 0.20. The two fields are visually indistinguishable at the resolution of the 21 x 21 grid. The periodic vortex pattern, locations of high- and low-velocity regions, and overall velocity magnitude are reproduced correctly by the Quantum Matrix formulation. Ultimately, this exploratory research demonstrates how emerging quantum techniques can be leveraged to push the boundaries of severe convective storm modeling.

498728.title: Turbulence Modeling of Tornadic Wind Field Using High-fidelity Coupled CM1–LES Simulations
498728.authors: Peng Yue, Missouri Univ. of Science and Technology, ROLLA, MO; and Y. C. Li, D. K. Fytanidis, M. Xue, L. Orf, and G. Yan
498728.abstract: To reduce the tornado induced damage to civil structures, it is important to understand the high-frequency turbulent fluctuations in tornadoes that govern transient aerodynamic loading on structures. An ideal approach is to collect the velocity data in the field during a variety of tornado events, at various heights and with various terrain/land cover conditions. However, collecting tornado data in the field is extremely difficult due to the destructive nature, small spatial scales, short lifetimes of tornadoes and the limitations of tornado track prediction. This motivated the authors to characterize turbulence in tornadic wind fields using computational fluid dynamics simulations. Two approaches are applied. The first approach is to minimize the mesh size in the large-eddy simulations (LES), hoping that the smaller eddies are directly resolved. The second approach is to generate artificial turbulence for the initial condition and at the time-dependent boundary conditions. To understand which approach performs better, the 24 May 2011 El Reno tornado is simulated using the two approaches. Herein, to apply time-varying inflow condition, the output of CM1 simulation is used to drive the LES simulations. Fig. 1 presents the contour of horizontal resultant velocity on the horizontal plane at the height of 10 m for various mesh sizes, using the first approach. As the mesh size decreases, the cell number is increased significantly; and more sizes of turbulence eddies can be resolved, indicated by the more complex contour color variation, representing more turbulent fluctuations, for the cases with smaller mesh sizes. Fig. 2 compares tornado wind speed on the horizontal plane at the height of 10 m height between the two approaches. For the case with smaller size, when artificial turbulence is applied, more flow fluctuations (turbulence) can be observed, especially in the region with lower velocities. More results are being extracted and will be presented in the AMS conference.

498730.title: Wildland Fire and Smoke Research and Tools at the U.S. Forest Service
498730.authors: Aaron Piña, U.S. Forest Service, Washington, DC
498730.abstract: Recent wildland fire and associated smoke events have raised the attention and concern of scientists, the public, and policymakers. The USDA Forest Service Fire, Fuels, and Smoke Research program supports research and development to improve and innovate science and tools related to fire weather and behavior, smoke from wildland fires, and air pollution and extreme weather events that affect forest management. The primary strategic goals of the program are 1) to transition fire weather and smoke research to operational tools for firefighters, land managers, and communities, and 2) to collaborate with federal, state, tribal, local, academic, and private partners on atmospheric science related effects on forest management such as fire weather and behavior, extreme wind and precipitation events, and smoke effects on communities. This talk will cover Forest Service Atmospheric Science R&D priorities, recent advances in fire weather and smoke science and technology, and future collaborative research directions and opportunities.

498731.title: Making Complex Satellite Algorithms Accessible: A Baseball Card Framework for Communicating NESDIS OCS Product in Practice Demonstrating Value
498731.authors: Vanessa Marie Escobar, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD
498731.abstract: The NOAA National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) Office of Common Services (OCS) develops and sustains operational algorithms that transform satellite observations into environmental products supporting weather forecasting, climate monitoring, water resource management, emergency response, and other mission-critical services. While these algorithms provide significant scientific and operational value, communicating their capabilities, how they are put into practice and the impacts to diverse audiences remains challenging. To address this need, OCS developed a standardized Algorithm Baseball Card framework that translates complex technical information into a concise, visually engaging communication product. Organized by algorithm portfolio, each Baseball Card summarizes the algorithm's purpose, inputs, outputs, operational status, applications, and downstream value across NOAA and partner organizations. Developed collaboratively with NOAA's Center for Satellite Applications and Research (STAR) and OCS Portfolio Managers, the cards provide a consistent method for communicating algorithm capabilities while maintaining technical accuracy. The Baseball Cards serve as more than technical summaries—they are stakeholder engagement and communication tools. Their familiar trading-card format creates an approachable, interactive experience that encourages discussion among scientists, developers, operational users, leadership, and external partners. By transforming complex algorithm portfolios into accessible visual stories, the cards help audiences understand how individual algorithms contribute to the broader satellite enterprise and support decisions that protect lives, property, and the environment. This presentation is designed to update the audience on the NESDIS products that are active and in play. It describes the strategy behind the development of the Algorithm Baseball Card framework, lessons learned. The NESDIS Baseball Card framework demonstrated how standardized visual communication can strengthen stakeholder engagement, increase awareness of NESDIS capabilities, and provide a scalable model for communicating complex scientific assets across NOAA.

498732.title: Trends in Congo Basin Precipitation and Temperature, and Their Impacts on the Tropical Forest
498732.authors: Kerry H. Cook, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX; and E. K. Vizy and I. Myrick
498732.abstract: Degradation in the Congolese tropical forest is documented in the literature, but attribution to forest disturbance and/or greenhouse gas-induced climate change is regional and complex. Here we consider observed trends in temperature and precipitation, compare these trends with predictions, and consider their impact on the health of the tropical forest. Building reliable precipitation datasets requires long, continuous records and these are rare in the Congo Basin which had experienced a decline in meteorological stations. Satellite-based precipitation datasets provide excellent areal coverage of Congo Basin precipitation, but these datasets are typically shorter than the decades-long records needed to establish trends in precipitation. In addition, satellite retrieval of precipitation values depends on algorithms that are developed by calibration with ground-based data which, again, are sparse. Consequently, it is difficult to analyze precipitation trends in the Congo Basin, and there is confusion in the literature. Here we update the analysis of precipitation trends using multiple satellite and ground-based datasets. In addition, we compare these trends with predictions from a high-resolution climate simulation of greenhouse gas-forced climate change in Central Africa, and consider the physical mechanisms that can change Congo Basin rainfall in response to greenhouse gas-forced climate change. We also examine current warming levels in the Congo Basin at high resolution in time and space and compare with the vegetation distribution. Tropical forests evolve under relatively constant temperatures in the absence of seasonal cycles, so they are particularly sensitive to temperature trends and threshold behavior is possible with the ongoing warming. Current warming in parts of the Congo Basin during some seasons is approaching levels at which reductions in photosynthetic activity are possible.

498733.title: Seeing What One View Cannot: From MISR's Multi-Angle Observations to the Future of Atmospheric Tomography (Core Science Keynote)
498733.authors: Larry DiGirolamo, University of Illinois at Urbana Champaign, Urbana, IL
498733.abstract: For more than twenty-five years, passive multi-angle satellite observations have transformed our ability to study aerosols, clouds, and atmospheric circulation. This presentation reflects on lessons learned from a career spent viewing the atmosphere from more than one direction. The Multi-angle Imaging SpectroRadiometer (MISR), which views Earth from nine directions spanning the visible to near-infrared spectrum, provided the first global retrievals of aerosol optical depth segregated by particle size and shape; produced the most accurate global passive satellite measurements of cloud height and motion; and recently enabled the detection of decadal-scale changes in atmospheric circulation. MISR also revealed the strong sensitivity of reflected sunlight to the three-dimensional structure of clouds and aerosols, exposing the widespread influence of 3D radiative transfer and the limitations of retrieval approaches built on one-dimensional assumptions. These limitations are particularly important for studies of aerosol-cloud interactions, where retrieval biases covary with cloud morphology and sun-view geometry, complicating efforts to distinguish true physical relationships from retrieval artifacts. As a result, many widely used passive satellite products remain ill-suited for robust quantification of aerosol-cloud interactions. To address these limitations, I will review recent advances in Atmospheric Tomography with 3D Radiative Transfer (AT3D), a new framework for retrieving the three-dimensional distribution of atmospheric properties directly from multi-angle observations. I'll share what I consider a real treat: the first application of AT3D to MISR observations, yielding tomographic retrievals of the three-dimensional cloud extinction field, validated against observations acquired during the NASA CAMP²Ex field campaign. I will also highlight recent advances in aerosol, water-vapor, and temperature tomography, demonstrating the growing ability of passive multi-angle remote sensing to reconstruct three-dimensional atmospheric structure. These developments point toward what I believe is the next major step in passive remote sensing: routine four-dimensional observations of atmospheric structure and evolution. Achieving this goal will require a constellation of pointable, high-resolution (~50 m) passive imagers that offers a low-cost, scalable pathway to combining atmospheric tomography with time-lapse stereography to simultaneously retrieve the three-dimensional distribution and evolution of clouds, aerosols, water vapor, temperature, and atmospheric motions. These measurements would substantially advance our understanding of cloud-aerosol-thermodynamic-dynamic interactions across scales while providing critical constraints for improving the next generation of large-eddy, weather, and Earth system models.

498736.title: Remote Sensing of MBL Cloud Properties from Surface, Airborne and Spaceborne 94-GHz Cloud Radars (Core Science Keynote)
498736.authors: Xiquan Dong, The Univ. of Arizona, Tucson, AZ
498736.abstract: Marine Boundary Layer (MBL) clouds have been the subject of considerable research because they strongly reflect incoming shortwave radiation and exert complex feedbacks on the climate system. Subtropical MBL cloud systems typically form over the cold eastern currents of the subtropical oceans, where persistent subtropical high-pressure systems maintain large-scale subsidence that caps MBL and favors extensive cloud development. In contrast, midlatitude MBL clouds are primarily associated with cyclonic systems and frontal activity. Abundant moisture supplied by ocean surface evaporation, together with cloud condensation nuclei, provides favorable conditions for the formation of MBL clouds. In warm MBL clouds, cloud droplets generally form near the cloud base through the activation of cloud condensation nuclei. As the droplets are transported upward in cloud updrafts, they grow by condensation and reach their largest cloud-droplet sizes near the cloud top. Through collision and coalescence, some droplets become drizzle-sized near the cloud top. These drizzle drops subsequently fall through the cloud, continuing to grow by collecting cloud droplets and smaller drizzle drops, and typically reach their largest sizes near the cloud base. Remote sensing, particularly using 94-GHz cloud radar, has become an indispensable tool for advancing our understanding of MBL cloud formation, macrophysical and microphysical properties and the processes governing their evolution. A major challenge in interpreting cloud radar observations, however, is that the measured radar reflectivity contains contributions from both cloud droplets and drizzle drops. Because radar reflectivity is proportional to the sixth power of particle diameter, the radar signal in drizzling clouds can be dominated by a relatively small number of large drizzle drops. Consequently, it is difficult to separate the contributions of cloud droplets and drizzle to the measured reflectivity and to accurately retrieve the microphysical properties of both cloud and drizzle. To address this challenge, Wu et al. (2020) developed an innovative retrieval framework that first partitions the observed radar reflectivity into cloud and drizzle components and then simultaneously retrieves the microphysical properties of both populations from ARM cloud radar observations. The retrieved cloud and drizzle microphysical properties were validated against aircraft in situ measurements collected during the ACE-ENA field campaign. Building on this retrieval framework, Dong et al. (2021) investigated the formation and growth of precipitation particles during the cloud-to-rain conversion process in warm MBL clouds and used the results to improve the parameterization of warm-rain microphysical processes. The Southern Ocean (SO) is one of the cloudiest and stormiest regions on Earth, with a mean total cloud fraction (CF) of ~70%, dominated by MBL clouds (below 3 km). A key scientific question is whether 94 GHz cloud radars deployed on surface-based, airborne, and spaceborne platforms can provide consistent measurements of cloud structures and their vertical distribution. Dong et al. (2025) compared cloud fraction (CF) and its vertical distribution derived from 94 GHz cloud radar observations across the three observing platforms and found that the more sensitive ARM surface-based and airborne cloud radars detected substantially more MBL clouds than the CloudSat and EarthCARE CPRs. Although the EarthCARE CPR represents a significant improvement over CloudSat in detecting low-level clouds, it still misses a substantial fraction of MBL clouds below approximately 1 km compared with ARM surface-based radar observations. This observational gap highlights an important limitation of current spaceborne cloud radar measurements for characterizing the lowest levels of MBL clouds and has implications for evaluating cloud processes and their representation in weather and climate models. Finally, I will briefly introduce other research areas from my group, such as aerosol-cloud-interactions, the impacts of clouds and radiation on Arctic sea ice changes, the formation and dissipation processes and their properties of deep convective clouds, and the global radiation budgets from our current NASA Libera project.

498739.title: How Do Clouds Impact the Arctic Surface Energy Budget? (Core Science Keynote)
498739.authors: Matthew David Shupe, CIRES, Boulder, CO
498739.abstract: Clouds are a leading driver of atmospheric variability in the Arctic, strongly modulating exchanges of energy at the surface and with potentially dramatic consequences for the cryosphere and Arctic climate. The magnitude and even sign of these cloud impacts depend strongly on cloud phase, which emerges from a complex interplay among aerosol, thermodynamic, and dynamic processes. Understanding the occurrence and properties of Arctic liquid-containing clouds, and the environmental conditions that govern them, is therefore critical for quantifying cloud influences on the Arctic surface energy budget. Here, observations from across the Arctic are combined with model simulations to examine the properties, distribution, and implications of Arctic liquid-containing clouds. Measurements from observatories spanning Arctic land, the Greenland Ice Sheet, and Arctic sea ice are used to quantify cloud impacts on all components of the surface energy budget and their evolution over the annual cycle. The role of environmental constraints in regulating the net surface cloud effect is explored, identifying key seasonal relationships, feedbacks, and buffering mechanisms that determine when and where clouds exert their strongest influence. Results from an observationally evaluated, regional model are then used to upscale these site-based insights to the pan-Arctic domain. The spatial and seasonal variability of cloud impacts on the surface energy budget is quantified, identifying hotspots where clouds exert particularly strong controls on the Arctic surface, including regions where clouds could contribute to variations in sea-ice conditions. Together, these observational and modeling perspectives provide an integrated view of how cloud phase and environmental state shape the Arctic surface energy budget from local to pan-Arctic scales. Finally, key uncertainties and priorities for future research needed to better understand and predict cloud–surface interactions in a rapidly changing Arctic are highlighted.

498743.title: Where's the Next Wildfire? Predicting Wildfires across the West Coast Using Past Wildfire Data
498743.authors: Staci M DeSchryver, ; and J. Tsiboah, A. Musthuri, A. Kalla, and L. Olson
498743.abstract: Across the west coast of the United States, wildfires are burning for an average of 8 months every year. These wildfires have not only become frequent but also unpredictable. This study explores wildfires and teh complex factors taht influence different wildfire behaviors and how this information can be used to minimize the harmful effects of these fires. Wildfires occur when an ignition source ignites combustible vegetation under weather conditions that allow the first to begin and the flames to spread. Natural causes, primarily lightning, account for only 15% of the causes of wildfires, while manmade causes, such as burning debris, fireworks, smoking, and campfires, account for the remaining 85%. Environmental conditions influence the behavior of a wildfire, such as low humidity, high winds, adn prolonged heat; conditions like cooler temperatures, lower wind speeds, and higher humidity can help prevent fires from occurring and spreading. Looking back at 35 years of past NASA data, the wildfire season has been starting months earlier adn ending months later compared to 30 years ago. What used to be a fire season that was 4-5 months has now increased to 7-10 months. Our method uses datasets of all wildfires on the West Coast. We then select specific sites and gather data from NASA satellites and the National Center for Environmental Information for a specific location, date, and time to cross-compare with teh weather, temperature, precipitation, etc i that area. We then apply this across the west coast to identify trends or mean thresholds that increase the likelihood of wildfires. From a manmade perspective, we also cross compare with tables of sold commercial products to determine whether fire and flammable products are sold in wildfire areas and whether this affects frequency. Wildfires are a destructive force, causing ecological destruction and damaging human health. The soot, ash, and debris from wildfires can make their way into water supplies, rendering them unsafe for consumption. Large wildfires can also degrade rthe soil and pave the way for invasive species to step in and interfere with the local ecosystem. Another dangerous aspect of wildfires is the smoke they release, which worsens as fires become more common. Through this study, our goal is to improve the predictability of wildfires, which can be used to minimize these disasters and their effects.

498744.title: Assessing the Regional Impacts of Climate Change and Adaptation Strategies
498744.authors: Staci M DeSchryver, ; and S. Harris, I. Mata, S. McMillan, J. McPeak, T. Bizuneh, V. Blakewell, and A. Abhilash
498744.abstract: Climate change is continuing to affect the Earth’s atmosphere and oceans, but the causes and impacts of climate change vary in different regions. This study examines the causes of climate change, such as rising global temperatures, in order to determine the social and environmental impacts of climate change in different regions. Through the use of high resolution climate projections, and focusing on the changes in precipitation, temperature extremes, and local weather patterns. We are able to analyze both historical trends and projected future changes across several key regions. For instance, in Southern Europe analyzing the impact of increasing sea levels on Venice. These differences show why climate change cannot be addressed effectively with a single approach for every region. Instead, understanding the specific risks faced by different communities can help improve climate adaptation strategies and planning for vulnerable areas. The anticipated results of our research seek to discuss and suggest possible adaptations to existing social and scientific approaches to natural disasters or extreme conditions caused by climate change.

498749.title: A CIROH Hydrometeorological Prediction Testbed Supporting the Advancement of CONUS-Wide Forecasting Capabilities (Invited)
498749.authors: Andrew W. Wood, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; and J. Sturtevant and S. Carney
498749.abstract: A key to the success of the forecast-oriented research in NOAA Cooperative Institute for R2O in Hydrology will be its ability to overcome the well-known ‘valley of death’ that slows the operational adoption of state-of-the-science modeling, methods and datasets in pragmatic hydrologic prediction operations and applications. With this motivation, we have designed and implemented a CIROH Hydrologic Prediction Testbed, also known as ‘HydrometBench’. HydrometBench is a CIROH-led research activity created to support the evaluation and benchmarking, selection and adoption of critical forecasting-relevant capabilities for transition into the National Water Model operations, including the Nextgen framework. The Testbed develops experimental ‘Protocols’ to assess and benchmark specific new techniques, models, model elements, workflows and datasets targeting distinct objectives (e.g., watershed-scale streamflow simulation, flash flood prediction, or sub-seasonal to seasonal water supply prediction) from an evidence-driven perspective. At present, there are few published and widely adopted benchmarks for US (or global) hydrologic forecast state-of-practice performance or skill, which makes it difficult to determine, quantitatively, the extent to which any new development in a forecasting system improves forecast skill. As protocols are developed, the testbed project is also working to construct and promulgate such benchmarks. To date, the CHPT has focused on a number of protocols, including short-to-medium range river forecasts, S2S runoff forecasts (e.g., water supply forecasting), meteorological forcings, and SWE estimation at catchment scales. Baseline capabilities for assessing performance are drawn from current working versions of NWS hydrologic forecasts and other NOAA products, including the current NWM and Nextgen capabilities as well as River Forecast Center (RFC) capabilities. The major outcome of this effort has been to establish a CIROH community Testbed practice that promotes the structured benchmarking of new hydrologic prediction science (models, methods, data, workflows), fostering evidence-based research assessment to support national water modeling and prediction services. This presentation reviews the CHPT philosophy and progress to date.
