498773.title: Effect of Boundary-Layer Thickness on Isolated Building Wakes at Different Aspect Ratios
498773.authors: Rahul Deshpande, RMIT University, Melbourne, Australia
498773.abstract: The three-dimensional (3D) wake of an isolated building is governed by the interaction between building-generated separated flow and the incoming atmospheric boundary layer. While building geometry is known to strongly influence the 3D wake structure, the role of the incoming boundary-layer thickness (δ) relative to building height (H) remains comparatively poorly understood. In particular, the ratio δ/H determines how far the building extends into the boundary layer, potentially altering the relative importance of base, tip and horseshoe vortices and the resulting characteristic frequencies observed in the 3D wake. This raises a fundamental question for urban boundary-layer flows: How does the building height relative to the incoming turbulent boundary layer modify the fundamental structure and evolution of its wake? We address this question through a systematic experimental study of the 3D wake of an isolated rectangular building at high Reynolds number. Experiments are conducted in the RMIT University industrial wind tunnel, with a 3 m wide, 2 m high and 9 m long test section. A turbulence-generating grid installed at the entrance to the test section produces a thick, highly turbulent wall flow representative of a suburban atmospheric boundary layer. The building is located 7 m downstream of the grid, where the incoming mean velocity profile has reached a nominal streamwise-invariant, self-similar state, with δ ≈ 1800 mm. The Reynolds number based on building height exceeds 10⁵ for all cases, placing the rectangular-building wake in a Reynolds-number-independent regime. The incoming velocity at building height is maintained at 5 m s⁻¹ for all experiments. A key feature of the experiment is the controlled variation of building aspect ratio, AR = H/D, and the boundary-layer thickness-to-building-height ratio, δ/H. Models with AR = 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 are considered. For AR = 0.5 and 2.0, matched-aspect-ratio configurations are achieved through two complementary geometric scalings: varying the spanwise width D while maintaining a fixed height H = 415 mm, and varying the building height H while maintaining a fixed D = 415 mm. This produces cases with identical aspect ratio but substantially different δ/H, enabling the influence of boundary-layer depth to be isolated from that of building geometry. The resulting parameter space provides a controlled framework for examining how the degree to which a building is submerged within the atmospheric boundary layer modifies its wake. Time-resolved 3D particle-tracking velocimetry (PTV) in the near wake, sampled at 1000 Hz, provides access to both the spatial structure and temporal dynamics of the flow. The measurements resolve the 3D mean flow, Reynolds stresses and turbulent kinetic energy production, while simultaneously capturing the temporal signatures of the characteristic wake structures. Particular attention is given to the formation, strength and interaction of tip vortices, vortex shedding, base vortices and the horseshoe vortex, and to the corresponding spectral signatures in the wake. Preliminary measurements reveal a marked difference from previous studies in which the incoming boundary-layer thickness was smaller than the building height (δ/H < 1). For the present fully submerged configurations (δ/H > 1), statistically significant base vortices are observed for all aspect ratios, manifested by strong upwash and streamwise-oriented vortical structures in the near wake. Furthermore, matched-AR cases with different δ/H exhibit appreciably different base-vortex and upwash strengths, demonstrating that boundary-layer depth can modify wake topology even when building aspect ratio is held constant. The presentation will examine how these changes in vortex strength influence the characteristic frequencies and spectral content of the wake across δ/H and AR, and compare the observed behaviour with established building-wake measurements and previous low-Reynolds-number studies. The results will provide new insight into how atmospheric boundary-layer depth governs the 3D structure and dynamics of isolated building wakes, with implications for understanding building–boundary-layer interactions in urban environments.

498791.title: The Austin City Digital Twin (AusTwin) for Urban Weather Extremes and City Solutions
498791.authors: Dev Niyogi, Univ. of Texas at Austin, West Lafayette, IN; and A. Patel, N. Sudharsan, A. R. Dallmann, and M. Coudert
498791.abstract: Cities worldwide are challenged by extreme weather events, including heat waves and rainfall events that trigger cascading environmental feedbacks affecting socioeconomic well-being and urban resilience. Accurate prediction and simulation of these city-scale meteorological processes remain fundamentally challenging due to inherent limitations in current Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models. These limitations stem from relatively coarse spatial resolution as well as limited process-scale understanding, which constrain adequate representation of the complex physiographical, physical, dynamical, and anthropogenic processes operating within urban environments. This talk presents a perspective on different work underway at The Extreme Weather and Urban Sustainability Lab (TExUS Lab) at the University of Texas at Austin, addressing city-scale challenges through synergistic integration of AI-based approaches with physics-based modeling frameworks. By combining data-driven AI methodologies with mechanistic understanding, we can develop robust city-centric simulation systems operationalized through a Digital Twin framework. Digital Twins offer emerging opportunities for targeted simulations, extreme weather prediction, and scenario analysis at scales relevant to urban decision-making, and for the development of the AUSTwin. The presentation highlights ongoing collaborative initiatives leveraging partnerships with UNESCO, the WMO/WCRP, and the UT City CoLab. These partnerships demonstrate engagement pathways for implementing integrated AI-physics modeling systems that capture multiscale urban processes, from urban heat islands to localized flooding patterns. The work highlights a framework for stakeholder-driven, hyperlocal forecasting that integrates how environmental predictions serve urban decision-making. By generating neighborhood-scale forecasts with embedded stakeholder engagement, this approach ensures relevance and usability for decision-makers. The convergence of Digital Twin technology, hybrid AI-physics modeling, and stakeholder co-design represents a practical approach for urban environmental modeling, on how cities utilize environmental data for informed decision-making, especially for weather extremes and urban sustainability.

498931.title: Strengthening U.S.–Kenya Partnerships for Climate-Resilient Urban Planning: Integrating Climate Science, Earth Observations and Adaptive Capacity in Nairobi, Kenya
498931.authors: Phoebe Murunga, Kenya Meteorological Services Authority, Kenya
498931.abstract: Rapidly growing African cities face increasing risks from climate change, including extreme rainfall, rising temperatures, flooding, and associated pressures on urban infrastructure, ecosystems, and livelihoods. Addressing these challenges requires stronger international partnerships that connect climate science, Earth observations, data and analytical capacity, local knowledge, and urban planning. This study examines the implications of climate change for urban sustainability in Nairobi City County, Kenya, while highlighting opportunities for U.S.–Kenya scientific collaboration in climate research, technology, knowledge exchange, and capacity development. The study adopts a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design informed by Ecological Resilience Theory, Urban Political Ecology Theory, and Ecological Modernization Theory. Four objectives guide the research: assessing historical trends and future projections of rainfall and temperature extremes; examining the influence of climate change on urban development and land-use change; evaluating community and institutional adaptive capacity; and assessing how urban planning and climate policies respond to climate risks and support sustainability. Historical climate data for 1980–2025 will be obtained from the Kenya Meteorological Department, while future projections to 2050 will be derived from CORDEX-Africa regional climate models. Mann-Kendall tests and Sen’s slope estimation will be used to assess climatic trends, while ETCCDI indices will characterize extreme events. Landsat and Sentinel-2 satellite imagery will be analyzed using supervised Random Forest classification to examine land-use and land-cover changes and the distribution of green, grey, and blue infrastructure. Household questionnaires involving 400 households across five sub-counties, together with key informant interviews with urban planners, climate experts, and government officials, will assess adaptive capacity and institutional responses. Policy documents published between 2015 and 2024 will also be reviewed to evaluate the integration of climate information into urban planning. The research provides a platform for strengthening international collaboration by bringing together meteorological observations, regional climate modelling, Earth observation technologies, geospatial analysis, and socio-economic knowledge. Such collaboration can support technical capacity development, methodological exchange, data sharing, and the co-production of actionable climate information between Kenyan and U.S. scientific and institutional partners. The study will generate location-specific evidence to inform climate-resilient urban planning, strengthen institutional coordination, identify opportunities for targeted adaptation investments, and demonstrate how sustained international partnerships can translate climate science and technology into locally relevant resilience solutions for rapidly urbanizing African cities.

498932.title: Impact of Climate Change on Tourism Potential in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
498932.authors: Billy Henry Jeffers, St Vincent and the Grenadines Meteorological Service, Argyle, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
498932.abstract: Economic diversification is a key strategy for Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, with the tourism sector playing a crucial role. The sector's recent expansion has been instrumental in generating economic growth and employment opportunities. However, tourism is highly vulnerable to the effects of climate variability and change. This research investigates the future impacts of climate change on the tourism sector through the year 2100, using an Outdoor Tourism Climate Index (OTCI). It is the first known study to examine this relationship for Saint Vincent and the Grenadines using future climate projections. Projections were made for the period 2015–2100 using four Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CIMP) 6 outputs under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) 2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. CIMP6 model outputs were statistically downscaled using data from the Saint Vincent and the Grenadines Meteorological Services, followed by the application of the OTCI formula. The results show that future warming is projected to result in a direct decrease in the OTCI scores and the corresponding attractiveness of the destination across both scenarios. Despite the overall decline, the peak tourism season from December to April remains largely within the "Acceptable" or "Good" category. Under the high-emission SSP5-8.5 scenario, October and November could become unsuitable by the 2060s. However, in the recent CMIP7 outputs, the high-emission scenario has been deemed “implausible, based on trends in the costs of renewables, the emergence of climate policy and recent emission trends.” 1 Even under less-extreme scenarios, the decline in climate suitability is likely to be worsened by the direct climate impacts of increased sea level rise, tropical cyclones and droughts. Hence the need for adaptation. Some adaptation has been developed in response to climate variability, such as the strong El Niño of 2026, which has caused drought and excessive heat in many Caribbean islands. Alerts of the impending strong El Niño were issued with lead time of months, due to advances in climate science, observations from the NOAA Tropical Atmosphere Ocean (TAO) buoys, numerical prediction models and coordination through the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). Therefore, climate sensitive sectors in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines had the opportunity to prepare for the impacts. In much the same way, the results of the climate change study offer valuable insights for the tourism industry to adapt to the projected changes and build a sustainable future. 1 Van Vuuren et al. (VVetal26), The Scenario Model Intercomparison Project for CMIP7 (ScenarioMIP-CMIP7), Geosci. Model Dev., 19, 2627–2656, https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/19/2627/2026/

498933.title: From Forecasts to Action: Strengthening Weather and Climate Communication forEffective Early Warning Services in Ghana
498933.authors: Maureen Abla Ahiataku, Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet), Accra, Ghana
498933.abstract: Effective early warning systems require more than accurate forecasts; they depend on translating scientific information into actionable messages that reach exposed and vulnerable populations. In Ghana, the Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet) is strengthening this forecast-to-action pathway through impact-based forecasting, implementation of the Common Alerting Protocol (CAP), strategic media engagement, stakeholder partnerships, and community-centered communication that aligns with the Early Warnings for All (EW4All) initiative. GMet is transitioning from communicating primarily meteorological hazards to delivering impact-based warnings that explain what weather and climate hazards mean for people, infrastructure, livelihoods, and critical services. CAP provides a standardized framework for disseminating structured alerts across multiple channels. Collaboration with radio and television stations, digital media platforms, government institutions, disaster management agencies, and local stakeholders support broader and more consistent warning dissemination. These efforts are reinforced through public engagement activities, including Meteorological Awareness Month (MAM), which strengthens public understanding of weather and climate information while promoting preparedness and risk reduction. As part of its communication strategy, GMet is also engaging youth through the Green Climate Club initiative. The program promotes climate awareness and participation in climate action by providing accessible weather, climate, and early warning information. It aims to develop a network of informed youth who serve as climate ambassadors within schools, communities, and social networks. This youth-centered approach expands communication pathways, encourages preparedness, and increases awareness of climate risks. Particular attention is given to vulnerable and underserved communities where access to digital technologies may be limited. To address this challenge, GMet is exploring multi-channel communication approaches that combine traditional media, digital platforms, community networks, youth climate ambassadors, and institutional intermediaries. These provide platforms to enhance mechanisms to assess feedback, identify communication gaps, and improve warning services. Ghana’s experience demonstrates that effective early warning communication is a continuous process involving forecast generation, impact interpretation, message development, dissemination, public engagement, and feedback. Strengthening these linkages enhances preparedness, improves warning usability, and supports more inclusive and people-centered early warning services nationwide.

498934.title: Digitizing Paper Based Archival Weather and Climate Data from NationalHydrological and Meteorological Services (NHMSs) using Artificial Intelligence(AI) Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for Data Rescue
498934.authors: Daison Lowe, Caribbean Institute for Meteorology and Hydrology, St. James, Barbados
498934.abstract: National Hydrological and Meteorological Services (NHMSs) in the Caribbean maintain decades of historical paper based weather and climate records which includes synoptic books rainfall and temperature tables stored in physical archives. The data from these records are valuable for climate change analysis, multi hazard warning systems and disaster risk management in the Caribbean. Manual data rescue requires a significant amount of time and labor to physically digitize scans and keying entries into a readable and editable format. While traditional rule based OCR software automates printed text conversion, it can struggle with complex table structures, decaying documents and varied handwriting legibility. Thus leading to low accuracy of extracted results. To streamline the digitization process, a platform was developed by CIMH using several open sourced AI OCR models and tools to upload, process and automate data extraction from paper based table records into a structured data format such as Comma Separated Value (CSV). The AI OCR models demonstrated a 80 to 90% accuracy of extracting data from printed tabular data. Performance on handwritten tabular data varied significantly from 40 to 60% depending on the legibility of the data, condition of the scans and table structure. Furthermore, each document processed by the AI OCR model takes 5 - 30 seconds to complete data extraction. Using open source AI OCR models offers a scalable and cost effective solution for data rescue in resource constraint environments. Additionally, because AI OCR models complete data extraction in seconds rather than minutes per document, labor costs for digitization drop significantly. While printed records are easily captured using AI OCR, handwritten tabular data still requires ongoing human intervention for validation. Keywords: data rescue, AI, OCR, weather data, climate data

498935.title: From Climate Data to Decision Support: Strengthening Climate Services in Ghanathrough the Ghana Climate Atlas
498935.authors: Ignatius Kweku Williams, Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet), Accra, Ghana; and M. A. Ahiataku, D. Tetteh, H. A. Yeboah, J. Amavih, C. Foriwaa Aggrey, E. Kpodo, A. S. Gyasi, S. Shepard Nangombe, and J. A. Stensballe
498935.abstract: The increasing impacts of climate variability and change are creating growing demand for accessible, reliable, and decision relevant climate information to support planning, investment, and climate risk management. However, a persistent challenge in many developing countries is the gap between climate data availability and institutional capacity to interpret and apply such information. The Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet), in collaboration with the Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI), is addressing this gap through the Ghana Climate Atlas by strengthening climate information infrastructure and institutional capacity for climate informed decision support. The Ghana Climate Atlas provides high resolution, downscaled seasonal and annual climate projections at approximately 4 km spatial resolution, enabling assessment of climate conditions and projected changes at district level up to 2100. An interactive Map Viewer and StoryMap present key indicators, including sea level rise, temperature, and rainfall, translating complex climate datasets into accessible information for relevant stakeholders such as planners, policymakers, and decision makers. The Atlas supports policy and investment planning and alignment with Ghana’s National Adaptation Plan, Nationally Determined Contributions, National Climate Change Policy, and the African Union Agenda 2063 for climate resilience. The Atlas uses the open-source Klimaatlas in Python (KAPy) framework to dynamically downscale WCRP CORDEX climate data from 50 km to 4 km resolution. KAPy harmonises CMIP and CORDEX data ingestion, performs bias correction, computes climate indicators, and conducts ensemble-based uncertainty analyses under Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) scenarios. Projections cover 2021–2100, referenced to the 1991–2020 climatological baseline. By 2081–2100 under RCP4.5, Ghana’s average annual temperature is projected to reach 29.2°C, 1.4°C above the 27.8°C baseline. Mean annual rainfall is projected to increase by 22 mm (1.8%) from 1,221 mm, while mean sea level is projected to rise by approximately 0.6 m. The next phase will expand the indicator suite. Ghana’s experience demonstrates how integrating climate data, digital infrastructure, visualization, and capacity building can support GMet’s transition from climate data provision toward sustainable, user focused, decision relevant climate information services. Keywords: Ghana Climate Atlas, Climate data, Climate Services, Downscaling, Geospatial Modelling, KAPy

498936.title: From International Capacity Development to Operational Climate Services: Experience from Madagascar
498936.abstract: How can international capacity development and technical partnerships help National Meteorological Services connect climate forecasts with operational decision-making? This paper explores this question through a case study of Madagascar, focusing on the links between technical training, regional exchange, and the use of seasonal and subseasonal forecasts for preparedness and planning. The case draws on technical training and professional exchange at the NOAA Climate Prediction Center’s International Desk through the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Volunteer Programme. This experience provided an opportunity to strengthen knowledge of climate forecasting and forecast interpretation, and to exchange technical expertise with international colleagues. The paper considers how such capacity development relates to the broader work of Madagascar’s Directorate General of Meteorology (DGM), including the production, interpretation, and communication of climate information for operational users. At the regional level, the Southern Indian Ocean Climate Outlook Forum (SWIOCOF) and the Southern Africa Regional Climate Outlook Forum (SARCOF) provide platforms for sharing seasonal outlooks and exchanging technical perspectives among participating countries. These exchanges complement cooperation with international technical partners, including universities and research institutions, and national collaboration between the DGM and humanitarian and development agencies. The paper examines how seasonal and subseasonal forecasts are used in Madagascar to inform climate-sensitive activities, including drought anticipatory action, agricultural planning, climate monitoring, and shorter-term preparedness. It considers the processes that connect forecast providers with operational users and the practical challenges of making forecast information useful for decisions. These include communicating forecast uncertainty, aligning information with operational timelines, and tailoring forecast products to different user needs. The discussion focuses on the complementary roles of international training, regional technical exchange, and national partnerships in strengthening climate services. It also considers how sustained interaction between meteorological services and forecast users can help identify information needs and improve the practical application of climate forecasts. By presenting Madagascar’s experience, this case study will share lessons on linking capacity development with the operational use of seasonal and subseasonal forecasts. It will identify opportunities for continued cooperation to improve forecast communication and support the integration of climate information into preparedness, anticipatory action, and planning.
